turns.content: What I witnessed: Rain was coming down hard on the West Landing, with the Heron at the planks for the last crossing of the evening and a goatherd and two goats already aboard. A young stranger came running down the landing from the toll road, soaked through, with a surveyor's chain coiled over one shoulder and a satchel of maps clutched against the rain. I heard the stranger say: "Does the ferry still run? Please tell me it still runs tonight." The stranger came aboard, dripping on the deck. Then I heard the stranger say: "I'm Wren, a surveyor's apprentice. The council sent me to map the marsh, and I've walked from the toll house since noon." What I did: I said 'She runs. This is the last crossing tonight, so you are in luck. Two coppers. Put the chain down by the rail and keep the maps away from the goats. They eat paper.' Then I take the two coppers, pull in the bow line, set the pole against the landing and push the Heron off into the current. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole in both hands, the West Landing going grey behind us in the rain. The air carried wet reeds and goat. How I came into it: tired, curious, wary.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: Wren has never crossed this river before and has nowhere arranged to sleep tonight. I based that on: Wren says: "Does the ferry still run? Please tell me it still runs tonight." and carries no bedroll, only a chain and a satchel of maps.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Halfway over the rain eased to a drizzle and the lights of the East Landing showed through it. Wren sat on the coiled chain by the rail with the satchel on both knees, watching where I set the pole. I heard Wren say: "How wide is it here? I can't see either bank properly." Then I heard Wren say: "Is there an inn on the town side? Somewhere that would take a wet surveyor?" The goatherd laughed into his collar and held his goats by the horns. What I did: I said 'A hundred and sixty paces at this crossing, more in spring. Do not try to chain it.' Then I lean on the rudder oar to bring the bow round against the drift and point with my chin at the lit windows along the waterfront. I said 'The Lantern Inn, there on the front. They may have a bed. It is market week, so they may not.' Then I ship the pole and let the Heron run the last of the way into the slack water by the landing. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my arm, the East Landing coming up out of the drizzle. The air carried rain on the river and smoke from the town chimneys. How I came into it: steady, amused, cautious.

What I witnessed: At the East Landing the goatherd led his goats off up the planks. Wren walked along the waterfront to the Lantern Inn with the satchel and went in at the front door. The inn's upper windows were lit, and lanterns of every colour hung inside the glass. A few minutes later Wren came back out and down to the landing, shoulders hunched against the rain. I heard Wren say: "Full. Drovers in every bed and two asleep on the settle. The woman said to try the chapel." What I did: Then I finish the knot on the stern post and look Wren over: soaked to the skin, shivering, holding the satchel as if it were worth more than a coat. I said 'The chapel sexton will put you on a bench under a drip. I have a spare room in my boathouse, just there. It has a bed and a stove. Pay me what the inn would have asked and it is yours.' Then I pick up the coil of chain before Wren can argue. What happened: I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with the chain over my arm, a few paces from the boathouse door. The air carried wet rope and chimney smoke. How I came into it: practical, tired, protective.

What I witnessed: Wren followed me into the boathouse and stood dripping on the boards, looking at the nets on the walls, the oars racked along the beams and the ladder to the loft. I heard Wren say: "You live in a boathouse?" At the spare room door I heard Wren say: "It's dry. That's all I wanted from today. Thank you, truly." Wren took the maps out of the satchel one by one and laid them across the table to dry, each corner weighted with a cup or a stone. What I did: I said 'The Heron lives outside it. I live in it.' Then I light the lamp and the stove, hang Wren's wet coat on the peg beside the stove, and put the kettle on. Then I fetch a spare blanket down from the loft and lay it on the bed in the spare room. I said 'Rent is four coppers a week. Help with a rope when I ask and I will not count the coppers too hard.' What happened: I was standing -- standing by the stove with the kettle starting to tick and Wren's maps curling on the table. The air carried wet wool and stove smoke. How I came into it: tired, warm, wary.

What I witnessed: Grey light came up over the river with the rain gone and mist lying on the water as far as the reeds of the West Landing. The Heron sat low at her mooring below the boathouse with a hand's depth of rainwater in her. From behind the spare room door came Wren's snoring, slow and heavy. What I did: Then I pull my boots on without lacing them and go down to the mooring with the bailer. Then I bail the Heron out, check the bow and stern lines for chafe, and wipe the rain off the rudder oar's grip. Then I come back up, set bread and a heel of cheese on the table beside the dried maps, and wake nobody. I said 'Sleep, then,' quietly, to the shut door. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the boathouse door with the bailer in my hand, looking at the mist on the water. The air carried cold river and wet planks. How I came into it: calm, alert, content.

What I witnessed: Wren came down to the East Landing with the chain over one shoulder and a heel of bread in one hand, while a carter backed a cart of turnips onto the Heron and two women with egg baskets sat down along the rail. I heard Wren say: "Can I ride over and back? I want to see the river before I see the marsh." The carter's horse stamped on the deck and the women held their baskets steady. What I did: I said 'Ride all day if you like. Stand clear of the horse and hold the rail when we leave the slack.' Then I chock the cart wheels, take the carter's fare and the women's, and push off. Then I walk the pole down the side of the Heron, stroke after stroke, while Wren watches where I set it. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole, the Heron out in the current and the mist thinning off the water. The air carried turnips, horse and river. How I came into it: easy, busy, curious.

What I witnessed: At the West Landing the carter drove his turnips off toward the toll road and the egg women walked after him. Wren stood at the top of the planks looking out over the reed marsh, brown and silver to the edge of sight, with water channels shining through it. Upstream, on its side channel, the old mill's wheel was turning. I heard Wren say: "That's all marsh? The council's map shows it as one blank with 'reeds' written across it." Then I heard Wren say: "Whose mill is that?" What I did: I said 'All marsh, and none of it blank. There are paths a cow can walk and paths that will swallow the cow.' Then I point up the side channel. I said 'That is the old mill. My oldest friend runs it, Ilse. We grew up in those reeds, the two of us.' Then I take the fares of two passengers waiting for the town side and wave them aboard. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the head of the Heron's ramp on the West Landing, looking upstream at the mill. The air carried reed and wet meal from the mill. How I came into it: fond, proud, watchful.

What I witnessed: After three more crossings the morning traffic thinned. Wren had filled a page with sketches of both banks and a column of numbers counting my pole strokes. At the East Landing Wren jumped off before the Heron touched. I heard Wren say: "I need chalk, twine and a bundle of pegs before I go anywhere near that marsh. Where's the market?" What I did: I said 'Up the lane and left at the chapel, into the market square. Tell the twine woman you lodge with me and she will not cheat you more than usual.' Then I make the Heron fast and hang a slate on the landing post: back within the hour. Then I take my purse for the month's landing dues and walk along the front toward the dock office. What happened: I was standing -- standing beside the landing post on the East Landing, the purse in my coat and the dock office ahead. The air carried tar and fish from the drying racks. How I came into it: businesslike, light, unhurried.

What I witnessed: Aldous Toller was at his desk in the dock office with the ledger open and a fresh council notice pinned to the wall behind him. He took my dues and wrote them in without looking up. I heard Aldous Toller say: "Read that before you go. From tonight the council closes the river after dark. Nothing moves on the Aune from dusk to dawn, ferry or skiff. A fine if they catch you, and they take the boat if they catch you twice." Then I heard Aldous Toller say: "It isn't the river they're nervous of. It's whoever's buying Oren Dask's green lanterns. The smugglers signal each other with them, green on the water at night, and the council wants the river empty so a green light shows." Then I heard Aldous Toller say: "Dask. The lantern-maker who took the rooms over the Lantern Inn last spring." What I did: I said 'Why now? And who is Oren Dask when he is at home?' Then I read the notice twice, standing. I said 'Twenty years I have crossed after dark when somebody needed it. Midwives. Drunks who live on the wrong side. They will lose me the evening trade to catch a few lights.' What happened: I was standing -- standing in front of the notice in the dock office with my empty purse in my hand. The air carried ink, tar and Aldous's pipe. How I came into it: angry, uneasy, stubborn.

inferences.text: I concluded that the curfew is meant for the green lanterns, but it is the Heron that will lose its evening crossings over it. I based that on: Aldous Toller says: "It isn't the river they're nervous of. It's whoever's buying Oren Dask's green lanterns."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren came back down to the landing with a bundle of pegs, a ball of twine and chalk in every pocket, and rode the next crossing with me beside a cart of split logs. I heard Wren say: "You've got a face like a shut door. What did the dock office want?" Then I heard Wren say: "The council never said a word to me about a curfew. I'm meant to be in that marsh at first light and out of it at dusk, and you're my only way over." What I did: I said 'From tonight nothing crosses after dark. Aldous says the council is nervous of whoever's buying Oren Dask's green lanterns. Dask makes lanterns over the inn, and the smugglers hang his green ones on their boats.' Then I said 'So you cross with me before dusk, every time, or you sleep in the reeds.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and set the Heron across the current toward the West Landing. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern, steering, with the West Landing ahead and the logs creaking in their chains. The air carried cut wood and river. How I came into it: irritated, protective, resigned.

What I witnessed: The last crossing of the day came in with the sun low over the marsh. On the East Landing Aldous Toller was nailing the council's notice to the landing post with a mallet, and a knot of people stood reading it. A carter swore at it and spat in the river. Wren read it out for the ones at the back: no boat on the Aune between dusk and dawn, by order of the council. I heard Aldous Toller say: "Heron tied and lamp out by dark, Mara. I don't want to be the one who writes your name in the fines book." What I did: I said 'You will not have to. I can tell when the sun goes down, Aldous.' Then I run the Heron's bow onto the landing, make her fast fore and aft, and double the stern line. Then I take my lamp down off the bow post, unlit, and carry it up to the boathouse door. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the boathouse door with my lamp in one hand, watching the people drift away from the notice. The air carried cooling mud and supper smells from the waterfront. How I came into it: bitter, tired, defiant.

What I witnessed: After supper Wren stood with me in the open boathouse door. The river was black from bank to bank without one boat light on it, the first such night I could remember. The town had its windows lit and the West Landing had nothing. Then, far down the river past the bend, a green light showed, blinked twice and went dark. A while after, another green light answered it from near the far reeds, and went dark too. I heard Wren say: "Was that one of them? The green?" Then I heard Wren say: "So the curfew works on everyone except the people it's for." What I did: I said 'That was green. Aldous will tell me tomorrow the council's men saw it too. I doubt they did.' Then I said 'Shut the door. The river is not ours tonight.' Then I bar the boathouse door and turn the lamp down. What happened: I was standing -- standing inside the barred door with the lamp turned low. The air carried cold off the water and lamp oil. How I came into it: uneasy, wry, restless.

inferences.text: I concluded that the curfew has not emptied the river, only emptied it of honest lights. I based that on: You see a green light blink twice far downriver after dark, and another green light answer it from near the far reeds.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren was up before me with the council's map pinned flat on the table under two cups and the bread knife, and a fresh sheet beside it already ruled into squares. I heard Wren say: "I need someone who knows which channels go through and which come to nothing. Could you take me in? Even an hour." Then I heard Wren say: "I'll pay for the hour the ferry stands still." What I did: I said 'Midday is slack. The carts come over in the morning and go home in the afternoon. I will tie the Heron on the West Landing at eleven and walk you in as far as the old mill.' Then I sit on the bench and splice the frayed end of a mooring line while Wren drinks tea standing up. I said 'Wear the boots, not those shoes. The reeds will keep the shoes.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the bench by the boathouse door with the spliced line across my knees. The air carried tea, tar and morning mist. How I came into it: willing, amused, careful.

What I witnessed: The first big crossing of the day was a red cow and the farmer who owned her. The cow refused the ramp until Wren pushed from behind and the farmer pulled from the front, and two women with egg baskets sat on the rail and laughed at all three. Out in the current Wren stood at the bow counting quietly. I heard Wren say: "Forty-two strokes from post to post. Is it always forty-two?" Then the cow leaned her whole weight against the rail and the Heron dipped on that side. What I did: I said 'Forty-two going over. Thirty-eight coming back, unless the wind is from the west. Then it is fifty and I swear the whole way.' Then I set the pole hard on the downstream side to bring the deck up against the cow's lean, and hold the rudder oar until the Heron sits level. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole braced, the Heron level again and the West Landing close. The air carried cow, eggs and river. How I came into it: cheerful, busy, steady.

What I witnessed: Along the reed path in from the West Landing the reeds stood well over both our heads, and the thump of the mill wheel came through them from upstream. At the fork Wren drove a peg, ran the chain out along the firm ground, and chalked the numbers on a board. I heard Wren say: "How do you know which one's real? They look exactly the same." Then I heard Wren say: "You grew up out here? In all this?" What I did: Then I tie the Heron at the West Landing, walk Wren in along the reed path to the fork, and show the deep channel and the false one. I said 'The false one has no current. Drop a reed in it and watch. The real channel takes the reed away.' Then I drop a reed in each, and the one goes and the other sits. I said 'Ilse and I grew up out here. I pulled her out of the river ice the winter I was seven, and that is how we met. By ten we knew every channel.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the fork of the reed path with the chain at my feet. The air carried mud, reed and wet chalk. How I came into it: fond, patient, easy.

What I witnessed: The path came out at the mill on its side channel, the wheel turning and the race loud under the floor. Ilse Harrow was in the mill doorway with flour to her elbows. She came out and held me by both arms. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Mara Vell, off her boat at midday. Has the river run dry?" Then she looked at Wren and the chain. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "And who's this, with the council's chain on?" I heard Wren say: "Wren. I'm mapping the marsh for the council, and Mara's showing me the way in." Ilse gave Wren a short nod. Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Sit, both of you, there's bread. And Mara, with this curfew my flour has to go over in the mornings or not at all. Will you take my cart at first light tomorrow?" What I did: I said 'The river is where I left it. Wren lodges in my spare room and pays on the day.' Then I sit on the mill step and take the bread. I said 'First light tomorrow. I will come over empty for your cart.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the mill step beside Wren with bread in my hand and Ilse leaning in the doorway. The air carried flour dust and the cold breath of the race. How I came into it: glad, easy, watchful.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: Ilse does not like the council's chain on the marsh, and she was civil to Wren for my sake. I based that on: Ilse Harrow says: "And who's this, with the council's chain on?" and gives Wren only a short nod.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Back at the West Landing a carter was waiting with an empty cart and a boy asleep in the back of it. Wren's board was full of chalk numbers and the chain was caked with mud to the handles. On the crossing Wren sat at the bow copying the chalk into a book before it rubbed off. I heard Wren say: "Who taught you the river? You don't use the pole like anyone I've watched." What I did: I said 'Petra. She ran this ferry before me, and she taught me the pole. I took the Heron over alone the first time at fifteen. She left her to me when she died, two winters ago.' Then I steer us round the snag below the West Landing and walk the pole down the length of the deck. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole, halfway over, the boy still asleep in the cart. The air carried mud, dry chalk and the river. How I came into it: quiet, fond, sad.

What I witnessed: The last crossing came in well before dusk. On the walk along the waterfront to the baker's hatch, the Lantern Inn's upper windows were hung inside with lanterns, dozens of them, brass and tin, clear glass and red and green, none of them lit. Wren stopped below them. I heard Wren say: "Is that where the lantern-maker works? The one Aldous named?" Then I heard Wren say: "There are as many green ones up there as all the other colours put together." What I did: I said 'That is his workshop, over the inn. Oren Dask, Aldous says. I have never been up there and I have no reason to go.' Then I buy a loaf at the baker's hatch and turn back toward the boathouse without looking up at the windows again. What happened: I was standing -- standing on the waterfront below the Lantern Inn with the loaf under my arm and the inn door shut on its step. The air carried new bread and the cold coming off the river. How I came into it: curious, guarded, contrary.

What I witnessed: After supper Wren laid a fresh sheet on the table and inked the day's work onto it by my lamp: the West Landing, the reed path, the fork with its deep channel and its false one, and the mill on the side channel, each with its numbers in small writing. I heard Wren say: "The council's blank is getting smaller. Before the frost I'll have every channel a boat can get down." Then I heard Wren say: "What will the council do with it, do you think? They never told me." What I did: I said 'Tax it, probably. Or sell it.' Then I lean over the sheet and put my finger on the false channel. I said 'Mark that one false, in big letters. Somebody will try it in the dark otherwise.' Then I turn the lamp wick up so Wren can see the small numbers. What happened: I was standing -- standing at Wren's shoulder by the table, the lamp turned up and the fresh ink shining. The air carried lamp oil and ink. How I came into it: thoughtful, uneasy, tired.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: Wren has not thought about what a map of every channel a boat can use is worth, to the council or to anybody who wants to move boats through the marsh unseen. I based that on: Wren says: "What will the council do with it, do you think? They never told me."

turns.content: What I witnessed: At first light the West Landing was white with mist. Ilse Harrow was already at the top of the planks with her handcart, eight sacks of flour roped on it and her shawl over her hair. Wren had come over with me and went straight to the ropes. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Eight sacks. That's what the curfew leaves me, one morning trip instead of my evening ones. The bakers won't wait on me now." Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Mind that top one, the seam's weak." What I did: I said 'Eight sacks is a light load. Back her down the ramp slow and I will take the weight at the bottom.' Then I take the handles from Ilse at the foot of the ramp and walk the cart onto the Heron, and Wren and I set chocks under both wheels. Then I lift the weak sack off the top and lay it flat by itself. What happened: I was standing -- standing on the Heron's deck at the foot of the ramp, my hands white with flour. The air carried mist, flour and wet planks. How I came into it: steady, useful, glad.

What I witnessed: Halfway over, with Wren at the bow watching the mist lift off the water, Ilse came back to the stern and stood by me at the rudder oar, speaking low. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Your surveyor. Is the council paying for a map of the marsh, or a map of my mill?" Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "I'm not asking you to spy, Mara. I'm asking what you think." She kept her eyes on Wren's back while she said it. What I did: I said 'I think Wren is paid to map the marsh and has not been told what for. Wren pays rent on the day, works from first light and asks a hundred questions. That is all I know, and now you know it too.' Then I lean on the rudder oar to bring the Heron in toward the East Landing. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my arm and Ilse beside me, the East Landing close through the thinning mist. The air carried flour and the mill smell on Ilse's shawl. How I came into it: honest, thoughtful, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: Ilse is more afraid for the mill than she is of Wren, and something has already made her think the council has its eye on the mill. I based that on: Ilse Harrow says: "Is the council paying for a map of the marsh, or a map of my mill?"

turns.content: What I witnessed: The last crossing of the day came in at dusk with a full deck, carters and market people crowding off onto the East Landing before the curfew closed the river. My own lamp slipped out of my wet hand as I unhooked it from the bow post, unlit, and smashed on the planks, glass and oil everywhere. People stepped back from it. Then a man stepped out of the crowd, a man in his forties in a good grey coat with soot on his fingers, holding up an unlit lantern glassed in green. I heard the man say: "You'll be wanting the green one, then." Some of the crowd laughed and some went quiet. Then I heard the man say: "Oren Dask. I make them, up over the inn. Take it. A ferry shouldn't go about without a lamp." Wren stood at my elbow, looking from him to me. What I did: I said 'You are the lantern-maker Aldous told me about.' Then I said 'A green lamp on a ferry, with this curfew. That is a poor joke at the end of a long day.' Then I take the lantern from him, because the other choice is no lamp at all, and set it on the landing post out of the broken glass. What happened: I was standing -- standing over my smashed lamp on the East Landing, with the green lantern on the post beside me. The air carried spilled lamp oil and wet planks. How I came into it: startled, wary, annoyed.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he made the joke in front of the whole landing on purpose, so that half the town would watch the ferry pilot take a green lantern from his hand. I based that on: Oren Dask says: "You'll be wanting the green one, then." and the crowd goes quiet.

turns.content: What I witnessed: The crowd thinned off the landing as the light went. Oren Dask crouched and helped Wren pick the larger pieces of my glass off the planks, and dropped them in the river. I heard Oren Dask say: "Brass frame, good glass, a wick that'll burn all night. It's a better lamp than the one you dropped." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "Green's what I had in my hand. A clear one costs more, and you'd only have said no to a gift that cost more." Then he touched his hat to Wren and to me, walked off along the front, and went in at the side door of the Lantern Inn. I heard Wren say: "So that's him. He's nothing like I pictured." What I did: I said 'Why green?' Then, when he had gone, I said 'Nor me.' Then I pick the green lantern off the landing post and turn it over in my hands. I said 'It stays dark. I will buy a plain one at the market.' Then I make the Heron fast for the night and walk to the boathouse with the lantern hanging unlit from my hand. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the boathouse door with the unlit green lantern in my hand, the river going dark behind me. The air carried cold off the water and kitchen smoke from the inn. How I came into it: unsettled, curious, contrary.

What I witnessed: We ate by a tallow candle, my lamp being in pieces. Wren kept looking at the green lantern where I had set it at the end of the table. I heard Wren say: "Will you use it? With the curfew, a green light on the Heron is about the worst thing you could show." Then I heard Wren say: "He knew who you were before you said a word. He knew it was your lamp that broke." What I did: I said 'I will not use it. I will hang it where I can see it and keep it dark.' Then I drive a nail into the beam beside the boathouse door and hang the green lantern on it. I said 'He knew me because everybody on that landing knows the ferry pilot. That is all that was.' Then I sit back down and cut the bread. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with the bread knife, the green lantern hanging dark on its nail by the door. The air carried stew and tallow smoke. How I came into it: stubborn, uneasy, tired.

What I witnessed: Wren held the candle close while I worked at the frame of my old lamp. The brass was bent flat on one side where it hit the planks, and the burner had a crack right through the collar. I heard Wren say: "Can it be saved?" Then I heard Wren say: "There's a tinker's stall at the market, I was there the other day. Pots and lamps all along the front of it." What I did: Then I bend the frame back over the edge of the table as far as it will go, fill the burner and try it. Oil weeps out through the crack. I said 'No. Petra bought this lamp before I ever stood on the Heron, and it has gone in the river at last, near enough.' Then I put the bent frame up on the shelf. I said 'The tinker, then. Tomorrow, after the morning crossings.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with oil on my fingers and the candle burning low between us. The air carried tallow and lamp oil. How I came into it: rueful, tired, resolved.

What I witnessed: Wren had gone to bed. From the boathouse step the river was black and quiet, with the Heron a darker shape at her mooring. Then a green light showed in the reeds below the West Landing, blinked twice, and went out. A moment after, a second green light answered it from downriver, nearer the town side, and went out too. No oar sounded and nobody called. What I did: Then I go out onto the step to check the Heron's lines before sleeping, and stand still until my eyes are used to the dark, watching both places for a long time. Then I check the bow and stern lines by feel. Then I go in, bar the door, and look at the green lantern hanging dark on its nail before I pinch out the candle. I said 'Not mine,' to nobody. What happened: I was standing -- standing inside the barred boathouse door in the dark with my hand still on the bar. The air carried cold river and candle smoke. How I came into it: uneasy, alert, alone.

inferences.text: I concluded that the green lantern on my nail speaks the same language as the lights in the reeds, and whoever was out on the water tonight would take a boat showing it for one of their own. I based that on: You see a green light blink twice in the reeds below the West Landing, and a second green light answer it from downriver.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren was up and dressed when I came out, the satchel packed and the chain coiled by the door. I heard Wren say: "I want the toll road edge of the marsh today, where the reeds meet the road. Can you take me over at midday, after the market?" Then Wren nodded at the nail by the door. I heard Wren say: "It's still there, then." What I did: Then I take the green lantern down and look it over in the daylight: a good brass frame, heavy green glass, a full wick, no oil in it. Then I hang it back on the nail. I said 'Still there. Still dark.' Then I said 'Midday, then. But you come back on the last crossing before dusk, or you spend the night in the reeds. I will not be fetching you.' Then I go down to bail the Heron. What happened: I was standing -- standing on the boathouse step with the bailer, the river grey under the morning mist. The air carried mist and wet rope. How I came into it: brisk, wary, ordinary.

What I witnessed: The first crossing carried a carter with four barrels of cider, a goatherd with three goats on a rope, and Wren at the bow with the satchel held high. Halfway over, one of the goats got its teeth into the satchel strap and Wren had to wrestle the strap back while the goatherd laughed. Through the mist the West Landing came up grey, with a figure sitting at the top of the planks, too far off to make out. I heard Wren say: "They eat leather too, then. Not just paper." What I did: I said 'They eat everything but rope. That is why goats ride at the stern.' Then I haul the goats back to the stern by their rope and tie them off on the cleat by my feet. Then I walk the pole down the deck and bring the Heron in toward the West Landing. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole and the goats at my feet, the West Landing close ahead. The air carried cider, goat and mist. How I came into it: amused, busy, easy.

What I witnessed: I met Oren Dask on the West Landing, sitting on a crate of lanterns at the top of the planks in the same grey coat, as if he had been waiting for the first ferry. The Heron had not carried him over the day before. He stood and lifted the crate once the cider barrels were off. I heard Oren Dask say: "Morning, ferry pilot. Have you lit the green one yet?" Then I heard Oren Dask say: "You should, the next time you're caught out after dark. Nobody on the water troubles a boat that shows green." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "How did I come over? I have my ways. A man who makes lights can always find his way in the dark." He paid the fare for himself and the crate and carried it aboard. What I did: I said 'I have not lit it, and I will not be out after dark. The council has seen to that.' Then I said 'How did you come over? I did not carry you.' Then I set his crate down on the deck by the rail, away from the ramp. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the head of the Heron's ramp on the West Landing, with Oren Dask aboard and Wren beside him. The air carried mist and new tin. How I came into it: suspicious, polite, cold.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he crossed the river last night after the curfew, under one of the green lights I watched from the step. I based that on: Oren Dask is on the West Landing at first light though the Heron did not carry him, and he says: "A man who makes lights can always find his way in the dark."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The market square was full for market week, with drovers' pens along the chapel wall and stalls in rows. The tinker's stall had pots, nails and buckets, and a row of empty hooks along the front. I heard the tinker say: "No lamps, not a one. Every lamp in Saltmere comes from the lantern-maker over the Lantern Inn these days, and he sells his own." Wren went off to the twine woman for more twine. At the rope stall next along, a tall lad with a burn-scarred left hand was haggling over a coil of rope, holding up the end to show the seller a frayed strand. He caught my eye across the stall, held it a moment, and looked away. I did not know his face. What I did: I said 'Then I will take a flask of oil and go without a lamp until I find one.' Then I buy a flask of lamp oil from the tinker and put it in my coat. Then I watch the tall lad at the rope stall until he pays and goes off with the coil over his shoulder, and I cannot say why I watch him. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the tinker's stall in the market square with the oil flask in my coat, looking after the tall lad. The air carried cattle, cider and hot pies. How I came into it: curious, annoyed, puzzled.

What I witnessed: At midday the Heron went over with nobody aboard but Wren, and the chain, the pegs and the new twine piled at the bow. Wren talked the whole way. I heard Wren say: "The road edge runs west from the toll house for a mile at least. If I chain it all today, the map has a south side by tomorrow." Then I heard Wren say: "I'll be on the landing before dusk. I promise." Wren jumped off at the West Landing and set off along the toll road with the chain over one shoulder. What I did: I said 'Before dusk means before the sun touches the reeds, not after. I wait a quarter of an hour on the West Landing and then I go home, because the curfew will not wait for either of us. Take this.' Then I give Wren my tin whistle off its cord. Then I push off from the West Landing and pole the Heron back across, alone. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern of the empty Heron in midstream, poling back toward the East Landing. The air carried warm reeds and dust off the toll road. How I came into it: uneasy, fond, busy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: Wren will work the chain until the light goes and only then remember the ferry. I based that on: Wren says: "If I chain it all today, the map has a south side by tomorrow."

turns.content: What I witnessed: On the last crossing the Heron reached the West Landing with the sun already low over the marsh. A woman with a crate of geese and a carter with an empty cart came aboard for the town side. There was no sign of Wren on the landing or along the toll road. The sun went down into the reeds. I heard the carter say: "Curfew's on us, ferry. Are we going, or are we sleeping here?" What I did: I said 'One more minute.' Then I walk to the top of the landing and call Wren's name toward the toll road three times, and listen, and hear only the reeds. Then I wait out the quarter hour I promised, and a little more. Then I said 'We go.' Then I push off from the West Landing in the last of the light with the carter, the geese and no Wren. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern of the Heron in the dusk, poling toward the East Landing and looking back at the empty West Landing. The air carried geese and the cold coming up off the water. How I came into it: worried, angry, torn.

What I witnessed: From the boathouse step, well after dark, there was a yellow lamp on the West Landing, swinging back and forth at the top of the planks the way someone swings a lamp who wants a boat. Then, faint across the water, came three blasts on a tin whistle. Out on the river, as the Heron came into the current, a green light blinked twice in the reeds downstream of the crossing and went dark. Nobody hailed me. What I did: I said 'That is my whistle,' to the dark. Then I take the green lantern Oren Dask gave me down from its nail, fill it from the flask of oil I bought at the market, trim the wick and light it. Then I hang the green lantern at the Heron's bow, cast off, and pole out onto the river after curfew toward the yellow lamp on the far side. I do not answer the green light in the reeds and I do not look at it twice. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern of the Heron in the middle of the black river, the green lantern burning at the bow and the yellow lamp on the West Landing ahead. The air carried cold water and hot lamp oil. How I came into it: afraid, determined, angry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the green lantern: whoever showed the light in the reeds took the Heron for one of their own boats, because nobody hailed me and the light went dark the way the ones I watched from the step did. I based that on: You see a green light blink twice in the reeds downstream and go dark, and nobody hails the Heron.

turns.content: What I witnessed: At the West Landing Wren was standing at the top of the planks with a borrowed lamp, soaked to the knees, the chain over one shoulder and the satchel of maps hugged against the cold: the same planks Wren came running down in the rain four nights ago to ask if the ferry still ran. I heard Wren say: "I lost the path in the reeds when the light went. I'm so sorry. The toll-keeper lent me this lamp." Then Wren saw the colour of the lantern at the bow. I heard Wren say: "Mara. That's the green one." What I did: I said 'Get in. Sit down. Say nothing until we are tied up.' Then I pole the Heron back across the black river with Wren silent at my feet. At the East Landing I make her fast, reach up to the bow, and pinch out the green lantern's wick between finger and thumb. I said 'Tomorrow you can tell me how a surveyor loses a path. Tonight you go to bed.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with the dark green lantern in my hand and Wren beside me. The air carried hot tin, wet wool and the river. How I came into it: relieved, shaken, cross.

What I witnessed: Wren was at the table before me with the kettle on, the bread cut and two cups set out. I heard Wren say: "I'm sorry. I'll say it once more and then I'll stop." Then Wren looked up at the green lantern back on its nail. I heard Wren say: "Was that the first time you'd lit the green one? Last night?" Then I heard Wren say: "The council would fine you for it. They'd fine me for being the reason." What I did: I said 'The first time. I would sooner it was the last.' Then I sit down and take the cup. I said 'Nobody is fining anybody. From today you carry a lamp of your own, and that whistle, and you are on the landing when the sun touches the reeds.' Then I put the flask of lamp oil on the shelf beside the bent frame of my old lamp. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with my tea, the green lantern hanging dark on its nail by the door. The air carried tea and cold lamp oil. How I came into it: tired, softened, firm.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: Wren is more frightened of having put me in the council's fines book than of the night lost in the reeds. I based that on: Wren says: "The council would fine you for it. They'd fine me for being the reason."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The morning's first crossing carried a cart of hay, two drovers with their dogs and a crate of hens, and Wren at the bow with the map book open, inking in the road edge from the chalk board before it rubbed away. The dogs lay down on the hay and would not get up. Across the water the West Landing stood clear in the sun, and the reeds downstream of the crossing looked like any other reeds. I heard Wren say: "The road edge goes in a long curve, not straight the way the council's map has it. Look." What I did: I said 'I have looked at that curve all my life. It is a curve.' Then I lean on the rudder oar to hold the Heron across the current, and look once at the reeds downstream of the crossing. Then I set the pole for the West Landing. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole, the hay cart creaking in its chocks and the West Landing ahead. The air carried hay, dog and sun on the water. How I came into it: steady, watchful, wry.

What I witnessed: I met Oren Dask again on the West Landing, standing by an empty crate at the top of the planks with his grey coat open in the sun. Once more the Heron had not carried him over. He waited until the drovers had driven the hay cart off. I heard Oren Dask say: "I hear the ferry showed green on the river last night. You'll be wanting a spare wick, then." He held one out between two fingers. Then I heard Oren Dask say: "No charge. I like to know my lanterns are working." Wren looked at me and said nothing. What I did: I said 'I fetched my lodger off this landing in the dark. It was the only lamp I had, as you know, since you sell all the others.' Then I take the wick, because I will need one. I said 'Your crate rides at the stern. Two coppers.' Then I take his fare, and he carries the empty crate aboard. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the head of the ramp on the West Landing with the wick in my coat and Oren Dask aboard behind me. The air carried hay dust and warm tar. How I came into it: wary, needled, honest.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: somebody who was on the river last night told him about the green light on the Heron before breakfast, so the lights in the reeds answer to him. I based that on: Oren Dask says: "I hear the ferry showed green on the river last night."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The reed path came out at the mill at midday, and Wren set to chaining the side channel from the race down to the river. Ilse Harrow came out wiping her hands and walked the bank with us while Wren pegged and chained. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Eight sacks went over the other morning and the bakers paid for seven. The weak one split on their floor and they say that's my loss." Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Take a sack of the second-grade for your boathouse. You're feeding two now." At the race Wren read the numbers off the chain aloud, and Ilse watched the chalk board as if it might bite. What I did: I said 'The weak sack. I laid it flat on the Heron, but it was weak before it came aboard. That is the bakers being bakers.' Then I take the sack of second-grade flour from Ilse and set it on my shoulder. I said 'Thank you. Wren eats like a drover.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the mill bank with the flour sack on my shoulder, beside Ilse, watching Wren chain the side channel. The air carried flour, wet stone and spray off the race. How I came into it: warm, easy, grateful.

What I witnessed: The chapel of the Drowned Saint was cool and empty but for the sexton sweeping the step, and the saint's niche by the river door held its usual small heap of coins, shells and twists of reed. Wren stood looking at the carved saint with the water carved round her knees. I heard Wren say: "Who was she? Every boat on this river has her painted on it somewhere." Then I heard the sexton say from the step: "Ferry folk's saint. She keeps those that cross in the dark." What I did: Then I put a copper and a twist of reed in the niche, the way Petra did after every crossing she made in the dark. I said 'Petra said she was a ferrywoman once, before the chapel. Nobody knows more than that. Petra never crossed at night without paying her after.' Then I said 'Neither will I.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the saint's niche in the chapel with Wren beside me and my hands empty. The air carried cold stone, candle wax and river damp. How I came into it: quiet, thankful, solemn.

What I witnessed: The curfew had closed the river an hour since. Wren had the new sheet spread on the table under the candle: the reed path, the fork, the mill race and the long curve of the road edge all inked in, and the false channel marked FALSE in big letters. I heard Wren say: "Another month or so and the marsh has a shape. Then I'll start on the side channels below the mill." Then Wren looked up at the green lantern on its nail. I heard Wren say: "Would you do it again? Cross after dark, for somebody else?" What I did: I said 'For somebody stuck on a landing who is mine to fetch, yes. For anybody else, the council can keep its river.' Then I put Oren Dask's spare wick in the drawer under the shelf, beside the oil, and do not look at the lantern. Then I said 'Bed. The goats come over at seven.' What happened: I was standing -- standing by the shelf in the boathouse with the drawer shut and the green lantern dark on its nail by the door. The air carried candle smoke, ink and new flour. How I came into it: tired, settled, uneasy.

What I witnessed: The sky was red in the east over the town and the swallows were skimming low over the water. Wren came aboard at the boathouse mooring with the chain over one shoulder and the satchel of maps under an arm. I heard Wren say: "Is that sky a bad sign or only a pretty one?" At the West Landing the goatherd was waiting at the top of the planks with three goats on a rope, to come over to the town. I heard the goatherd say: "Both, if you ask my knees." What I did: I said 'Bad. There is a blow coming up the river by dark.' Then I hold the Heron against the planks with the pole while Wren jumps off. Then I said 'You are on this landing by four today, not at dusk. Four, Wren. In what is coming I will not cross for anybody.' Then I drop the ramp for the goats. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the bow of the Heron at the West Landing with the pole planted and the goats coming down the planks. The air carried damp reeds, goat and a wind with rain behind it. How I came into it: watchful, brisk, uneasy.

inferences.text: I concluded that a hard blow is coming up the Aune by dark: the sky is red over the town, the swallows are down on the water and the wind is backing into the south. I based that on: The sky is red in the east over the town and the swallows skim low over the water.

turns.content: What I witnessed: The goats stood in a knot at the bow and would not settle. A carter with an empty cart and his horse came aboard behind them for the town side. The wind backed into the south while we were on the water, turning the reed tops silver, and the river began to stand up in short ridges off the bar. I heard the carter say: "Will you run tonight, ferry? I've a load to bring back from the toll road." I heard the goatherd say: "She'll not. Look at her face." What I did: I said 'Not tonight. Last crossing at four, and I may not make that one. Bring your load tomorrow.' Then I chock the cart wheels and walk the pole down the deck. Then I lean on the rudder oar to hold her bow up into the wind while the pole bites. Then I said 'Hold the horse's head. If he dances, I put you both off on the bar.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with one hand on the rudder oar and the pole under my arm, halfway over. The air carried goat, horse and the first cold breath of the south wind. How I came into it: brisk, wary, dry.

What I witnessed: Oren Dask came down the steps from the side door of the Lantern Inn with a crate on one shoulder and set it on the landing beside the Heron's post. I heard Oren Dask say: "Morning, ferry pilot. There's weather coming up the river." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "Will you run in it tonight, or is the river shut to honest folk and the other sort alike?" He looked up at the sky and smiled as if it had told him a joke. Then I heard Oren Dask say: "This wants to be on the West Landing before noon. Will you take it?" What I did: I said 'Nobody runs in what is coming, honest or otherwise.' Then I take his fare and lift the crate aboard by its rope handles, heavy and clinking with glass. Then I said 'It goes now or not today. After four the Heron is tied double below my boathouse and stays there.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the East Landing planks beside the Heron's post with the stern line in my hand. The air carried coal smoke from the inn chimney, flattened by the wind. How I came into it: guarded, dry, curious.

What I witnessed: Three blasts on the tin whistle came across the water from the West Landing before I was halfway over, and Wren was waiting at the top of the planks with the satchel wrapped in oilcloth and the chain coiled over one shoulder. Behind the landing the reeds went down flat under the wind and the first rain came over the river in grey sheets. I heard Wren say: "Four, as ordered. The far stakes are already under water." Then I heard Wren say: "Does the Heron mind this kind of weather?" What I did: I said 'The Heron minds nothing. I mind for her. Sit on the cart rail and hold on with both hands.' Then I drive the pole in hard by the bow and walk it back, aiming her nose high above the East Landing because the current is setting west. Then I put my weight on the rudder oar through every gust. Then I said 'Last crossing. Nobody else gets on this boat today.' What happened: I was standing -- standing braced at the stern with both hands on the rudder oar, mid-river, the rain coming sideways. The air carried rain, cold and reed. How I came into it: strain, resolve, alert.

What I witnessed: Rain hammered the boathouse windows and the wind rattled the door on its bar. We ate late, by a tallow candle, with the stove ticking hot. Then a thump came from overhead in the net loft, and a long scrape after it, like something dragged across the boards. Wren looked up at the loft hatch with the spoon halfway to the bowl. I heard Wren say: "What was that? Is something up there?" Then nothing more came from the loft, only the wind on the roof and the river roaring below the boathouse. What I did: I said 'That is the gable shutter. The latch has not held since the day I bought this place. Or rats coming in out of the wet. Eat your soup.' Then I sit still and listen with my spoon down. Then I said 'If it is the shutter, the old nets will be soaked by morning. I will see to it when the river lets me.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with my bowl in front of me and my eyes on the loft hatch. The air carried wet wool, soup steam and tallow smoke. How I came into it: tired, wary, stubborn.

What I witnessed: Down at the mooring below the boathouse the river was up over the second step of the slip, brown and fast, and the Heron was straining at her lines. A branch as long as the boat came down on the current and struck her quarter. Wren came down the slip behind me holding the lamp high against the rain. I heard Wren say: "Tell me where to hold it." What I did: I said 'High, and on my hands, not on the water.' Then I wade down the slip to my knees and take a second turn of the stern line round the post. Then I double the bow line and make it fast on the ring. Then I take the pole and fend the branch off her quarter until the current carries it away. Then I said 'She will hold now. Inside, before the lamp goes out.' What happened: I was standing -- standing knee-deep on the slip below the boathouse with the pole across my body. The air carried rain and the cold breath of the flood. How I came into it: strain, resolve, cold.

What I witnessed: Wren hung the lamp on its peg by the spare room door and wrung out a sleeve over the stove. Then a scrabbling came from the net loft overhead, then a bump, then quiet, then the scrabbling again, quick and short. I heard Wren say: "There it is again. That isn't the shutter." What I did: I said 'No. Rats. Every high water drives them up off the slip, and a loft full of old nets is a palace to a rat.' Then I bang the broom handle twice on the boards under the hatch, and listen, and nothing answers. Then I said 'There. I will buy a trap when the market is up. Go to bed, Wren.' Then I bar the door and pinch out the candle. What happened: I was standing -- standing under the loft hatch in the dark with the broom in my hand and water running out of my boots. The air carried wet rope, candle smoke and mud. How I came into it: tired, irritated, wary.

inferences.text: I concluded that rats have come up into my net loft out of the flood, the way every high water drives them in off the slip. I based that on: You hear a scrabbling in the loft overhead, then a bump, then quiet, then the scrabbling again, quick and short.

turns.content: What I witnessed: In the grey light the river was high and brown to the top step of the East Landing, carrying branches, a hen coop and a cartwheel past the end of the planks. Folk from the town stood along the landing in shawls, looking at the water. Slates off the chapel roof were broken in the lane behind them. I heard Wren say: "The marsh must be a lake this morning. All my stakes." What I did: I said 'Your stakes are where the river put them. Mine is the boat.' Then I go down to the mooring below the boathouse and look the Heron over: lines held, no planks sprung, a scrape of bark along her quarter. Then I come back up to the end of the landing. Then I said 'She held. Nothing crosses until the water drops, so we have a morning with nothing to do but wait for it.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the end of the East Landing with my arms folded, watching the current. The air carried mud, wet leaves and chimney smoke. How I came into it: relieved, restless, tired.

What I witnessed: Aldous Toller was at his desk in the dock office with the dock book open and the river gauge chalked on the slate behind him. I heard Aldous Toller say: "Over the third mark, Mara. Nothing crosses till it's back under. That's the river's order before it's the council's." Then I heard Aldous Toller say: "My boy's home from upriver, from his mother's people. Nineteen, and too quiet by half. I'll bring him round to you when the water's down. He's handy with a rope." Wren stood in the doorway reading the gauge marks on the slate. What I did: I said 'The river's orders I take. The council can wait its turn.' Then I lean on the doorframe and read the gauge for myself. Then I said 'Bring your boy when you like. If he can coil a line and keep his mouth shut, I can use him.' Then I said 'Write me down for the first crossing when it drops.' What happened: I was standing -- standing in the dock office doorway with one shoulder on the frame. The air carried ink, wet coats and the river through the open door. How I came into it: impatient, dry, steady.

What I witnessed: Half the stalls were up in the market square and the rest still under canvas weighted with stones. The baker's woman lifted two loaves off her board for me. I heard a seller say: "The chapel lost a dozen slates and the sexton's up his ladder already." Wren bought a stoppered bottle of ink at the next stall and held it up to the light. I heard Wren say: "The good ink. The map has earned it after last night." What I did: I said 'Two loaves. And a bundle of candles from the chandler, and grease for the lines.' Then I count my coins out onto the board. Then I put the loaves in my basket under a cloth. Then I said 'That is the last of the week's fares gone. The curfew halves my crossings and the river has had the rest.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the baker's board in the market square with the basket on my arm. The air carried warm bread and wet straw. How I came into it: grudging, practical, tired.

What I witnessed: The river was back under the third mark by noon, still brown and fast. At the West Landing Wren set off along the reed path with the chain to look for the stakes. I met Oren Dask on the West Landing; he was standing by a cart of covered crates at the top of the planks, as if he had been waiting for the first boat. I heard Oren Dask say: "The ferry runs again. I knew the river couldn't keep you long." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "Take me back over when you go? The crates stay here for a carter who's waiting on the road to dry." He lifted a corner of the canvas to show me lamp glass packed in straw. What I did: I said 'When I have a full deck. I do not cross half empty for one man and his smile.' Then I make the bow line fast to the ring at the foot of the planks. Then I said 'You were on this side before the river dropped. I did not carry you.' Then I look at the glass under the canvas and say nothing more about it. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the foot of the West Landing planks with the bow line in my hand and Oren Dask leaning on the cart. The air carried mud, crushed reeds and straw. How I came into it: guarded, curious, dry.

What I witnessed: Wren sat at the table with the marsh map pinned flat under four stones, inking in the flooded channels by the candle. Then a thump came from overhead in the loft, then a long creak, like a weight going slowly over a board, then nothing. Wren stopped the pen and looked up at the hatch. I heard Wren say: "Your rats are heavy." What I did: I said 'That is the timbers. A boathouse drinks the rain for a week and talks all night while it dries out.' Then I go on knotting the torn mesh of the net across my knees. Then I listen for it again and hear only the river. Then I said 'And if it is rats, they are welcome to the old nets. They are not welcome to my bread.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the stool by the stove with the net across my knees and the netting needle in my hand. The air carried wet ink, tar and stove heat. How I came into it: tired, dismissive, uneasy.

What I witnessed: A drip had started in the corner over the woodpile where the storm had lifted a shingle, and it ticked into the tin cup I set under it. Wren rolled the map, tied it with tape and watched the drip. I heard Wren say: "How long have you had this place?" Then I heard Wren say: "Did it leak when you bought it?" What I did: I said 'Since I was twenty-two. Six years of fares bought it, every copper. It leaked then, and the slip was half full of silt. I spent a whole autumn on the roof and in the mud.' Then I bank the stove and shut the damper. Then I said 'It leaks less now. One shingle is nothing. Bed, Wren. The water will be down by morning and I want the early crossing.' What happened: I was standing -- standing by the stove with the poker in my hand and one ear on the drip. The air carried banked coals, wet wood and the river going quieter. How I came into it: tired, fond, quiet.

What I witnessed: Mist lay on the river so thick the West Landing came out of it only at the last pole-length. Wren stepped off with the chain and the satchel and went along the reed path toward the marsh. Ilse Harrow was coming down the mill path with flour on her sleeves and her shawl pinned crooked. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Mara. The storm packed my sluice full of branches and the wheel won't turn. I've been at it since first light with a rake." Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Can you come over at noon with a boathook and a strong back?" What I did: I said 'Noon. I will bring the long hook, and bread, because you will not have eaten.' Then I hold the Heron against the planks with the pole while a carter leads his horse off. Then I said 'Leave the rake. You will only push the branches in deeper.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the bow holding the Heron against the West Landing planks. The air carried mist, river weed and flour dust. How I came into it: warm, brisk, concerned.

What I witnessed: The boathouse was empty and the stove gone cold. The cloth I had wrapped round the half loaf lay on the floor under the shelf, and the shelf was bare beside the oil flask. There were no crumbs on the shelf or the floor and no tooth marks in the cloth. The whole loaf was still in the basket by the door where I left it last night. What I did: I said 'Well. Somebody has had my breakfast.' Then I pick up the cloth, shake it out and look at it in the light from the door. Then I look up at the loft hatch, shut, and at the ladder under it. Then I said 'A rat that size should be paying fares.' Then I cut the whole loaf in two and wrap one half for Ilse. What happened: I was standing -- standing by the bare shelf with the bread cloth in my hand. The air carried cold ashes and the damp of the night. How I came into it: puzzled, annoyed, hungry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the bread: a rat dragged the half loaf off the shelf in the night, or Wren took it for the marsh before we went down to the boat and never said so. I based that on: The cloth that wrapped the half loaf is down on the floor under a bare shelf, with no crumbs and no tooth marks.

turns.content: What I witnessed: A carter drove a cart of cabbages down onto the Heron at the East Landing, and a woman brought a sow and six piglets on a rope behind him. The piglets went everywhere but into the pen at the bow. I heard the woman say: "They've never been on water. Their mother has, and she hated it." The current was running fast and brown along the bar. What I did: I said 'Then she and I agree. Put her at the bow and the little ones will follow her in.' Then I chock the cart wheels and drop the rail behind the sow. Then I push off and walk the pole, keeping well above the bar. Then I said 'Nobody stands up until we touch. A piglet overboard is a piglet gone, and I am not swimming for pork.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole in both hands, mid-river. The air carried cabbage, pig and the cold off the water. How I came into it: amused, brisk, steady.

What I witnessed: The mill sluice was packed with branches and reeds the storm had driven down the side channel, and the wheel stood still over the race. Ilse Harrow was out on the sluice walk with her skirts kilted up and her arms muddy to the elbow. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "The wheel's stood two days. Two days of nobody's grain." Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Since the curfew the town folk bring me half what they did. They can't get their flour home across the river after dusk." Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "You look like you've not slept." What I did: I said 'I think rats have got into my loft. The storm drove them in, and they have had me up two nights.' Then I set the long hook into the jam and haul beside Ilse until the first branch comes free. Then I work the rest loose one by one until the water drops through and the wheel groans and turns. Then I said 'There. Eat that bread before you thank me.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the sluice walk at the old mill, soaked to the knees, with the hook in my hands. The air carried wet flour, weed and the clatter of the wheel. How I came into it: satisfied, warm, tired.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: the mill is in worse trouble than she lets on -- two days without the wheel frightened her more than the work did, and the curfew has cut her trade in half. I based that on: Ilse Harrow says: "Since the curfew the town folk bring me half what they did.".

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren was knee-deep at the edge of the reed marsh, pulling a survey stake out of the mud where the flood had laid it flat. Three more stakes were floating in the open water beyond. I heard Wren say: "Half a week's work, gone east with the current. I'll have to chain the whole north edge again." Then I heard Wren say: "What do the marsh folk call this channel? The council's old map just says 'water'." What I did: I said 'That is the Eel Cut. The one past it with the leaning willow is Willow Reach. Every channel from here to the weir has a marsh name, and not one of them is on any council map.' Then I wade out and pull the nearest floating stake in with the hook. Then I said 'Put the names on yours. Somebody should.' What happened: I was standing -- standing ankle-deep in the reed marsh with a muddy stake in each hand. The air carried rotting reed, mud and the cry of a heron out on the open water. How I came into it: fond, patient, wry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: getting the marsh right matters more to Wren than drawing what the council asked for -- nobody at the council wants the marsh folk's names. I based that on: Wren says: "What do the marsh folk call this channel? The council's old map just says 'water'.".

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren sat on the cart rail with the muddy stakes bundled across both knees. Two marsh women sat at the bow with baskets of eels in wet sacking. I heard Wren say: "The council told me the curfew was to stop smuggling. Is there really that much to stop?" I heard one of the women say: "There's that much to stop, and less on our tables for the stopping of it." What I did: I said 'The council sees a boat at night and thinks of thieves. I see the midwife who cannot cross, and eels going off on the wrong bank.' Then I put my shoulder to the rudder oar and bring her bow round for the East Landing. Then I said 'Draw your map, Wren. Leave the council's business to the council.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern leaning on the rudder oar, with the East Landing coming up. The air carried eel slime, wet sacking and the town's smoke. How I came into it: bitter, protective, tired.

What I witnessed: Wren dropped the stakes by the door and hung the chain on its peg. I heard Wren say: "Bread? No. I didn't take any bread this morning. I had an apple from the market and that was all." Then I heard Wren say: "Maybe your rats really are as big as they sound." What I did: I said 'Then something walked off with half a loaf in the night, and it was not you and it was not me.' Then I take the half loaf that is left, put it in the tin box under the bench and set a flat stone on the lid. Then I said 'Let it gnaw tin.' Then I look up at the loft hatch, shut and quiet, and sit down to grease the mooring lines. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the bench with a mooring line across my knees and the grease pot beside me. The air carried tallow, mud and stove heat. How I came into it: uneasy, stubborn, dry.

What I witnessed: Aldous Toller came out of the dock office onto the dock with a tall lad a step behind him. The back of the lad's left hand was scarred shiny and puckered from an old burn, and I knew him: the tall lad haggling over a coil of rope at the market stall, who caught my eye and looked away. I heard Aldous Toller say: "Mara, this is my son, Bram. Bram, this is Mara Vell, who has the Heron." I heard Bram Toller say: "I saw you in the market. At the rope stall." He put the scarred hand behind his back. Then I heard Bram Toller say: "I can coil a line. My mother's brother ran a barge upriver and I worked it three summers." What I did: I said 'I remember you. You showed the seller a frayed strand and bought the coil anyway.' Then I look him over: long arms, steady feet, a waterman's squint. Then I said 'Your father says you can keep your mouth shut. That is half the work.' Then I said 'Dawn tomorrow at my mooring. If you are late, you are not my deckhand.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the dock outside the dock office door with Wren beside me. The air carried tar, river and the dock office stove. How I came into it: curious, measuring, dry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Bram Toller: he is ashamed of the burned hand and will hide it from passengers, but he does not shy from work, and he met my eye this time instead of looking away. I based that on: Bram Toller puts the scarred hand behind his back and says: "I can coil a line.".

turns.content: What I witnessed: I met Oren Dask on the East Landing at dusk as Wren and I came along the waterfront from the dock. He had a lantern in his hand, plain glass, already burning. He fell into step beside us as far as the door of the Lantern Inn, where the windows were bright and the coloured lanterns hung from the beams inside. I heard Oren Dask say: "Come in and eat, the pair of you. The stew is better than the company, and the company is paying." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "You've never once set foot in the Lantern, have you? People will say I've offended you." He laughed behind us when we walked on. What I did: I said 'People say what they like. I have soup at home and a new deckhand to break in at dawn.' Then I keep walking past the inn door toward the boathouse. Then I said over my shoulder 'Another night, Oren.' What happened: I was walking -- walking along the East Landing toward the boathouse with Wren beside me and the inn's light behind us. The air carried stew, lamp smoke and the river cooling. How I came into it: wary, tired, amused.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he wants me at his table for more than stew -- a ferry pilot who eats on his coin is a ferry pilot who owes him a favour. I based that on: Oren Dask says: "Come in and eat, the pair of you. The stew is better than the company, and the company is paying.".

turns.content: What I witnessed: Bram Toller was waiting at my mooring in the grey light before I had the boathouse door unbarred, with a coil of his own line over one shoulder. Wren came aboard with the sketching board to draw the banks from the water. Bram took the bow line off the ring, coiled it clean and stowed it without being told, keeping his left hand in his sleeve. I heard Bram Toller say: "Where do you want me when we land?" What I did: I said 'At the bow with the pole ready to hold her off the planks. Watch me, not the passengers.' Then I push off and walk the pole down the deck while Bram copies me on the other side. Then I said 'Not bad. Lean into it more and let the pole do the work. The river will take it off you if you fight it.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my hand, mid-river, with my new deckhand at the bow. The air carried morning mist and fresh tar. How I came into it: hopeful, critical, brisk.

What I witnessed: Bram jumped down onto the West Landing planks and held the Heron against them with the pole while a carter led his horse off. Wren sat on the cart rail sketching the line of the landing and the mouth of the mill channel. I heard Bram Toller say: "Why does the council care who crosses at night? Upriver nobody counts the boats." I heard Wren say: "The council says it's smugglers." What I did: I said 'The council cares because somebody is making money that the council is not. The rest of us pay for it in daylight.' Then I take the carter's fare and drop it in the box. Then I said 'Bram. Do not say that sort of thing in the dock office. Your father writes everything down.' Then I take the pole back and wait for the next cart. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the foot of the West Landing planks with the fare box under my arm. The air carried horse, mud and the thump of the mill wheel. How I came into it: dry, guarded, wry.

What I witnessed: Oren Dask came down the East Landing steps with a crate of lamp glass and paid his fare to Bram, who looked at the coin as if it might bite. I heard Oren Dask say: "Aldous's boy, back from upriver. Mind she doesn't work you to the bone, lad." Then he stood at Wren's elbow and looked at the drawing of the marsh shore on the sketching board. I heard Oren Dask say: "Will your map show the little channels, the ones behind the reeds? Or only the big water the council cares about?" I heard Wren say: "Everything that will float a boat, if I can chain it." What I did: I said 'Stand clear of the board, Oren. And clear of my deckhand's ear.' Then I push off and walk the pole while Bram takes the other side. Then I said 'If you want to know the channels, ask the eels. They know them better than Wren and me together.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my hand, mid-river. The air carried lamp oil from the crate and the cold of the morning water. How I came into it: wary, protective, curious.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he wants to know what Wren's map will show of the small channels behind the reeds, and a lamp-maker has no business with channels no cart can reach. I based that on: Oren Dask says: "Will your map show the little channels, the ones behind the reeds?".

turns.content: What I witnessed: The chapel of the Drowned Saint was empty but for the sexton at the top of a ladder by the north wall, nailing back the slates the storm had taken. A patch of grey sky showed through the roof and puddles stood on the flags beneath it. The saint's niche by the river door held its heap of coins, shells and twists of reed, and two candles burned in the stand beside it. What I did: I said 'Good day' to the sexton and nothing else. Then I put a coin in the niche and light a candle for Petra from one of the two. Then I stand in front of the saint with my hat in my hands. Then I said 'The river came over the third mark this week and the Heron held, Petra. Your knots. And I have a deckhand now. You would have had him in tears by noon.' What happened: I was standing -- standing before the saint's niche with my hat in my hands. The air carried candle wax, wet stone and the tap of the sexton's hammer. How I came into it: quiet, grieving, steady.

What I witnessed: The ironmonger's stall at the corner of the market square was hung with hooks, hinges and two kinds of rat trap. Wren picked up the big spring trap and worked the jaw with a thumb. I heard Wren say: "This one would take a hand off. Is it for rats or for burglars?" I heard the ironmonger say: "For rats the size of burglars, mistress. Yours for the price of a crossing and a half, and I'll throw in the bait hook." What I did: I said 'A crossing and a half for one rat. The rat should pay it.' Then I count the coins onto the board and take the trap and the bait hook. Then I said 'It goes at the foot of the loft ladder. Whatever has been eating my bread will have to come down past it.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the ironmonger's stall in the market square with the trap under my arm. The air carried iron, wet straw and frying fish from the next stall. How I came into it: grim, amused, determined.

What I witnessed: Wren sat at the table inking the channel names into the marsh map in small careful letters: Eel Cut, Willow Reach. The loft hatch was shut at the top of the ladder, and nothing moved up there while we were in. I heard Wren say: "If it catches something, I don't want to be the one who finds it." What I did: I said 'Then you will not be. I find everything in this house sooner or later.' Then I set the trap at the foot of the loft ladder, bait a rind of cheese on the hook and pull the jaw back until it catches. Then I said 'Mind your feet on the way to bed. Cheese, not bread. I am not feeding it any more of my bread.' Then I wipe my hands and go back down to Bram and the Heron. What happened: I was standing -- standing in the boathouse door with my back to the trap and the river bright below. The air carried cheese, ink and stove heat. How I came into it: grim, careful, satisfied.

What I witnessed: The carter I had brought over whipped his horse up from the West Landing planks and away along the toll road. Ilse Harrow came down the mill path with a basket of eggs under a cloth. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "For yesterday's work, and don't argue. The wheel's turned all day." Then I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Sit a minute. You and I haven't sat on a step together since the spring." The sun went down toward the reeds while we talked, and the river turned the colour of slate. What I did: I said 'A minute.' Then I sit on the landing step beside Ilse with the basket on my knees, and we talk about the crooked letters I painted on the Heron's bow and the winter I pulled her out of the river ice. Then I look up and see how low the sun has got. Then I said 'Ilse, the dusk. I have to go now or I will be on the water when it falls.' Then I put the eggs in the bow and take the pole. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the bow of the Heron at the West Landing with the pole in my hands. The air carried cold off the water and flour dust from the mill. How I came into it: warm, rueful, hurried.

What I witnessed: The sun went into the reeds behind me before I was halfway over, and the watch's skiff came out from under the chapel steps with a lamp in its bow and two of the council's men at the oars. I heard one of them say: "You're on the water after dusk, ferry. That's a fine, and it's written. Tie up at the inn jetty, and the boat stays there till dawn." The windows of the Lantern Inn were bright over the jetty, gold and red and green through the coloured glass. I met Oren Dask at the inn, by the hearth in the common room under a ceiling hung with lanterns. I heard Oren Dask say: "Well. The dusk has done what I never could, and got the ferry pilot in at the Lantern's door." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "I'll send the pot-boy round to your boathouse with word." What I did: I said 'Not by choice.' Then I tie the Heron to the inn jetty with a double turn on both lines. Then I go up the jetty steps and in at the door of the Lantern Inn, and ask the woman at the tap for a room at the front over the jetty, because I am not leaving my boat on a public jetty with the council's men rowing about. Then I said 'Tell Wren the dusk caught me on the water.' Then I sit where Oren points and let him put a bowl of stew in front of me. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on a bench in the common room of the Lantern Inn with the stew in front of me. The air carried stew, pipe smoke and lamp oil. How I came into it: annoyed, wary, hungry.

What I witnessed: The room the woman gave me had a narrow bed, a jug and basin, and a window over the jetty where the Heron rode dark at her lines. Through the ceiling came the tap of glass from Oren Dask's workshop above, then Oren Dask's voice, low, and another man's, then a door and boots going down the back stair. Far down the river a green light showed low on the water, blinked twice and went dark. The watch's lamp went slowly past the jetty and on toward the chapel steps. What I did: I said nothing. Then I sit on the bed in my coat with my boots on, where I can see the Heron from the window. Then I count the watch's passes: two in the hour. Then I lean back against the wall with my hands behind my head and listen to the workshop over me until it goes quiet. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting up on the inn bed in my coat and boots with my back to the wall and my face to the window. The air carried cold glass, old smoke and the river under the jetty. How I came into it: sleepless, watchful, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: his workshop does its real business after dusk -- voices and boots on the back stair at night, and a green light out on the river while the watch was looking at the chapel steps.
