I based that on: You hear Oren Dask's voice, low, through the ceiling, then a door and boots going down the back stair.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Grey light was on the river and the Heron rode easy at the inn jetty, both lines as I had left them. The common room was empty but for the woman at the tap raking out the hearth, with bread and small beer set on the end of a table. Oren Dask came down the stair in his shirtsleeves with soot on his fingers. I heard Oren Dask say: "Up before the bread's cold. Spoken like a pilot." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "Put your coin away, Mara. I've settled the room, for the pleasure of saying the ferry slept at the Lantern." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "Come up to the workshop at noon. I've something to put to you." What I did: I said 'I pay for my own beds.' Then I put the coin on the table by his hand and leave it there. Then I eat the bread standing up. Then I said 'Noon, if the river lets me.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the end of the table in the common room of the Lantern Inn with the bread in my hand. The air carried cold ash, small beer and the river through the open door. How I came into it: stiff, grateful, wary.

What I witnessed: Wren was at the boathouse door, red-eyed from sitting up, before I had the Heron tied at her mooring. I heard Wren say: "The boy from the inn came round and said the dusk caught you on the water. I sat up anyway." Then I heard Wren say: "Did they fine you?" The rat trap at the foot of the loft ladder was still set, the cheese rind still on the hook, the jaws open. What I did: I said 'They fined me, and it is written in their book. I slept at the Lantern Inn in my boots, with Oren's stew in me.' Then I make the Heron fast at her mooring and come up. Then I crouch by the trap and look at it. Then I said 'Not even a sniff. Our rat does not care for cheese.' Then I put the kettle on the stove for us both. What happened: I was crouching -- crouching by the trap at the foot of the loft ladder. The air carried a cold stove, tar and the river. How I came into it: tired, puzzled, fond.

What I witnessed: Aldous Toller stood on the East Landing with the dock book under his arm as Bram and I brought the Heron round from her mooring. I heard Aldous Toller say: "The watch has the Heron in its fines book for last night, Mara, so I've had to put her in mine." Bram looked down at the planks and grinned. Wren came aboard with the chain for the marsh. I heard Bram Toller say: "Did you really sleep at the Lantern?" What I did: I said 'Write that the dusk caught me two lengths out and I did as I was told, for once.' Then I take the fares and put Bram on the bow pole. Then I push off. Then I said 'Bram, stop grinning. A pilot who sleeps at an inn is a pilot who talked too long on the wrong bank.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my hand and the East Landing falling behind. The air carried morning cold and wet planking. How I came into it: rueful, brisk, dry.

What I witnessed: The inn's back stair went up past the rooms to a door at the top of the house, and behind it was Oren Dask's workshop: a long bench under the skylight, sheets of tin, a rack of coloured glass in green, red and amber, and half-made lanterns hanging from every beam. I heard Oren Dask say: "You'll be wanting the green one lit tonight, then." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "Three sacks to the West Landing, after dark. Two of my lads will bring them to your mooring. Hang the green one at the bow and nobody on the far side will trouble you. The watch keeps to the chapel steps after ten." Then I heard Oren Dask say: "It pays three nights' fares." He turned a pane of green glass to the light and did not answer when I asked what was in the sacks. What I did: I climb the inn's back stair for the first time, all the way to the top of the house, and go in at Oren's door. Then I said 'What is in the sacks?' Then I said 'The council has taken my evening trade and has me in its fines book once. Twice and they take the Heron.' Then I said 'Three nights' fares. And if they take her, you buy me another.' Then I put my hands in my coat pockets and look at the green glass instead of at him. What happened: I was standing -- standing in Oren Dask's workshop at the top of the Lantern Inn with my back to the door. The air carried hot solder, lamp oil and sawdust. How I came into it: uneasy, tempted, guarded.

inferences.text: I concluded that Oren Dask's sacks hold something the watch would take my boat for: he pays three nights' fares for one crossing, knows where the watch will be after ten, and will not say what is in them. I based that on: Oren Dask says: "Three sacks to the West Landing, after dark." and turns the green glass to the light instead of answering.

turns.content: What I witnessed: The boathouse was bright with afternoon sun through the open door, the dust standing in it. Then a slow creak came from overhead in the loft, a board taking a weight and giving it back, then a soft knock, like a knee or an elbow against the net-bales, then nothing. After that there was only the river and a gull, and nothing more from the loft. The rat trap at the foot of the ladder was still set, the cheese rind untouched. What I did: I stand still in the middle of the floor with the bread knife in my hand and listen. Then I said, under my breath, 'Rats do not walk like that. Not in broad day.' Then I look at the hatch a long time and do not go up, because Bram is waiting at the landing with a cart already on the Heron. What happened: I was standing -- standing in the middle of the boathouse floor with the bread knife in my hand and my eyes on the loft hatch. The air carried sun-warmed tar and dust. How I came into it: uneasy, alert, stubborn.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the loft: whatever is up there may be no rat at all. A rat runs and scrabbles; this crept slowly in broad day with the weight of something big, and it will not touch cheese. I based that on: You hear a slow creak overhead in the loft, a board taking a weight and giving it back, then a soft knock.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren's door was shut and the line of candlelight under it had gone out. Two men came along the slip in the dark with three sacks between them, hoods up, and set them in the Heron without a word. The watch's lamp was far down by the chapel steps. What I did: I set a heel of bread on the top rung of the loft ladder, right under the hatch, as bait, and leave the trap where it is below. Then I take the green lantern Oren gave me down from its nail, put in his spare wick from the drawer, fill it, light it and hang it at the bow. Then I said to the two men 'Tell Oren three sacks, and I counted them.' Then I push off from my mooring after curfew and walk the pole out into the black river with the green lantern burning at the bow. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern of the Heron in the dark, mid-river, with the green light on the water ahead of me. The air carried cold, river mist and hot lamp oil. How I came into it: tense, defiant, alert.

What I witnessed: The boathouse was dark and still when I came up from the mooring with the Heron's deck empty behind me. In the glow from the stove door the top rung of the loft ladder was bare: the heel of bread was gone, not a crumb on the rung or on the floor beneath it, no gnawed crust anywhere. The trap at the ladder foot was still set with its cheese rind. What I did: I pinch out the green lantern and hang it back on its nail by the door. Then I climb up and run my fingers along the top rung, and it is dry and clean. Then I come down and stand at the foot of the ladder and look up at the shut hatch. Then I said, under my breath, 'Rats leave crumbs.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the foot of the loft ladder with my hand on the rung. The air carried stove ash, river and hot lantern oil. How I came into it: cold, certain, afraid.

inferences.text: I concluded that whatever lives in my loft is no rat: it took the heel of bread whole off the top rung, left not one crumb, and has walked past the cheese in the trap for two days. I based that on: The top rung of the loft ladder is bare, the heel of bread gone, not a crumb on the rung or on the floor beneath it.

turns.content: What I witnessed: The lamp burned steady in its glass as I climbed. The hatch lifted under my hand and the loft opened above me: the net-bales stacked to the rafters, coils of old rope, and the gable shutter unlatched and pulled to. Behind the net-bales at the back of the loft came breathing, quick and shallow, and then it held. A board creaked back there, once. What I did: I take Wren's lamp down from its peg by the spare room door, light it at the stove and turn the wick up. Then I climb the loft ladder with the lamp in one hand and the bread knife in my belt, and say nothing. Then I push the hatch up with my head and shoulders and hold the lamp up into the loft. Then I step off the ladder onto the loft boards and stand still with the lamp high. What happened: I was standing -- standing in the boathouse loft with the lamp held high and the open hatch behind my heels. The air carried old nets, tar, dust and something like wet wool. How I came into it: frightened, resolute, angry.

What I witnessed: A man was crouched behind the net-bales at the back of the loft, knees drawn up, one arm over his eyes against the lamp. He was thin to the bone and unshaven, in a blue coat torn at the shoulder, its buttons cut off and the threads left hanging. The last crust of my bread was in his hand. I heard the man say: "Don't shout. Please. I'll go. It was only bread." Then I heard the man say: "My name's Tobin. Tobin Reyes. I came in through your shutter in the storm. I've touched nothing but the bread." What I did: I said 'Come out from behind there where I can see your hands.' Then I keep the bale between us and hold the lamp up while he comes out on his knees. Then I said 'That is a soldier's coat with the buttons cut off.' Then I said 'Sit down before you fall down, Tobin Reyes. Nobody is shouting.' What happened: I was standing -- standing over him in the loft with the lamp held high and the hatch at my back. The air carried wet wool, old nets and lamp smoke. How I came into it: shock, anger, pity.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin Reyes: he has run from soldiering -- a soldier's blue coat with the buttons cut away is a deserter's coat -- and he has lived in my loft on my bread since the storm night. I based that on: The man wears a blue coat torn at the shoulder, its buttons cut off, and says: "I came in through your shutter in the storm.".

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Tobin sitting against the net-bales with my old blanket round his shoulders and the torn blue coat folded on his knees. I heard Tobin say: "I was in the council's river watch, at the post below the second bend. Pressed into it in the spring. I walked off a week before the storm and kept to the reeds." I heard Tobin say: "When the storm broke I came across on a drifting log and climbed in under your eaves. The bread was me. I'm sorry about the bread." I saw Wren sitting on the top rung of the ladder with the lamp, listening. I heard Wren say: "Nobody else needs to know he's here, Mara." What I did: I said 'Why did you walk off.' Then I wait while he looks at his hands and does not answer. Then I said 'Keep your reasons for now. You stay up here by day, you keep away from the hatch when the door is open, and you come down only when the shutters are closed.' Then I take the lamp from Wren and hang it on the rafter hook. What happened: I was kneeling on the loft boards between the net-bales and the hatch. The air carried tar, old rope and wet wool. How I came into it: wary, tired, protective.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin Reyes: he is holding back the real reason he left the river watch; he answered everything except why. I based that on: he told me where he served and how he crossed in the storm, then looked at his hands and said nothing when I asked why he walked off.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Tobin wake when the hatch lifted and reach for the blue coat before he saw it was me. I saw a dark bruise along his ribs where his shirt rode up. I heard Tobin say: "That's more bread than I've had in a week. Thank you." I heard Tobin say: "A sergeant's boot. The night before I left." I saw Wren pass up a jug of water and then go down with her surveyor's chain over her shoulder and her satchel of maps. I heard Wren say: "I'll be on the north reed beds all day. If anyone asks, I've seen nothing but herons." What I did: I said 'Eat slowly or it will come back up.' Then I set bread, a heel of cheese and two apples on a sack beside him. Then I said 'Who gave you those ribs.' Then I said 'The first carts come down at seven. When you hear the landing bell, keep still and keep away from the gable.' What happened: I was crouched at the loft hatch with one foot on the ladder. Grey light came through the gaps in the roof boards. How I came into it: careful, protective, uneasy.

What I witnessed: I saw Bram coiling the bow line, the burn-scarred left hand holding the coil and the right one laying it down. I saw two carters and a woman with a basket of eggs on the deck, and Wren on the stern thwart with her chain across her knees. I heard Bram say: "There's council men in my father's office since first light. Asking after a deserter, they said. A man in a blue coat." I saw Wren look down at her map case and say nothing. What I did: I said 'Then they had better ask the river.' Then I set the pole against the bottom and walk it back along the deck, and the Heron slides off the East Landing. Then I said 'Bram, take the bow and watch for snags off the shoal.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and bring her round into the current for the West Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern with both hands on the rudder oar, halfway across the Aune. The air carried river mist and the wet hay on the carts. How I came into it: guarded, steady, alert.

inferences.text: I concluded that the council's men have come to Saltmere for the man in my loft, and that they started at the dock office, so Aldous will know all their questions by noon. I based that on: Bram said council men had been in his father's office since first light asking after a deserter in a blue coat.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw a new notice pinned beside the tide board with the council's seal at the foot. I saw that it read: "Tobin Reyes, deserter from the council's river watch. Twenty-eight years, dark hair, thin, last seen in a torn blue coat. Two silver marks for word that leads to him." I heard Aldous say: "They want every boatman keeping an eye out. You most of all, Mara. Every soul who crosses goes through your hands." I heard Aldous say: "Two marks. There's folk in this town would sell their own mother for two marks." I heard Aldous say: "The marsh first, they told me. Then the landings, if the marsh gives them nothing." What I did: I said 'Then let us hope the man has more sense than to come to the ferry.' Then I pay the week's crossing tolls into his tin and watch him write them in the book. Then I said 'Are they searching the town or the marsh.' Then I put my cap back on and go out without looking at the notice again. What happened: I was standing in the dock office doorway with the tolls paid. The air carried lamp oil and damp paper. How I came into it: cold, careful, watchful.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Aldous Toller: he has no more love for the council's men than I do, but he will do what their notice asks if he thinks it keeps his dock quiet. I based that on: he told me every boatman should keep an eye out, then spat about folk who would sell their mother for two marks.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw two of the council's men come down the East Landing in blue coats with brass buttons, leading a long-legged hound on a cord. I heard the older one say: "Have you carried a man alone in a blue coat this last week? Dark, thin, keeps his head down." I heard the younger one say: "He'll have cut his buttons off by now." I saw the hound put its nose over the gunwale and sneeze at the river. I saw them get off at the West Landing and go up the toll road toward the reed marsh with the hound pulling ahead. What I did: I said 'I carry whoever pays. I have had no soldier on this deck this month but the two of you.' Then I take their coins and push off with Bram on the bow. Then I put them ashore at the West Landing and stand off from the planks while they climb out. Then I turn the Heron for home with the deck empty. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in midstream with Bram at the bow. The air carried wet dog and river weed. How I came into it: tense, wary, relieved.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin flat behind the net-bales when the hatch lifted, then sit up when he saw my face. I heard Tobin say: "I heard the bell and the carts and a dog somewhere across the water. Was that for me?" I heard Tobin say: "If they've a hound, it'll find my track at the reed edge where I came ashore. Not past the water, though. Water takes the scent." What I did: I said 'Two of them and a hound, gone up the toll road to the marsh. They asked me if I had carried you. I told them I had carried no soldier, which is so.' Then I hand him a bowl of eel soup and a spoon. Then I said 'Your track ends at the river and the river is a hundred yards wide. Eat.' Then I check that the gable shutter is barred from the inside. What happened: I was sitting on an upturned crate in the loft while Tobin ate. The air carried eel soup and dust. How I came into it: steady, uneasy, practical.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren knee-deep at the edge of the north reed beds with a ranging pole, her chain laid out along a line of white stakes. I saw, far off toward the old duck hides, two blue coats moving and a hound working the reeds. I heard Wren say: "They've been beating the reeds since noon. They asked me if I'd seen anyone. I told them I'd been looking through a sight glass all day and seen a great many reeds." I heard Wren say: "The north channel isn't on any of the council's old maps. It's on mine now." What I did: I said 'That channel is where Ilse and I set eel traps when we were girls.' Then I hold the end of her chain while she reads the distance and writes it in her book. Then I said 'Come back with me on the next crossing. I want you home before those two come back down the road.' What happened: I was standing on a hummock of firm ground at the edge of the north reed beds with mud to my ankles. The air carried marsh gas and crushed reed. How I came into it: watchful, fond, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: she is better at turning a question aside than I am; she answered the council's men with the plain truth and gave them nothing. I based that on: she said she told them she had been looking through a sight glass all day and seen a great many reeds.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Tobin come down the ladder slowly after I barred the door and closed the shutters, and sit at the end of the table nearest the dark. I saw Wren unroll her map across the table and weight the corners with my tin mugs. I heard Tobin say: "The watch post is about here. Below the second bend. I came up this side of the water, through all of this." I saw him trace a line through the reed marsh with one finger. I heard Wren say: "That's four miles of reed. You must have been in the water half the way." What I did: I said 'Supper first, maps after.' Then I ladle out barley and onions and put the bread in the middle of the table. Then I said 'If anyone knocks after curfew, Tobin goes up and pulls the ladder after him, and Wren and I are two women eating supper.' Then I eat standing by the shutter, listening to the landing. What happened: I was standing by the barred shutter with a bowl in my hand. The air carried barley, onions and lamp smoke. How I came into it: watchful, warm, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw three carts waiting on the East Landing, a goatherd with eleven goats, and Bram already on the Heron bailing last night's rain out of the bilge. I heard Bram say: "Rained in the night. I've had forty buckets out of her already." I saw Wren come down from the boathouse with her chain and satchel and stand among the goats. I heard the goatherd say: "Do the goats go first or the carts? Last time the brown one went over the side." What I did: I said 'Goats first, in the middle, and you hold the brown one by the horns this time.' Then I take the bucket from Bram and bail while he unships the boarding plank. Then I said 'That is good bailing, Bram. Now get the plank under the first cart wheels.' Then I count the carters' coins into my pouch. What happened: I was standing on the East Landing beside the Heron's bow with a full pouch and wet sleeves. The air carried goat, rain and wet planking. How I came into it: busy, brisk, cheerful.

What I witnessed: I saw Oren Dask at a trestle in the market square with lanterns hung from a pole, brass ones, tin ones and two with green glass. I heard Oren say: "Mara Vell. You'll be wanting oil for the green one, then. The nights are drawing in." I heard Oren say: "No? Well, it keeps. The council's men are thick on the ground this week. Bad for trade, men in blue coats." I saw him smile and look past me at the river while he said it. I heard the baker say: "Four loaves, Mara? Are you feeding a regiment?" What I did: I said 'I came for bread, not oil.' Then I buy four loaves and a bag of oats from the baker beside him and a second wool blanket from the old woman at the end of the row. Then I said 'I have a surveyor lodging with me, and surveyors eat like horses.' Then I walk out of the square with the blanket over my shoulder. What happened: I was walking out of the market square toward the landing with my arms full. The air carried fresh bread and warm lamp oil. How I came into it: guarded, irritated, careful.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: the council's men worry him more than he lets on, and not for the reason he gave me. I based that on: he said men in blue coats were bad for trade, and he smiled and looked past me at the river while he said it.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw a carter lead a grey mare with a swollen near foreleg onto the deck while his two sons pushed the cart on behind. I heard the carter say: "She went lame on the toll road. I'll walk her the last mile if you get us over." I heard Bram say: "Why do you hold her so far upstream before you turn? We lose a good minute." I saw Bram watch the water where I pointed, then lean on the pole the way I showed him. What I did: I said 'Because the eddy off the shoal will take her stern round if we come at it square. Petra held her high, so I hold her high.' Then I give Bram the pole and let him take the Heron across the slack water while I keep the rudder oar. Then I said 'Feel that pull under the pole. That is the shoal edge. Lean into it, not against it.' Then I take the pole back for the landing and we put the carter and his mare ashore on the West Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern with my hand on the rudder oar and the Heron's bow against the West Landing planks. The air carried horse sweat and river silt. How I came into it: patient, content, focused.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin turn the torn blue coat over in his hands when I asked him for it. I heard Tobin say: "It's the only coat I've got. It's the only thing they ever gave me that was any use." I saw him put on the old oilskin jacket I had brought up; the sleeves came down past his knuckles. I heard Tobin say: "Whose was this?" What I did: I said 'Petra. She taught me the river and left me the Heron. She has been dead two winters and she would not grudge it.' Then I roll the blue coat tight and push it down into the bottom of the oldest net-bale, under the cork floats. Then I take Wren's sewing scissors and cut his hair short above the ears while he sits on the crate. Then I said 'There. Now you look like a boatman and not a notice on a wall.' What happened: I was standing behind Tobin in the loft with the scissors in my hand and dark hair on the boards around the crate. The air carried oilskin and dust. How I came into it: practical, sad, determined.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse come down the mill path pushing a handcart with four flour sacks, flour on her sleeves to the elbow. I heard Ilse say: "Two for the baker and two for the chapel. They pay on the day, both of them, which is more than the council ever does." I heard Ilse say: "Your blue-coat friends tramped through my reed bed yesterday and broke my eel weir. Not so much as a sorry." I saw her sit down on a sack and rub her wrists. What I did: I said 'They are no friends of mine. They came through the dock office yesterday morning and went up the toll road with a hound.' Then I help her heave the sacks onto the deck one by one. Then I said 'I will come up and help you mend the weir when the crossings are quiet.' Then I wait on the West Landing planks for the last carter before we cross. What happened: I was standing on the West Landing with flour down my shirt beside the loaded Heron. The air carried flour dust and wet reed. How I came into it: fond, easy, guarded.

What I witnessed: I saw the two council's men come down to the West Landing caked in black mud to the thigh, the hound limping on a cut paw. I heard the older one say: "You could hide a regiment in that reed and never find a bootlace." I heard the younger one say: "We'll be back with ten men and a boat. He's in there or he's drowned." I saw Wren come down behind them with her chain coiled and her face very still, and step aboard last. I heard Wren say: "They asked me where the dry ground was. I showed them on the map. That's all." What I did: I said 'The marsh has drowned better men than either of you. Stay on the planks and you will both get home dry.' Then I take their fare and pole them across without speaking. Then I hold the Heron against the East Landing while they climb off and walk up toward the dock office. Then I step ashore and make the bow line fast. What happened: I was standing on the East Landing beside the tied-up Heron with Wren next to me. The air carried black marsh mud and wet dog. How I came into it: grim, relieved, wary.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin sitting on the floor with his back to the warm stove, mending a tear in one of my nets with small neat knots. I heard Tobin say: "My mother's in a village two days down the river. They'll be watching her door. That's the first place they'd look." I heard Tobin say: "I can mend nets and pole a punt and dig a ditch. I was never any use for what the watch wanted." What I did: I said 'Those knots are better than mine.' Then I sit on the bench and take the other end of the net across my lap. Then I said 'When the search moves on, there are boats going down to the coast every week. A man who can pole can work his passage.' Then I said 'Not yet. Not while they are still beating the reeds.' What happened: I was sitting on the bench by the stove with half a net across my lap, and Wren was writing up her field book at the table. The air carried warm iron and tarred twine. How I came into it: calm, thoughtful, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse waiting alone at the end of the West Landing planks with an empty basket and her shawl wet with mist. I heard Ilse say: "They came to the mill at dawn, two of them in blue coats, banging on my door with a stick." I heard Ilse say: "They're after a stranger in a blue coat. Mara, have you seen a stranger in a blue coat? Anywhere on your side? Around the boathouse?" I saw her watch my face, the way she has watched it since we were seven. What I did: I said 'No. I have not seen anyone around the boathouse.' Then my stomach turned over, and I kept my eyes on the far landing. Then I push off and walk the pole down the deck. Then I said 'If they bang on your door again, send for Aldous. They have no business with a miller.' What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in midstream with Ilse on the thwart in front of me. My stomach was still turning. The air carried mist and cold river. How I came into it: sick, steady, ashamed.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: she was not asking idly; the council's men frightened her at her own door, and she came to me first because she trusts my word. I based that on: she said they banged on her door with a stick at dawn, and she watched my face while she asked about the stranger in the blue coat.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Ilse walk up from the East Landing toward the market with her basket and not look back. I saw Bram come down the landing at a run, late, with a coil of new rope over his shoulder. I heard Bram say: "Father had me counting barrels. Sorry. What's the matter? You've a face like a wet week." I saw a farmer drive four bullocks onto the deck and Bram go to their heads. What I did: I said 'Nothing that is yours to carry. Get those bullocks tied short.' Then I run the new rope through my hands and said 'That is good hemp.' Then I push off for the West Landing with the bullocks shifting on the deck. Then I keep my eyes on the water and say nothing more the whole way over. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron with four bullocks shifting on the deck and Bram at their heads. The air carried cattle and wet hemp. How I came into it: quiet, heavy, distracted.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin put down the net he was mending when I came up the ladder. I heard Tobin say: "Ilse. Is that the friend you grew up with?" I heard Tobin say: "Then I've made you say a hard thing to the one friend you've had all your life. I'll go tonight. I'll take my chances in the reed." I saw him start rolling up the blanket. What I did: I said 'Ilse asked me this morning if I had seen a stranger in a blue coat. I told her I had seen no one around the boathouse.' Then I take the blanket out of his hands and put it back on the boards. Then I said 'You will not go into the reed with ten men coming to beat it. You will stay until the search moves on, and then we will see.' Then I sit on the crate until he sits down too. What happened: I was sitting on the crate in the loft facing Tobin, the blanket back on the boards between us. The air carried damp twine and dust. How I came into it: tired, firm, guilty.

What I witnessed: I saw the taproom of the Lantern Inn half full of carters at their noon meal, and Oren Dask coming down the back stairs from his workshop with soot on his fingers. I heard Oren say: "Mara. Sit, sit. The pie's mutton today and better than it looks." I heard Oren say: "They tell me the blue coats were banging on the miller's door on the West Landing at dawn. Hard on a widow, that. Is she a friend of yours?" I heard Oren say: "If they come knocking at your boathouse, you send for me. I know which of them drinks." I saw him laugh and not answer when I asked him why. What I did: I met Oren at the foot of the inn stairs and let him steer me to a bench by the window. Then I said 'She is the oldest friend I have.' Then I eat the mutton pie and pay the girl at the counter for it myself before he can. Then I said 'Why would they knock at my boathouse.' What happened: I was sitting on a bench by the taproom window of the Lantern Inn with an empty plate. The air carried mutton, ale and lamp soot. How I came into it: wary, puzzled, guarded.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he keeps closer track of the council's men than a lantern-maker has any need to, and he wanted me to know it. I based that on: he knew before noon that they had banged on Ilse's door at dawn, and he told me he knew which of them drinks.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Wren come down to the West Landing early with her chain in two pieces, one link sprung open. I heard Wren say: "It caught on a stake and snapped. I need a smith or a pair of pliers." I saw a hen get out of a crate a woman had set on the bow and run along the gunwale flapping. I heard Wren say: "Mara, the mill race isn't on the council's map at all. Can you show me where it runs into the side channel?" What I did: I said 'Grab it by the legs, not the wings.' Then I catch the hen myself against the rudder post and hand it back to the woman. Then I close the sprung link of Wren's chain with the pliers from my tool box. Then I said 'I can show you the race better than any map. I am going up to the mill this afternoon to help Ilse with her weir. Come with me after the next crossing.' What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron with the pliers in my hand and Wren's chain whole again. The air carried hen feathers and river water. How I came into it: amused, busy, fond.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse standing in the doorway of the old mill with a paper in her fist and the broken eel weir still down in the race below. I heard Ilse say: "Leave the weir. Read this. The council's men nailed it to my door while I was at market." I heard Ilse say: "It's an eviction notice. For the mill. Signed by Councillor Hesk." I saw that the paper read: "The mill, its race and its ground to the reed edge are to be vacated by the first frost, by order of the council of Saltmere." I heard Ilse say: "Councillor Hesk. I've never laid eyes on the man. He's never set foot on this side of the water." I saw Ilse look past me at Wren and her chain. I heard Ilse say: "First they send a surveyor. Then they send this." What I did: I said 'Who is Councillor Hesk.' Then I read the eviction notice through twice, slowly. Then I said 'Wren maps reeds, Ilse. She did not write this.' Then I put my arm round her shoulders and feel her shaking. Then I said 'This mill has stood since before either of us was born. A paper does not undo that.' What happened: I was standing in the mill doorway with my arm round Ilse and the notice in my other hand. The air carried wet stone, flour and the water of the race. How I came into it: shocked, angry, protective.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Councillor Hesk: he wants the West Landing for something and wants it quickly; nobody clears a working mill by the first frost for no reason. I based that on: the notice Ilse showed me gives her until the first frost to leave the mill, its race and its ground to the reed edge.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Wren sit on the stern thwart with her satchel of maps held against her chest all the way across. I heard Wren say: "The clerk who gave me my orders said the council wanted the marsh drained one day, for grazing. He never said a word about the mill." I heard Wren say: "If my map is what they use to put her out, I'll tear it up." I heard Wren say: "Who is Hesk, Mara? I never once heard the name in the council office." What I did: I said 'Neither had I until an hour ago.' Then I steer the Heron wide of the shoal in the low afternoon light. Then I said 'Do not tear up anything yet. A map that shows the mill race may be the thing that keeps the mill. Keep drawing.' Then I make the Heron fast at the East Landing and wave the waiting carts down to the plank. What happened: I was standing on the East Landing with the bow line in my hands and Wren beside me. The air carried cold river and the smell of the town's ovens. How I came into it: angry, thoughtful, tired.

inferences.text: I concluded that Wren did not know her survey could be used against Ilse, and that she will side with Ilse if it comes to it. I based that on: she said the clerk told her the marsh was to be drained for grazing and never mentioned the mill, and she said she would tear up her own map.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Tobin awake already, splicing an eye into the end of Bram's new hemp rope by the light through the gable cracks. I saw his hands stop on the rope when I said the name. I heard Tobin say: "Hesk. I know the name. It was on the orders at the post, at the bottom of every one. That's all I know about him." I saw Wren pass the water jug up through the hatch and go down again to lace her boots. I heard Tobin say: "Let me do something for her. I can carry sacks at night. Nobody looks twice at a man carrying sacks." What I did: I said 'The council has ordered Ilse out of her mill by the first frost. Councillor Hesk signed it.' Then I said 'You will carry nothing at night across a river with a curfew on it. Finish that splice. That rope is going on the Heron today.' Then I leave his bread and cheese on the sack by the hatch. Then I go down the ladder without looking back at him. What happened: I was standing at the foot of the loft ladder in the boathouse. The air carried new hemp and the cold of the morning. How I came into it: grim, wary, determined.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin Reyes: Councillor Hesk's name means more to him than a signature at the foot of the post's orders. I based that on: his hands stopped on the rope when I said the name, and he told me it was on the orders at the post and that was all he knew about him.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Bram on the bow with the boarding plank and Wren on the stern thwart with her chain. I heard Bram say: "Father's had to pin a copy of the miller's notice in the office window. Folk were reading it before he'd got his coat off." I heard Bram say: "There's three more like it for the West Landing, he says. The net sheds and the old tannery. All signed by Hesk." I saw a carter on the deck spit over the side at the name. What I did: I said 'Three more.' Then I lean on the pole and walk her off the East Landing. Then I said 'Bram, tell your father I will be in to see him after this crossing.' Then I take the Heron over with the carter's barrels lashed amidships and Wren looking at the West Landing as if she were measuring it. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in midstream with my hands on the rudder oar. The air carried wet barrel staves and river mist. How I came into it: angry, intent, steady.

What I witnessed: I saw the copy of Ilse's notice in the dock office window and four people outside reading it. I heard Aldous say: "Hesk wants the whole West Landing cleared before winter. The mill, the net sheds, the old tannery. Don't ask me what for. They don't tell a dockmaster anything." I heard Aldous say: "Councillor Hesk doesn't come down to the river. Never has. He sends paper and men in blue coats." I heard Aldous say: "If Ilse wants to fight it, she'll need it in writing to the council, with names under it. Mine'll be one of them." What I did: I said 'Then put your name down first, so the others are not afraid to.' Then I lean on his counter and read the notice again through the window glass, backwards. Then I said 'She will fight it. I have known her since she was seven and she has never let go of anything in her life.' Then I go out past the people at the window. What happened: I was standing outside the dock office among the folk reading the notice. The air carried tar and a cold wind off the river. How I came into it: resolute, angry, hopeful.

What I witnessed: I saw Oren Dask sitting on a crate of lantern glass at the end of the West Landing planks with a pack on his back, waiting for the ferry. I heard Oren say: "There she is. I've been out to the toll road houses selling wicks. They buy wicks out there like bread." I heard Oren say: "Bad business about the mill. Hesk's a cold fish. Keep the green one dry, Mara; the glass cracks if it's left out in the cold." I heard Oren say: "Everyone on the river knows of him. Nobody knows him." I saw him look up the mill path toward the old mill while he talked, and then away. What I did: I met Oren on the West Landing and lifted his crate of glass aboard myself, carefully, because he asked me to mind it. Then I said 'You know Councillor Hesk.' Then I said 'The green one is on a nail in my boathouse, and it can stay there.' Then I wait on the planks with him for the carter coming down the toll road. What happened: I was standing on the West Landing beside the Heron with Oren next to me and his crate of glass at my feet. The air carried river cold and the smell of lamp wicks. How I came into it: wary, curious, cool.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he knows more of what Councillor Hesk wants with the West Landing than he says. I based that on: he called Hesk a cold fish, then said everyone on the river knows of him and nobody knows him, and he looked up the mill path and away while he talked.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Wren on her knees on a board laid over the mud at the edge of the side channel, drawing the mill race into her map with a fine pen. I heard Wren say: "There. The race, the sluice, the weir, the mill ground to the reed edge. All of it, true to a foot." I heard Wren say: "If the council wants to say there's nothing here but reed, they'll have to say it over my map." I saw ten of the council's men far off on the north reed beds, in a line, beating the reed with poles. What I did: I said 'Petra used to say a true map is a hard thing to argue with.' Then I hold the board steady while she blots the ink. Then I said 'Ten of them now. They came back with their boat and their ten men, the way the young one said they would.' Then I watch the line of blue coats work away from the side channel toward the north. What happened: I was crouched on the board at the edge of the side channel beside Wren, below the old mill. The air carried wet ink and marsh mud. How I came into it: proud, uneasy, watchful.

What I witnessed: I saw a sergeant of the council's men with a grey moustache step onto the deck at the West Landing alone, his boots white with dried marsh mud. I heard the sergeant say: "Your deserter's not in the reed, ferrywoman. Ten men for two days and nothing but frogs." I heard the sergeant say: "So he crossed. When we're done on this side, we'll go through every boathouse and loft on the East Landing, one by one." I saw Wren on the stern thwart with her map case on her knees, and Bram look up from the bow line at the sergeant's boots. What I did: I said 'He is not my deserter. You will find a great many nets and a great many rats in the lofts on the East Landing.' Then I take his fare and pole him across without hurrying. Then I said 'Bram, the bow line.' Then I keep my hands steady on the rudder oar until he is off the deck and walking up toward the dock office. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron against the East Landing, my hands still on the rudder oar. The air carried dried mud and cold river. How I came into it: frightened, steady, defiant.

inferences.text: I concluded that the council's men will come to my loft in the end; they have given up on the reed, and the boathouses on the East Landing are next. I based that on: the sergeant said ten men found nothing in the reed in two days, so the deserter crossed, and they would go through every boathouse and loft one by one.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Wren and Tobin at the table with the shutters barred and the lamp turned low. I heard Tobin say: "The loft is the first place they'll look. Every man in the watch looks in a loft first. I've done it myself." I heard Wren say: "What about the boat? Under the deck boards of the Heron?" I heard Tobin say: "They'd put the hound aboard her to sniff the boards. No." What I did: I said 'There is an old eel-well under the floor by the slip. It has been dry for years.' Then I pull up the two short boards by the slip and hold the lamp down so they can see the stone box under them, big enough for a man folded double. Then I said 'If they come, you go in there, the boards go back, and I put the net-bales on top.' Then I set the boards back and walk on them until they stop creaking. What happened: I was standing on the floorboards by the slip with the lamp in my hand. The air carried old stone, eel slime and lamp oil. How I came into it: careful, frightened, resolved.

What I witnessed: I saw fog so thick on the East Landing that the Heron's bow was grey at ten paces and the far bank was gone. I heard a carter say: "Are you crossing or aren't you? I've cabbages for the toll road houses." I heard Bram say: "I can't see the end of the plank, never mind the shoal." I saw Wren sitting on her chain box at the head of the landing with her collar up. I heard Wren say: "I'll stay on this side today and ink the map at the inn. Nobody can chain a marsh they can't see." I heard a boat's oars somewhere out on the river, and men's voices, and then nothing. What I did: I said 'Nobody crosses until I can see the shoal posts. Cabbages keep. People do not.' Then I ring the landing bell three times so anyone on the water knows where the landing is. Then I sit on a bollard with Bram and share a heel of bread while we wait. Then I said 'Those oars are the council's boat. They are searching the reed from the water now.' What happened: I was sitting on a bollard on the East Landing in the fog beside Bram, the bell rope in my hand. The air carried wet fog and cabbage. How I came into it: patient, cold, uneasy.

What I witnessed: I saw the fog lift off the water in strips until the shoal posts showed. I saw the council's boat, a long grey skiff with six men at the oars and the sergeant in the stern, pull past us downstream toward the reed. I heard the sergeant call across the water: "Morning, ferrywoman. Keep your eyes open." I heard the cabbage carter say: "They're wasting their time. Any man with sense is three counties off by now." What I did: I said 'Bram, push off. Slow, and keep her out of their wash.' Then I lift a hand to the sergeant and nothing more. Then I bring the Heron across behind the skiff's wake with the cabbage cart lashed amidships. Then I said 'Any man with sense would be, yes.' What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in midstream with the fog gone off the river. The air carried cabbage and a cold wet wind. How I came into it: steady, watchful, tense.

What I witnessed: I saw the chapel of the Drowned Saint empty but for the sexton sweeping wet leaves out of the porch. I heard the sexton say: "Ilse Harrow was here at first light. She wants the chapel to put its name to a letter to the council about her mill. I said I'd ask." I heard the sexton say: "The chapel's never set its name against the council, mind. Not in my time." I saw the Drowned Saint over the altar with her hands full of river weed, the paint flaking off her feet. What I did: I said 'Then the chapel can keep its quiet and lose its miller.' Then I sit on the back bench for a while with my cap in my hands, the way Petra used to before a hard crossing. Then I said 'Ask them anyway. Ask them twice.' Then I go out past the sexton and his broom into the square. What happened: I was standing in the chapel porch with wet leaves round my boots. The air carried cold stone, candle wax and wet leaves. How I came into it: bitter, sad, quiet.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren eat a whole bowl of the inn's pea soup without looking up from her inked map. I saw Oren Dask come down from his workshop with a pane of green lantern glass in his hand, holding it up to the window light to look for flaws. I heard Oren say: "Surveyor! They tell me you've put the mill race on your map. The council won't thank you for that." I heard Oren say: "Mara, there's a man in the taproom offering two marks for a deserter, and nobody's selling. This is a better town than it looks." I heard Wren say: "How do you know what's on my map?" I saw him smile and not answer, and set the green glass on the table between us. What I did: Wren and I met Oren in the taproom of the Lantern Inn, and he sat down at our table without asking. Then I said 'Everyone seems to know what is on that map before the ink is dry.' Then I put coins on the table for the soup. Then I said 'We are going. The one o'clock crossing will not pole itself.' What happened: I was standing at our table in the Lantern Inn taproom with my cap in my hand and Wren rolling up her map beside me. The air carried pea soup and pipe smoke. How I came into it: uneasy, suspicious, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse come aboard at the West Landing with a letter folded in her apron pocket and her jaw set. I heard Ilse say: "I've written it. Aldous says it can sit on his counter for names, and the sexton says he'll ask the chapel. Now I need twenty names." I heard Ilse say: "Hesk can send all the paper he likes. My man's father built that weir and I'm not leaving it to the frost." I heard Ilse say: "At least I've still got you, Mara. You've never once told me a wrong word in thirty years." I heard Bram say: "I'll put my name to it, if a deckhand's name counts." What I did: I said 'A deckhand's name counts the same as anyone's on a letter like that.' Then I take the letter and write my name under hers, on my knee, while Bram holds the Heron against the current, and then I hand the pencil to Bram. Then I give the letter back to her without meeting her eyes. Then I pole the rest of the way across without saying anything more. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron with Ilse's letter signed and my stomach tight. The air carried cold wind and wet wool. How I came into it: loyal, guilty, determined.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: she is leaning on me harder than she lets anyone see, and the one thing she is sure of this autumn is my word. I based that on: she said she still has me and that I had never told her a wrong word in thirty years, with the council's notice in her apron and her jaw set.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Tobin at the table with the shutters barred, showing Wren how to tuck a long splice, his hands over hers on the rope. I heard Tobin say: "Over one, under one, and pull it tight before the next tuck, or it'll draw apart under load." I heard Wren say: "It's like closing a traverse on the map. You check every leg or the whole thing's wrong." I saw Wren laugh for the first time in two days. What I did: I said 'If either of you makes a splice that draws apart on my ferry, you swim the rest of the way.' Then I warm tar in the small pot on the stove and dip the cut ends of the new rope. Then I hang the finished rope on the peg by the door to go aboard in the morning. Then I said 'That is a good rope. Thank you, Tobin.' What happened: I was standing by the stove with the tar pot, Wren and Tobin bent over the table behind me. The air carried hot tar and hemp. How I came into it: warm, easy, content.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren step aboard with her chain and Bram cast off the bow line. I heard Bram say: "They've changed the notice in the office. Five silver marks now for the deserter, Tobin Reyes. Father says it's the most the council's ever put on a man." I heard Bram say: "Five marks. I could buy a boat of my own for five marks." I saw Wren stop winding her chain, and then go on winding it. What I did: I said 'You could buy half a boat for five marks, and the other half would sink.' Then I push off and take the Heron out into a brisk west wind with whitecaps on the reach. Then I said 'Wren, sit low. Bram, take the bow and lean on the pole when I call it.' Then I hold her across the wind to the West Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in midstream in a stiff west wind. The air carried spray and cold. How I came into it: tense, quick, wry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Bram Toller: five marks is a great deal of money to a deckhand who wants a boat of his own, and he said so aloud on my deck. I based that on: he told me the reward for the deserter had gone up to five marks and said he could buy a boat for five marks.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I saw Ilse's letter on Aldous's counter with fourteen names under it now, some written and some only marks. I heard Aldous say: "The sergeant and his ten have taken their boat back down to the post. Called back for a week or two, he said. They'll be back." I saw Oren Dask come in out of the wind to pay the duty on a crate of lantern glass, read the letter over my shoulder, and sign it with a long flourish. I heard Oren say: "There. Fifteen. A lantern-maker's name is worth something to a miller; she buys my lamps." I heard Aldous say: "Hesk won't read it. But somebody on that council might." What I did: I met Oren at the dock office counter and moved aside to let him sign. Then I said 'A week or two is a long time on a river.' Then I read down the names and find Bram's, written large and careful. Then I said 'Keep it here where people can sign it, Aldous. More of them come through your door than through the chapel's.' Then I put my cap on and go out into the wind. What happened: I was standing on the step of the dock office with my collar up. The air carried tar, wind and wet paper. How I came into it: relieved, hopeful, wary.

What I witnessed: I saw Bram at the chandler's stall in the market square haggling over a coil of tarred rope for the Heron, his burn-scarred left hand on the coil. I heard Bram say: "Six coppers. It's frayed at the end, look. Six." I heard the chandler say: "Seven, and I'm robbing myself." I saw that the old clothes seller had a man's grey wool shirt and a pair of patched boots on her trestle. What I did: I said 'Seven, Bram, and stop insulting the man. The end is not frayed.' Then I buy the grey wool shirt and the patched boots from the clothes seller without saying who they are for. Then I said 'Carry the rope down to the Heron and coil it in the stern locker.' Then I tuck the shirt and boots under my arm and go down toward the landing. What happened: I was walking out of the market square with a bundle under my arm. The air carried tar, wool and roasting chestnuts. How I came into it: brisk, amused, watchful.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren standing on the dry ridge above the north channel with her map pinned to a board, most of the sheet inked in now. I heard Wren say: "The north beds are done. Three more days and the whole marsh is on paper." I heard Wren say: "Where did you and Ilse set your eel traps? I want to put the old places in. Somebody should remember them." I saw her pen waiting over the paper. What I did: I said 'There, where the channel bends twice, and there, under the alders. Ilse went through the ice by that second bend the winter we were seven, and I pulled her out.' Then I point the places out one by one while she marks them with small crosses. Then I said 'Put them on your map. But do not write our names beside them.' Then I walk back with her along the ridge toward the West Landing. What happened: I was walking along the dry ridge of the reed marsh beside Wren with the wind at our backs. The air carried dry reed and cold water. How I came into it: fond, wistful, calm.

What I witnessed: I heard Tobin turn over on the loft boards above me, and after that the boathouse was quiet but for the river under the slip. I saw the grey shirt and the patched boots folded on the bench where I had left them for him. I saw Wren's door shut and no light under it. What I did: Then I sit by the stove with my hands round a cup gone cold. Then I think back on lying to Ilse on the Heron, when she asked if I had seen a stranger in a blue coat and I told her I had seen no one around the boathouse. Then I think that it was the first lie I have ever told her, and that only yesterday she said I had never told her a wrong word in thirty years. Then I said 'Petra, I have told Ilse a lie, and I would tell it again.' Then I bank the stove and go to bed. What happened: I was sitting on the bench by the banked stove in the dark boathouse. The air carried cold ash and the river. How I came into it: guilty, tired, resolved.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren at the table under the window with the marsh sheets weighted flat by the salt crock, inking in the reed channels west of the mill from the notes of the day before. I heard Wren say: "The side channel behind the mill bends twice before the weir, not once. I've had it wrong all week." I heard Tobin shift on the loft boards overhead, and the ladder creak once and go still.
What I did: I said 'Then put the second bend in. The river does not care what you had all week.' Then I cut the heel off the loaf and set it on a plate with a cup of milk at the foot of the loft ladder, and knock twice on the bottom rung. Then I take my coat off the peg and look out through the river doors for the mist. Then I said 'First ferry at half past seven. Bring the chain if you want the west side today.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the river doors of the boathouse with my coat half on. The air carried cold river mist and the smell of Wren's ink.
How I came into it: rested, calm, watchful.

What I witnessed: I saw Bram waiting on the East Landing with the bow pole already over his shoulder, a goatherd with six goats roped in a string, and a carter with a cart of cabbages for the toll road. I saw Wren come down the slip with the surveyor's chain coiled over one arm. I heard the goatherd say: "Mind the brown one, she bites." I heard Bram say: "Mist's lifting off the middle. We'll see the West Landing by halfway."
What I did: I said 'Goats amidships, cart forward, wheels chocked. Wren, stand by the rail and keep the chain off the deck.' Then I lean on the rudder oar to bring the Heron's head up into the current. Then I call the stroke and watch Bram walk the pole back. Then I said 'Aim high, Bram. The current sets toward the West Landing this morning. We land square or we land in the reeds.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern of the Heron with the rudder oar under my arm, in the middle of the river. The air carried goat and wet cabbage leaves.
How I came into it: calm, brisk, content.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse waiting on the West Landing in her floury apron with a folded letter in her fist. I saw Bram make the Heron fast, and Wren go off up the toll road with the chain. I heard Ilse say: "The council clerk has written. Councillor Hesk has read my objection, and the eviction notice stands. Out by first frost, mill and land." I heard Ilse say: "He's never once set foot on this side of the river, and he wants my mill." I saw the letter in the clerk's hand: the eviction notice signed by Councillor Hesk stands, and she may bring her papers to the clerk in two days.
What I did: I said 'Read it to me again, slowly.' Then I said 'Two days. Take the deed and every tally book you have, and I will carry you over myself.' Then I hold her by both arms until her hands stop shaking.
What happened: I was standing -- standing on the West Landing with Ilse's arms in my hands and the letter crushed between us. The air carried wet meal from the mill and the smell of the marsh.
How I came into it: content, steady, easy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Councillor Hesk: he wants the mill land for something he has not written on the notice, or he would have crossed the river once to look at what he is taking. I based that on: Ilse says: "He's never once set foot on this side of the river, and he wants my mill.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I met Oren in the taproom of the Lantern Inn at noon. I saw Oren at the corner table under the window with a tray of lantern glass beside his bread. I heard Oren say: "Mara Vell, out of the wind for once. Sit. The stew's mutton today, and it's paid for." I heard Oren say: "I've a crate of glass going west in the morning for the drovers' inns on the toll road. Put me on your first crossing and keep it off the wet." I heard Oren say: "Green glass sells best out there. They like a lantern that looks like a secret."
What I did: I said 'I can pay for my own stew.' Then I sit down across from him and eat it anyway. Then I said 'First crossing is half past seven. The glass rides amidships, and you hold it yourself if the river is rough.' Then I watch him lift a pane of green glass to the window and turn it in the light.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting inside the Lantern Inn across the table from Oren, my bowl empty. The air carried mutton fat, tobacco and wet wool.
How I came into it: worried, angry, hungry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he pays for other people's dinners so that the whole taproom owes him a little, and a little is all he ever asks back at first. I based that on: Oren says: "Sit. The stew's mutton today, and it's paid for.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Tobin come down the loft ladder once I had the river doors barred, thin in my old grey jersey, and sit on the upturned crate by the stove. I saw Wren spread the torn eel net over the table. I heard Tobin say: "Give me the mesh needle. I can't sit up there another hour counting rafters." I heard Tobin say: "Do the council's men ever come down to the boathouses after dark?" I heard Wren say: "Not since I've lodged here. They keep to the dock and the inn."
What I did: I said 'Here. Small meshes. Make them big and the eels laugh at us.' Then I hand Tobin the mesh needle and the twine. Then I shutter the lamp so only the table is lit. Then I said 'They come when they come. If they knock, you go up the ladder and pull it up after you, and we are a ferry pilot and a surveyor mending a net.'
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with half the eel net across my knees. The air carried tar, stove heat and the river under the floor.
How I came into it: wary, tired, amused.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: being shut in frightens Tobin more than being caught, and it is in the idle hours that Tobin starts listening to every board in the place. I based that on: Tobin says: "I can't sit up there another hour counting rafters.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Aldous come out of the dock office with the dock book under his arm while Bram untied the Heron's bow line, and a new paper nailed to the dock office door. I heard Aldous say: "Council's men came down the toll road at last light asking after a deserter. Young, thin, a blue coat if it's still being worn. There's a reward on the door." I heard Aldous say: "They asked would anyone have crossed one. I told them the ferry doesn't run after dark, which is the council's own rule." I saw Bram read the paper over his father's shoulder.
What I did: I said nothing about the deserter. Then I read the paper on the door from where I stand. Then I said 'The council made the rule. Let the council keep it.' Then I take the stern line from Wren and coil it on the deck, and step aboard.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the Heron's stern on the East Landing with the coiled line at my feet. The air carried cold and the tar on the dock posts.
How I came into it: rested, steady, alert.

inferences.text: I concluded that the council's men are working along the landings now, and Tobin must keep off the slip and away from the windows in daylight while that paper hangs on the dock office door. I based that on: Aldous says: "Council's men came down the toll road at last light asking after a deserter.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Oren come down the landing at the last minute with his crate of lantern glass on a handbarrow, behind a carter with a cart of barrels for the toll road. I saw Oren sit on the crate amidships with his boots braced against the barrels' chocks, and Bram at the bow pole. I heard Oren say: "Steady hands on that oar, Mara. There are forty panes in here and I've counted every one." I heard Oren say: "The drovers' inns hang a green lamp over the door for luck now. Saltmere's fashion has gone up the toll road ahead of me."
What I did: I said 'Then sit still and keep counting.' Then I take the Heron off the East Landing and lay her head up into the current. Then I call the stroke to Bram and hold her steady through the middle. Then I said 'Green lamps over inn doors. The council will be pleased.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my arm, the West Landing a pole's length off. The air carried barrel staves and river weed.
How I came into it: guarded, tense, uneasy.

What I witnessed: I saw the market square full of carts, and the pitch seller's barrels by the chapel steps. I heard the pitch seller say: "Pitch is dear this month. The council's buying it all for the dock posts." I heard the cheese woman say to her neighbour: "They're putting the widow off the old mill by frost. Councillor Hesk's own order. Thirty years that mill fed half this town." I saw Wren buy a twist of ink powder and put it in a pocket.
What I did: I said 'A pot of pitch and two balls of the tarred twine. And a loaf, and that end of cheese.' Then I count the coins into the pitch seller's palm. Then I said to the cheese woman 'The widow has a name. It is Ilse Harrow, and she is not off it yet.' Then I hand the loaf to Wren to carry.
What happened: I was standing -- standing in the market square with the pitch pot hooked on two fingers and Wren beside me. The air carried hot pitch, cheese rind and horses.
How I came into it: dry, steady, watchful.

What I witnessed: I saw Oren come back aboard at the West Landing with his crate empty, and a carter with a cart of reed bundles for the East Landing. I felt the rudder oar shiver under my hands in the middle current. I saw, when I leaned out over the stern, a crack along the grain of the rudder blade, a hand's length up from the tip, dark with water. I heard Oren say: "Sold the lot at the first inn. That oar of yours is groaning, Mara." I heard Bram say from the bow: "You're steering heavy. Something wrong at the back?"
What I did: I said 'The blade is cracked along the grain. Not bad yet.' Then I ease off the rudder oar and let the pole do more of the work. Then I said 'Long easy strokes, Bram. I do not lean on this blade again until I have looked at it dry.' Then I bring the Heron in toward the East Landing, a little below the mark.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with one hand light on the rudder oar, coming in below the mark. The air carried river weed and dry reed dust.
How I came into it: irritable, practical, loyal.

inferences.text: I concluded that the rudder blade will have to be replaced before the autumn floods; a crack that runs along the grain never closes again, it only runs further. I based that on: You see a crack along the grain of the rudder blade, a hand's length up from the tip, dark with water.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Ilse come aboard at the West Landing with a satchel holding the mill deed and three tally books. I saw Bram at the bow pole, and Wren make room for Ilse on the bench and show her the marsh sheet with the mill channel drawn in. I heard Ilse say: "Does the council's map show my water rights? The sluice, the weir, the race?" I heard Wren say: "It shows what's there. What it means in law isn't mine to draw." I heard Ilse say: "Then draw them dark, so nobody can say they missed them."
What I did: I said 'Sit, Ilse. You will want your legs for the clerk.' Then I steer wide of the snag line with the rudder oar held light, because of the crack. Then I said 'Wren draws true. That is worth more to you than a friend who draws kindly.' Then I hand Ilse up onto the East Landing.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern at the East Landing, watching Ilse go up into the square with the satchel. The air carried mist off the water and new bread from the bakery.
How I came into it: uneasy, careful, rested.

What I witnessed: I saw Aldous at his high desk in the dock office with the dock book open. I heard Aldous say: "You came in below the mark yesterday, and again this morning. Petra did that in her last year, when the oar was going." I heard Aldous say: "There's a seasoned ash plank in the back store, left from the new dock steps. Take it. Call it the council's contribution to the ferry, since they've never made one." I heard Aldous say: "And the fine for crossing after curfew is doubled from today."
What I did: I said 'The rudder blade is cracked along the grain. I was going to ask at the timber yard.' Then I go into the back store and heft the ash plank onto my shoulder. Then I said 'Thank you, Aldous. Write it in the book however you like.' Then I sign the morning tally under his finger.
What happened: I was standing -- standing in the dock office doorway with the ash plank on my shoulder. The air carried ink, damp paper and lamp oil.
How I came into it: hopeful, protective, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the curfew: doubling the fine is aimed at whoever runs the green-lantern crossings, and the council knows any crossing in the dark needs a boat like mine. I based that on: Aldous says: "And the fine for crossing after curfew is doubled from today.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Ilse on her knees before the Drowned Saint with a candle lit in the row for the dead and the satchel at her feet, and Wren waiting just inside the door. I heard Ilse say: "The clerk says the notice stands. Councillor Hesk won't hear me before the date on it, and after the date there's nothing left to hear." I heard Ilse say: "I lit one for him. He'd have known what to say to them. I only know how to run the stones." I heard Ilse say: "I'll take it to the full council if I have to stand in the square and shout."
What I did: I said 'Then we stand in the square together. I can shout louder than you.' Then I kneel down beside her on the cold flags. Then I said 'You learned those stones alone, and the carters came back to you one by one. The council cannot take that from you.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing in the chapel door with the satchel on my shoulder and Ilse's arm through mine. The air carried candle wax and cold stone.
How I came into it: grateful, wry, anxious.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse: losing the work frightens her more than losing the walls; the stones are the thing she taught herself after the drowning. I based that on: Ilse says: "I only know how to run the stones.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Tobin come down the ladder after I had barred the river doors and go straight to the stern of the Heron in her berth. I saw Tobin run a thumb along the rudder blade by the lamp and press, and the crack open and close like a mouth. I heard Tobin say: "That's past a patch. It runs up into the shoulder where the blade meets the loom. You want a new blade scarfed on and lashed." I heard Tobin say: "I've planed ash before. Give me a sharp iron and an evening." I saw Wren hold the lamp closer and say nothing.
What I did: I said 'Aldous gave me a plank. It is against the wall behind you.' Then I lay my own hand on the blade where Tobin pressed and feel the crack move. Then I said 'Tomorrow evening, when the last crossing is in. I will sharpen the plane irons in the morning.' Then I pour three cups of small beer.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the edge of the Heron's berth with my hand on the rudder blade. The air carried tar and lamp oil.
How I came into it: sad, stubborn, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw an ox-cart of turnips come aboard at the West Landing for the last crossing, and Wren come aboard behind it with the chain. I felt the current take the Heron broadside in the middle of the river. I heard a crack like a green stick breaking at the stern, and saw the rudder blade split open along the old line and trail loose on its lower half. I heard Bram say: "She's not answering! Mara, she's going down onto the bar!"
What I did: I said 'Wren, take the spare pole. Both of you push off on my word. The oar is no use, we steer with the poles.' Then I ship the rudder oar inboard before the blade goes. Then I take the stern pole and we walk her off the bar. Then I said 'Not the landing. Home, into the boathouse slip.' Then I bring her into the boathouse slip on the poles with Bram and Wren.
What happened: I saw the carter lead the ox off up the slip, cursing. I was standing -- standing in the boathouse slip up to my shins with the Heron's bow line in my hands and the cracked rudder oar lying across her stern. The air carried ox, wet turnips and river mud.
How I came into it: careful, uneasy, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw the light go off the river and Wren bar the river doors. I saw Tobin come down the loft ladder in my grey jersey with the sleeves pushed up. I heard Tobin say: "Get it on the trestles, blade toward the lamp." I saw the cracked blade, once the rudder oar lay across the trestles, split from the tip right up into the shoulder, and the old lashing round the joint gone soft and black.
What I did: I said 'We repair the rudder oar tonight. The Heron does not cross tomorrow without it.' Then I lift the rudder oar off the Heron's stern with Tobin at the loom end and lay it across the two trestles. Then I cut the old lashing away with my knife, turn by rotten turn. Then I knock the cracked blade off the loom with the mallet and stand it against the wall. Then I said 'There. Now we know the worst of it.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the trestles in the boathouse with the bare loom of the rudder oar under my hands and Tobin across from me. The air carried old tar and wet ash wood.
How I came into it: alarmed, sore, determined.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren trace the old blade's outline onto Aldous's ash plank with a stub of chalk. I heard Wren say: "Drawn true. Cut outside the line, plane down to it." I saw Tobin test the edge of the plane iron on a thumbnail. I heard Tobin say: "Thinner at the tip than the old one. The old one was too fat, that's half of why it split."
What I did: I said 'Then we plane it down to the line and no further.' Then I cut the rough shape of the new blade out of the plank with the bow saw, along the chalk. Then I clamp it to the bench and plane one face while Tobin planes the edges, long strokes down the grain with the shavings curling onto the floor. Then I sight down the new rudder blade against the lamp for twist. Then I said 'It is flat. Petra would have found something wrong with it anyway.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the bench planing the new rudder blade, ankle deep in ash shavings, with Tobin at the other end. The air carried fresh-cut ash and lamp oil.
How I came into it: determined, focused, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin cut the long scarf on the heel of the new blade. I heard Tobin say: "Bring it up. Let's see where it rocks." I saw the new blade sit on the loom and rock at the heel, and Tobin take three shavings off and try it again, and again, until it sat down tight with no lamplight under it. I heard Wren say: "No gap. I'd pass that on a survey."
What I did: I cut the matching scarf on the loom of the rudder oar. Then I said 'Hold it there. Do not breathe on it.' Then I bore two holes through blade and loom together with the auger while Tobin holds the fitting tight. Then I drive two oak pegs through and trim them flush. Then I lift the end of the rudder oar and feel the new blade's weight against the old loom. Then I said 'It fits. Now it has to stay fitted.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the trestles with the auger still in my hand and the new blade pegged to the loom. The air carried ash dust and sweat.
How I came into it: absorbed, content, steady.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren hold the lamp low over the joint so the light fell on the scarf. I saw Tobin take the tarred twine I bought in the market and lay the first turns of the lashing tight against the pegs. I heard Tobin say: "Heave on every turn. A loose turn is a broken blade in a month." I heard Tobin say: "You've done this before, with the old woman. You know the count."
What I did: I said 'Eighty turns, Petra said, then twenty back over the top. She never told me why eighty.' Then I take the bitter end and heave each turn of the lashing tight round a belaying pin while Tobin lays it. Then I count the turns aloud. Then I hitch off the lashing and cut the twine. Then I said 'Eighty and twenty. If it fails now, it was Petra who was wrong.'
What happened: I was kneeling -- kneeling by the trestles with the new lashing hard under my palms. The air carried tar and hemp.
How I came into it: careful, satisfied, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw the pitch melt in the pot on the stove, and Tobin brush it hot over the lashing until the twine was black and shining. I saw Tobin and Wren take up the loom end of the rudder oar. I heard Tobin say, once it hung on the Heron's stern pin: "Swing it. Full over and back." I heard the new blade go through the water of the slip clean, with no shiver in the loom. I heard Tobin say: "That's a blade. I'm going up before I fall asleep on your floor."
What I did: I take the blade end and carry the rudder oar to the Heron with them, and hang it back on her stern pin. Then I swing it full over and back three times. Then I said 'That is a blade. The repair is done, and the oar is better than the one Petra left me.' Then I said 'Go up, Tobin. Thank you.' Then I watch Tobin climb the loft ladder, and wipe the pitch off my hands with a rag.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the Heron's stern in the slip with my hand on the mended rudder oar. The air carried warm pitch and the river.
How I came into it: steady, focused, warm.

What I witnessed: I saw, when I opened the river doors of the boathouse to let the pitch smell out, a red glow across the river on the West Landing where the old mill stands. I heard the chapel bell begin to ring hard behind me. I saw flames come up through the mill roof, and Wren come out of the spare room pulling on boots. I heard Bram say from the top of the slip: "The mill! Mara, the mill's burning!" I saw Bram run down the slip and jump aboard. At the mill I saw marsh folk throwing buckets from the race, and Ilse in the door of the sack store, coughing, dragging a sack by its neck.
What I did: I said 'Wren, the bow pole. Bram, the other one. Push.' Then I pole the Heron across with them in the dark, curfew or no curfew, by the light of the burning mill, steering on the new blade. Then I run up the mill track from the West Landing. Then I said 'Ilse! Leave them, I have them!' Then I drag sacks out of the burning sack store two at a time onto the grass with Ilse, and go back in under the smoke for more.
What happened: I was kneeling -- kneeling in the mill yard among the sacks we dragged out, coughing, with the old mill burning above me. The air carried smoke, scorched flour and hot stone.
How I came into it: proud, tired, content.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse sit down hard in the mill yard and not get up, coughing until she retched, her lips grey in the glow of the embers, the roof fallen in and the flames gone down. I heard Ilse say: "I can't get my breath. Mara, I can't get my breath." I saw Wren take her other arm. When we came up from the East Landing I saw the sexton holding the chapel door open with a lamp, and a pallet laid down in the vestry. I heard the sexton say: "Lay her there. Keep her sitting up. I'll fetch water and vinegar."
What I did: I said 'Wren, her other arm. We are taking her across.' Then I carry Ilse down the mill track between us and lay her in the Heron on my coat. Then I pole her across to the East Landing, smoke-sick and coughing, with Wren holding her up.
