Then I walk her up to the chapel of the Drowned Saint with Wren and prop her sitting up against the vestry wall. Then I said 'Breathe slow, Ilse. You are out. You are across the river.'
What happened: I was kneeling -- kneeling by Ilse's pallet in the chapel vestry with her hand in mine. The air carried the smoke in our clothes and cold candle wax.
How I came into it: frightened, fierce, breathless.

What I witnessed: I saw the mill roof fallen in between its walls, and Aldous and the townsmen I poled back over with him throwing buckets from the mill race on the smoking sack store wall. I saw a fallen roof beam, still smouldering at one end lying across the last sacks we had not got clear. I saw Bram take hold of the beam with his bare hands to drag it off them. I heard Bram cry out, and saw him let go, his palms white and blistering, the old forge scar on his left hand black with soot. I heard Aldous say: "Bram! Get him to the water!"
What I did: I said 'Bram, here, to the race. Hands in. Keep them in.' Then I drag Bram by the elbows to the edge of the mill race and push both his hands under the water. Then I hold them there while he shakes. Then I tear the hem off my shirt, wet it, and wrap his palms loosely. Then I said 'You will keep your hands, Bram. Do not take hold of burning things again.'
What happened: I was kneeling -- kneeling at the edge of the mill race holding Bram's wrapped hands down in the cold water, with Aldous beside us. The air carried smoke, steam and wet ash.
How I came into it: shaken, tender, exhausted.

What I witnessed: I saw the town gathered on the East Landing at dawn, carters and market sellers and chapel folk, looking across the grey river at the smoke going up from the old mill. I saw Bram on a bollard with his hands wrapped in my shirt and Aldous standing beside him, and Wren coming down from the chapel. I heard the sexton say, loud enough for the whole landing: "That fire was set. I rang the bell and I watched it from the chapel step. It caught at both ends at once, the sack store and the wheel house. A fire doesn't jump across a yard by itself." I heard the landing go quiet.
What I did: I said 'Who was over there before the bell? Did anyone see a boat?' Then I look round at the faces on the landing. Then I said to Wren 'Ilse is asleep in the vestry. Be there when she wakes. She should not hear this from a crowd.' Then I sit down on the edge of the Heron's deck with my head in my hands.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the edge of the Heron's deck at the East Landing with soot to my elbows. The air carried cold dawn and the burned mill across the water.
How I came into it: frightened, grim, exhausted.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the fire: whoever set it wanted Ilse off the mill sooner than the council's paper could put her off, or wanted something inside it gone. I based that on: The sexton says: "It caught at both ends at once, the sack store and the wheel house.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Ilse awake on the vestry pallet, her eyes red from the smoke, and Wren on a stool beside her with a bowl of the sexton's broth. I heard the sexton say at the vestry door: "She keeps the vestry as long as she needs it." I heard Ilse say: "The sexton told me. Set, he says. Both ends at once." I heard Ilse say: "There's nothing left for Councillor Hesk to put me off but the stones and the wheel. He can have them. He can have the ash." I saw Ilse cough until she had to hold the wall.
What I did: I said 'You are alive, and so is everyone who went in after you. That is something.' Then I take the bowl from Wren and hold it for her. Then I said 'The sexton says you keep the vestry as long as you need it. Anything you want from the other side, I will carry.' Then I sit down on the floor by the pallet until she sleeps again.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the vestry floor with my back to the wall and Ilse asleep beside me. The air carried broth, wax and the smoke still in her hair.
How I came into it: exhausted, angry, numb.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse: she is giving the mill away out loud so that nobody can take it from her; she stood dry-eyed at the grave the same way and wept that night in the mill kitchen. I based that on: Ilse says: "He can have them. He can have the ash.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Wren take the bow pole in Bram's place, since Bram's hands are wrapped, and plant it too far forward and nearly go in after it. I saw a carter with a cart of hurdles for the toll road, and two marsh women going home. I heard the carter say: "They're saying in the square it was that deserter. The one the council's men are after. Burned the mill for the sacks, or for spite." I heard one of the marsh women say: "Folk will always blame the one they can't see."
What I did: I said 'Wren, plant it by your feet, not out in front of you. Lean, then walk it back.' Then I steer us across the middle current on the new blade and feel it hold. Then I said to the carter 'Were you over there last night? I was. Say what you saw, or say nothing.' Then I hold her head up for the West Landing.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in mid-river with the rudder oar under my arm. The air carried wet ash blowing off the mill and the river.
How I came into it: grieving, tender, tired.

What I witnessed: I saw Bram on the dock office bench with his hands dressed in goose grease and linen, and Aldous at the high desk, grey in the face. I heard Aldous say: "The council clerk was down at first light. Councillor Hesk's word: the notice stands. Burned or not, the mill land goes to the council at first frost." I heard Bram say: "I'm sorry, Mara. I can't hold a pole. The sexton says a fortnight." I heard Aldous say: "He'll hold nothing till it's healed. He had one burn off a forge already. That was plenty."
What I did: I said 'Bram, you pulled a burning beam off the last of her sacks. Do not be sorry to me.' Then I sit down on the bench beside him. Then I said to Aldous 'The land, and not the stones. Hesk wanted the ground under it all along.' Then I write the morning crossings into the dock book myself, since Aldous has not.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the dock office bench beside Bram with the dock book on my knee. The air carried goose grease and wet ink.
How I came into it: protective, sharp, tired.

What I witnessed: I met Oren at the Lantern Inn, the first time I had seen him since the fire. I saw him come down the stair from his workshop into the taproom with a small brass lantern in his hand, clear glass all round, and set it on the table in front of me. I heard Oren say: "For the widow's vestry. A sickroom wants a steady flame, not a candle that gutters every time the door opens." I heard Oren say: "I watched it from my window the whole night. I've never seen a glow like it on the river. Was anyone hurt?" I heard the carters at the next table talking about the deserter.
What I did: I said 'Bram burned his hands on a beam. Ilse is smoke-sick in the vestry. Nobody died.' Then I turn the brass lantern round in my hands. Then I said 'Thank you. I will carry it up to her.' Then I watch his face while the carters talk.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting in the Lantern Inn taproom with Oren's brass lantern in my lap. The air carried ale, stew and the smoke still in my coat.
How I came into it: bitter, fond, weary.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he watched the mill burn from his window all night while half the town carried buckets, and he was in no hurry to tell me why he stayed up there. I based that on: Oren says: "I watched it from my window the whole night.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Tobin come down the ladder before I had the river doors barred, and stop on the bottom rung. I heard Tobin say: "I saw it from the loft window. The whole sky over the marsh. Is your friend alive?" When I told Tobin what the square is saying, I heard Tobin say: "Then I've brought it on you. If they come looking for whoever burned a mill, they'll look harder than they ever would for a deserter. I can go tonight, up the river in the dark." I heard Wren say: "Go where? The council's men are on the toll road."
What I did: I said 'Ilse is alive. She is in the chapel vestry, coughing.' Then I bar the river doors. Then I said 'You were at those trestles with Wren and me all evening, and up that ladder when the glow came. I can swear to that. You stay.' Then I set the bread and the brass lantern Oren sent for Ilse on the table.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table across from Tobin with the shutters closed. The air carried bread, damp wool and old smoke.
How I came into it: wary, groggy, grateful.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: Tobin would rather walk out into the council's hands than have this boathouse searched on Tobin's account. I based that on: Tobin says: "Then I've brought it on you. I can go tonight, up the river in the dark.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw thin smoke still going up from the old mill as we came off the East Landing, white now instead of black. I saw Wren at the bow pole, planting it by the feet this time and walking it back the way I showed. I saw a goatherd with four goats for the toll road. I heard Wren say: "I'll have to mark the mill as burned on the map. A ruin, a hatch and the word. It feels like signing something." I heard Wren say: "Is this how Petra taught you? Plant, lean, walk?"
What I did: I said 'Mark it true. Ilse will want it marked true, more than anyone.' Then I hold the Heron's head up into the current on the new blade. Then I said 'That is how Petra taught me. Plant by your feet, and pull it free before the river keeps it.' Then I look up the side channel at the black shell of the old mill while the goats complain.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in mid-river with the burned mill off the bow. The air carried wet ash, goats and the river.
How I came into it: steady, sad, rested.

What I witnessed: I saw the side door of the boathouse open and Ilse come in out of the light with my coat folded over her arm, the coat I laid her on in the Heron the night of the fire. I saw her stop when she saw Tobin at the Heron's bow with the pitch brush, in my grey jersey, in daylight; I had let Tobin down to help with the seams behind the barred river doors. I saw Wren at the stern seams stop work and look at me. I heard Ilse say: "I didn't know you had anyone in. Who's this, Mara?" I saw Tobin put the brush down and wait for me.
What I did: I said 'This is my cousin, from downriver. Come up to work the bow while Bram cannot.' Then I said 'Mam had people downriver. We never saw much of them.' Then I take my coat from her and hang it on the peg so I need not look at her. Then I put the brass lantern Oren sent into her hands.
What happened: I lied to Ilse. It was the second lie I have told her, and it came out smooth and easy, easier than it should have. I saw Ilse look at Tobin a long while and then sit down on the crate by the stove. I heard Ilse say: "You never once said you had cousins." I was standing -- standing by the coat peg with my face hot. The air carried pitch and the river.
How I came into it: sad, patient, steady.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse: she knows I have no cousins downriver and has decided not to say so yet, which is worse than if she had said it. I based that on: Ilse says: "You never once said you had cousins.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw the market square quieter than usual, and the talk at every stall about the fire. I saw Oren at his lantern stall under the dock office wall, hanging new lanterns on the pole, red ones and clear ones and two green ones at the end. I heard Oren say: "Mara. Did the widow like her lantern?" I heard Oren say: "The council's doubled the curfew fine, and now every carter in Saltmere wants a lantern that shutters. A frightened town is good for my trade." I saw Wren buy a yard of linen and a pot of comfrey salve from the herb woman, for Bram.
What I did: I said 'She took it. She did not say whether she liked it. She is not liking anything this week.' Then I said to Oren 'Good for your trade. Not good for much else.' Then I take the linen from Wren and walk on.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the edge of the market square by the chapel steps with the linen for Bram under my arm. The air carried tallow, wet stone and comfrey.
How I came into it: ashamed, cornered, uneasy.

What I witnessed: I saw Bram on the dock office bench with his hands in their dressings, trying to turn a page of the dock book with his wrists, and Aldous take the book away from him. I heard Aldous say: "The council's men are about the landings now, both sides. Still after their deserter, and now asking who was on the river the night the mill burned." I heard Bram say: "Let me come out on the Heron. I can call the stroke even if I can't pole." I saw Bram wince when I unwrapped the linen.
What I did: I said 'Hold still.' Then I unwrap Bram's hands, spread the comfrey salve over the blisters with two fingers, and wrap them again in clean linen. Then I said 'You can call the stroke tomorrow, from the bench, with your hands in your lap.' Then I said to Aldous 'Let them ask. The ferry carries anyone who pays.'
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the bench beside Bram with the salve pot in my hand. The air carried comfrey, goose grease and ink.
How I came into it: wary, tired, curt.

What I witnessed: I saw two of the council's men waiting at the West Landing with their pikes and the council's badge on their coats, mud to the knee from the toll road. I saw Wren move the chain off the bench to make room for them. I heard the older one say: "We're after a deserter. Young, thin, came this way in a blue coat. You'd have seen everyone who crossed this month, ferrywoman." I heard the younger one say: "And the night the mill burned. Who crossed that night?"
What I did: I said 'I carry whoever pays, and I watch the river, not coats.' Then I take the Heron off the West Landing. Then I said 'The night the mill burned I crossed four times, with buckets and townsmen and a sick woman. Ask the dockmaster. He crossed with me.' Then I hold the rudder oar steady and say nothing more.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in mid-river with my eyes on the water and the two council's men at my back. The air carried wet wool, mud and pike oil.
How I came into it: tender, uneasy, steady.

inferences.text: I concluded that the council's men now want their deserter for the fire as well as for deserting, so every question about the one is a question about the other. I based that on: The younger one says: "And the night the mill burned. Who crossed that night?".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Tobin come down when the river doors were barred and sit by the stove with the eel net, not mending it. I heard Tobin say: "Wren told me about the council's men on the ferry." I heard Tobin say: "And your friend. You lied to her for me this morning, to her face, with me standing there holding a pitch brush." I heard Wren say: "She's sharper than either of you think. She looked at Tobin like a sum that doesn't add up."
What I did: I said 'I did. I lied to Ilse, and now I carry it.' Then I take the mesh needle out of Tobin's hand and finish the row myself. Then I said 'If the men from the council come into this boathouse, you are my cousin to them too, and you do not open your mouth.' Then I bank the stove for the night.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting by the stove with the eel net across my knees and Tobin beside me. The air carried tar and the cold coming off the river.
How I came into it: guarded, cold, tense.

What I witnessed: I saw Bram on the bench amidships with his wrapped hands in his lap, calling the stroke, and Wren at the bow pole answering it. I saw a hay cart for the toll road and a crate of hens. I heard Bram say: "Plant. Lean. Walk it back. Again." I heard Wren say: "Bram, if you call it any faster I'll be in the river." I saw the old mill come up black on the West Landing as the mist lifted, the wheel still standing in the race.
What I did: I said 'He calls it the way Petra called it to me. Too fast, and right.' Then I hold the Heron's head up into the current on the new blade. Then I said 'Bram, slower through the middle. Let her drift down onto the mark.' Then I look at the black wheel in the race until we are past it.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in mid-river with the hay cart in front of me and the burned mill off the bow. The air carried hay, hens and wet ash.
How I came into it: rested, heavy, resolved.

What I witnessed: I saw the chain flash once far up the mill track, where Wren had gone with Bram to measure what is left of the old mill, and then only reeds. I saw a marsh woman come down the track with a bundle in her apron: Ilse's copper kettle, blackened, and a grey shawl scorched along one edge. I heard the marsh woman say: "Found these in the yard under the kitchen window. Take them to her, would you? I can't look at her yet." I heard Wren call down from up the track: "Forty-two links from the door to the wheel. Same as before. The walls haven't moved." I heard Bram call: "The wheel's still turning, Mara. Slowly."
What I did: I said 'I will take them to her.' Then I wrap the kettle in the shawl and stow it under the stern bench. Then I said, loud, up the track 'Forty-two links. The walls are still hers.' Then I sit on the landing post and wait for the next fare.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting alone on the West Landing post with my back to the burned mill. The air carried wet ash and marsh mud.
How I came into it: fond, sad, steady.

What I witnessed: I met Oren on the West Landing in the middle of the morning. I saw him come down the toll road with a purse at his belt and wait at the landing post while I loaded a cart of reed bundles. I heard Oren say: "Spent the night at the drovers' inn at the head of the road. They pay in silver up there." I saw Oren take the spare bow pole without being asked and plant it like someone who has done it in the dark. I heard Oren say, at midstream: "I've a load going over tonight. Ten o'clock, the cart in the inn yard. Light the green one when the chapel bell's done, not before. Same as always." I heard Oren say: "Double, this time. The council's doubled their fine, so I'll double mine."
What I did: I said 'Bram cannot pole, and the council has men on both landings.' Then I said 'Double. And it goes to Ilse, not to me.' Then I said 'Ten, then. If the bell is late, I am late.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in mid-river with Oren poling at the bow. The air carried reed dust and the river.
How I came into it: sad, quiet, patient.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he has poled this river in the dark many more times than he has asked me to carry his carts, and he no longer troubles to hide it from me. I based that on: You see Oren take the spare bow pole without being asked and plant it like someone who has done it in the dark.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Ilse asleep on the vestry pallet with Oren's brass lantern on the sill above her and a bowl scraped clean on the floor. I saw the sexton in the doorway with a broom. I heard the sexton say: "She ate. First bowl she's finished since the fire. Don't wake her." I heard Ilse breathing slow, with a catch in it but no cough.
What I did: I said 'I will not wake her.' Then I set Ilse's copper kettle down by the pallet with the scorched grey shawl folded on top, where she will see them first when she wakes. Then I stand a while at the foot of the pallet. Then I said to the sexton, low 'When she wakes, tell her the walls stand. Wren measured them. Forty-two links, door to wheel.' Then I go out quietly.
What happened: I was standing -- standing in the chapel porch with my cap in my hands. The air carried candle wax, cold stone and broth.
How I came into it: wary, tempted, resolved.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin come down the ladder when I had the river doors barred, and Wren look up from the map with the old mill hatched in black. I heard Tobin say: "You're going out tonight. You've been looking at that green lantern since supper." I heard Tobin say: "Bram can't pole. Let me take the bow. It's dark, and nobody on the river after curfew is going to ask me my name." I heard Wren say: "I'll keep the lamp out and the doors barred, and if anyone knocks, nobody's home."
What I did: I said 'It is a cart for Oren, over to the West Landing and back. You do not look under the canvas, and you do not speak to the men on the other side.' Then I take the green lantern down from its hook, unlit, trim the wick with my knife and fill it from the oil can. Then I said 'Tobin, the bow. Wren, the doors.' Then I wait by the river doors for the chapel bell.
What happened: I was standing -- standing by the river doors with the green lantern, still unlit, in my hand. The air carried lamp oil and the cold off the river.
How I came into it: tender, quiet, sad.

What I witnessed: I heard the chapel bell finish ten. I saw a covered cart come down from the Lantern Inn yard to the landing with a carter at the ox's head, the load roped down under canvas. I heard Oren say from the dark by the inn yard gate: "Keep the flame low. They only need to see it, not read by it." I saw Tobin lead the ox aboard and take the bow pole. Past the middle of the river I saw a green light answer from the reeds by the West Landing, once, and go out. I saw Tobin put a hand on one of the sacks under the canvas, take it away, and say nothing for the rest of the crossing.
What I did: I light the green lantern Oren gave me and hang it at the bow, the first time I have lit it since the fire. Then I said 'Push, Tobin. Long and quiet.' Then I take the Heron out into the dark after curfew on the new rudder blade, with the green lantern burning low at the bow. Then I said 'Do not look at the cart. Look at the light in the reeds.' Then I bring us in where the reeds give way, hand the ox rope to the man who comes out of them, and push off again for home.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in mid-river in the dark, the cart gone, the green lantern still burning at the bow and Tobin a shape beside it. The air carried wet reeds, ox and hot lamp tin.
How I came into it: tense, resolved, alert.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: something under that canvas frightened Tobin more than the council's men ever have, and it was not the dark. I based that on: You see Tobin put a hand on one of the sacks under the canvas, take it away, and say nothing for the rest of the crossing.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren was at the table with the porridge pot, the marsh map weighted flat with two mugs. Tobin came down the loft ladder with his blanket round his shoulders and sat on the low stool away from the water door. The green lantern hung on its nail by the door, its chimney still sooted from last night. I saw Tobin look at it and look away, twice. I heard Wren say: "The north dyke path is two chains shorter than the old map says. Somebody walked it drunk." I heard Tobin say: "Is there salt?" What I did: I said 'Salt's in the crock by the stove.' Then I hang my damp coat on the hook and ladle porridge into three bowls. Then I said 'Eat, then back up the ladder before the landing wakes. The carters come early on a dry morning.' Then I open the water door and check the Heron's bow line. What happened: I was standing -- standing in the water door with the bow line in my hand and the mist sitting on the river. The air carried woodsmoke and wet rope. How I came into it: tired, watchful, fond.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: the green lantern unsettles him. He looked at it on its nail and looked away twice, the way a man looks away from a face he knows. I based that on: Tobin looks at the green lantern by the door and turns his eyes from it, twice.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Seven of the council's men in blue coats came down the hill road onto the East Landing, a sergeant in front with a paper in his fist, and went straight into the dock office. Bram came running along the planks with both hands bandaged from the mill fire, held up in front of him. I heard Bram say: "They're searching every shed and every boat on the landing. Father says they're after a deserter. They start at the north quay and work down." I heard Wren say: "The north quay first. Then the boathouse comes near the end." What I did: I said 'Thank you, Bram. Go back to your father and keep those hands out of the wet.' Then I turn and walk back along the planks toward the boathouse, not running. Then I said to Wren 'The first crossing goes early today. Bring the goatherd down from the steps if he's there, goats and all.' What happened: I was walking -- walking fast along the landing planks with Wren beside me. The air carried tar, wet rope and boot grease. How I came into it: alarmed, careful, protective.

What I witnessed: The goatherd brought nine goats down the steps and stood among them with his crook. Tobin lay flat in the bow under the folded nets and a goat hurdle; I could see nets, not him. As I poled off, the sergeant came out of the dock office and stood at the end of the landing watching the Heron go. I heard Tobin say from under the nets, very low: "Is he still looking?" I heard Wren say: "He's turned back to the sheds." I heard the goatherd say: "Early for you, ferrywoman." What I did: I said 'Quiet now. The goats are louder than you are.' Then I pole us off the steps and lean on the rudder oar to set the bow upstream of the current. Then I said to the goatherd 'Dry morning. The carters will be lining up by eight.' Then I keep the Heron on its usual line, no faster than any other morning. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my arm, halfway across. The air carried goat and river mist. How I came into it: tense, steady, defiant.

What I witnessed: At the West Landing the goatherd drove his goats up the toll road and never looked back. Tobin came out from under the nets with chaff in his hair. Wren led us up the dyke path into the reeds, map case under one arm, to the old reed-cutters' hut. Half the roof is down but the back room is dry. I heard Wren say: "The hut's marked as a ruin on the council's own map. Nobody walks a mile of mud to search a ruin." I heard Tobin say: "How long do I stay?" What I did: I said 'Until I come back at dusk. Maybe two dusks.' Then I set the bread in its cloth and the water skin on the dry boards. Then I said 'Ilse and I sat out a hailstorm in here when we were girls. It has held this long, it'll hold you. Don't light anything.' Then I take one last look down the path behind us. What happened: I was standing -- standing in the hut doorway with the reeds higher than my head. The air carried mud and cut reed. How I came into it: anxious, determined, tender.

What I witnessed: The sergeant and two of his men came to the boathouse door with pikes. One climbed the loft ladder and drove his pike into every net-bale; the other turned back the blanket in Wren's room. I heard the sergeant say: "We're after a deserter. Tobin Reyes. Twenty-eight, thin, dark hair, last seen in a torn blue coat. Seen anyone like that about this landing?" I heard the sergeant say to Wren: "You're the council's surveyor. You lodge here?" I heard Wren say: "In the spare room, since the first week of the survey." I heard the man in the loft call down: "Nets and an old blanket. Nothing else." What I did: I said 'Nobody sleeps under this roof but me and the surveyor, and the rats in the loft.' Then I hold the sergeant's eye on that lie until he looks away first. Then I stand at the foot of the ladder with my arms folded until the man comes down. Then I said 'Mind the third rung, it's split.' What happened: I was standing -- standing by the ladder watching their blue backs go out along the planks. The air carried wet wool and pitch. How I came into it: defiant, wary, relieved.

What I witnessed: The council's men stood at the head of the landing stopping every cart and lifting every sack. Oren came down from the Lantern Inn with a jug and a string of cups and poured for the sergeant, laughing with him like an old friend. Bram sat on a bollard with his bandaged hands in his lap. When I tied up, Oren strolled along the planks to the Heron's bow. I heard Oren say: "No green tonight, Mara. Let the lantern sleep till these gentlemen have gone home." I heard Bram say: "They put a pike through every bale on the north quay. Father's furious." I heard Wren say: "They searched the boathouse too. They found the rats." What I did: I said 'I wasn't going to wake it.' Then I make the bow line fast to the iron ring. Then I said to Bram 'Take the fares from the next lot. Coins in the tin, not in your hands.' What happened: I was crouched -- crouched at the bow ring with the line in my fist, watching Oren's back go away up the landing. The air carried cider and river mud. How I came into it: uneasy, guarded, irritated.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he pours for the council's sergeant so the sergeant drinks instead of looking. He was laughing with the man searching the landing, then telling me to keep the green lantern dark. I based that on: Oren pours cider for the sergeant and says: "No green tonight, Mara."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The hut was as I had left it. Tobin was sitting in the dark of the back room with his knees drawn up; he had eaten half the bread and saved half. I heard Tobin say: "Did they say my name?" I heard Tobin say: "Then it'll be on paper in every village up the toll road by the end of the week." What I did: I said 'They said it. Tobin Reyes, twenty-eight, thin, a torn blue coat. They didn't find a hair of you.' Then I set down the pot of stew and my old grey blanket. Then I said 'One more night out here. They've searched the boathouse, so it's the safest place on the landing, but not while they're drinking at the inn.' Then I put the blanket round his shoulders and go before the light does. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the hut door with the last light going red over the reeds. The air carried cold mud and stew. How I came into it: protective, weary, grim.

What I witnessed: Mist lay on the river so thick the West Landing was gone. Wren was up before me, inking the dyke paths onto the marsh map by the lamp. Along the waterfront the council's men were shouting for their breakfast at the Lantern Inn. I heard Wren say: "Did he have enough blanket, do you think?" I heard Wren say: "If they ask for a guide through the marsh, I can walk them up the north dyke. It loops a mile before it goes anywhere." What I did: I said 'He had my grey one. He'll have been cold, but cold isn't caught.' Then I eat a heel of bread standing up at the stove. Then I said 'If they ask you, take them the long way. If they don't ask, don't offer.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the water door looking into the mist toward the marsh. The air carried wet smoke and lamp ink. How I came into it: worried, restless, grateful.

What I witnessed: Aldous was nailing a notice to the dock office door. It offered ten silver from the council for word of a deserter, thin, dark, about twenty-eight, last seen in a torn blue coat. Bram sat inside by the stove with his bandaged hands on his knees. I heard Aldous say: "The warrant's got Councillor Hesk's name at the bottom. Hesk wants this one found, and the sergeant means to search the West Landing and the marsh today." I heard Bram say: "They'll want the ferry for it." I heard Aldous say: "Ten silver. I've known men sell their own brothers for less." What I did: I said 'They'll get the ferry. It goes where it's paid to go.' Then I read the notice twice from top to bottom. Then I said 'Ten silver is a lot of money for one runaway soldier.' What happened: I was standing -- standing in the dock office doorway with the notice at the height of my eyes. The air carried damp paper and coal smoke. How I came into it: uneasy, guarded, cold.

What I witnessed: The sergeant and four of his men came down the steps with pikes and a coil of rope and paid for the crossing in council chits. The other two stayed on the East Landing watching the steps. I heard the sergeant say: "Surveyor. You know these reeds. You'll show us the paths." I heard Wren say: "The north dyke first, then. It's the driest." I heard one of the men say: "Smells like a drowned dog out there." What I did: I said 'Fare's paid. Stand in the middle and keep your pikes upright.' Then I pole off the steps and bring the Heron round into the current with the rudder oar. Then I watch the far reeds come up out of the mist and keep my face still. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the oar under my arm, five blue coats gone grey with damp in front of me. The air carried mist and wet wool. How I came into it: anxious, controlled, watchful.

What I witnessed: Wren led the council's men away up the north dyke and the reeds closed behind their pikes. Up the side channel I could see the black shell of the old mill. Then I met Oren on the West Landing; he came down the toll road walking beside a carter's wagon of crated lantern glass. I heard Oren say: "Good morning, Mara. Waiting on the council's pleasure?" I heard Oren say: "Glass from upriver. Half of it cracked, as usual. A lantern is only as honest as its glass." I heard Oren say: "Don't look so grim. Whoever they're after, he's long gone up the road." What I did: I said 'I'm waiting on fares. Same as every morning.' Then I help the carter rope his crates to the Heron's rails. Then I said 'You're cheerful for a man whose night trade has been stopped.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the West Landing steps with one hand on the rail, looking at the reeds where Wren had gone. The air carried wet ash from the mill and river mud. How I came into it: tense, wary, impatient.

What I witnessed: Wren brought the council's men back down the north dyke at noon with mud to their knees and nothing in their hands. Oren's glass crates rode in the middle of the deck, and Oren stood beside the sergeant all the way across talking about the price of lamp oil. I heard the sergeant say: "Nothing out there but birds and a mill gone to charcoal." I heard Oren say: "Then you'll be wanting a hot dinner. The inn does a mutton pie on a cold day." I heard Wren say to me, low: "We never went within half a mile of the hut." What I did: I said 'Hold the crates, the pull is strong at the middle.' Then I lean on the rudder oar through the midstream pull. Then I said to Wren, low, 'Good. Thank you.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the East Landing coming up, the men's boots steaming on the deck boards. The air carried mud and wet straw from the crates. How I came into it: relieved, careful, grateful.

What I witnessed: Ilse was on her knees in the sexton's kitchen at the chapel house, putting her few things back into a bundle; the council's men had searched the chapel house that morning and tipped everything out. Her knuckles still had soot in the creases. I heard Ilse say: "They turned my bundle out on the floor. Everything I carried out of the mill fits in one cloth, Mara, and they turned it out looking for a soldier." I heard Ilse say: "My husband's father built that wheel. Six men to hunt one runaway, and not one of them to ask who set my mill alight." What I did: I said 'I know. It's wrong, and none of it is your doing.' Then I kneel beside her and help fold the shawl, the two shirts and the tin of buttons back into the cloth. Then I said 'I'll come by tomorrow. Eat something before then.' What happened: I was kneeling -- kneeling on the chapel house floor with Ilse's bundle tied between us. The air carried candle wax and old soot. How I came into it: sorrowful, angry, tender.

inferences.text: I concluded that Ilse's grief for the mill has turned to anger at the council, and anger will carry her further than grief would. I based that on: Ilse says: "Six men to hunt one runaway, and not one of them to ask who set my mill alight."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Tobin came out from under the nets as soon as the water door was shut behind the Heron, stiff from the hut and the crossing, and went straight up the loft ladder. In the loft, by the lamp, his face was grey. I heard Tobin say: "That sergeant. I know him. He had the granary watch before me, before I--" Then he stopped. I heard Tobin say: "It doesn't matter. Is that soup?" What I did: I said 'It's soup, and it's hot.' Then I set the bowl down beside the net-bales and hang the lamp on the beam, well clear of the nets. Then I said 'Before you what?' Then I sit and wait while he eats and says nothing more. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on a net-bale in the loft with my back against the slope of the roof. The air carried tar, soup and old net. How I came into it: relieved, puzzled, watchful.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: something happened at the council's granary that he has not told me. He knew the sergeant from the granary watch and bit off his own sentence. I based that on: Tobin says: "He had the granary watch before me, before I--" and then: "It doesn't matter."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Rain on the roof boards since before light. Wren had the marsh map spread on the table with the lamp pulled close. Tobin sat on the floor by the stove mending the bow net, well back from the water door. I heard Wren say: "Rain's in for the day. The ink won't dry and the reeds won't hold a chain." I heard Tobin say: "I can mend the stern net too, if there's twine." What I did: I said 'Twine's in the chest under the ladder. Keep back from the door while the inn's full of blue coats.' Then I go out into the Heron's stern well with the scoop and bail last night's rain over the side. Then I fill the kettle and set it on the stove. What happened: I was standing -- standing in the stern well of the Heron with the bailing scoop, rain running off my hat brim. The air carried wet wood and tea. How I came into it: calm, cautious, settled.

What I witnessed: A farmer's cart of turnips and a woman with two hens in a basket crossed east to west in the rain. Bram rode at the bow with the fare tin under his arm and his bandaged hands wrapped in oilcloth. I heard Bram say: "Father says the sergeant asked about you last night. Whether you ever cross after dark." I heard Bram say: "Father told him you keep the curfew like everybody else on this river." I heard the farmer say: "Curfew. The council can't keep its own bakers in flour, but it can keep the river shut." What I did: I said 'Your father's a sensible man.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and bring the bow round for the West Landing. Then I said 'Keep that tin out of the rain, Bram.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern in the rain with the turnip cart dripping in the middle of the deck. The air carried rain and turnip tops. How I came into it: uneasy, steady, wry.

inferences.text: I concluded that Aldous covered for me with the sergeant without being asked, which means he knows, or guesses, that I cross after dark. I based that on: Bram says: "Father told him you keep the curfew like everybody else on this river."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The rain had eased to drizzle. The council's notice was nailed to the market well too, ten silver for a deserter in a torn blue coat, and a fishwife was reading it aloud to anyone near. I heard the fishwife say: "Ten silver for a runaway. Nobody's offered a copper for the one who burned Ilse Harrow's mill." I heard the baker say: "Loaf's up a copper again. The council says its stores are short, and the council should know." I heard Wren say: "Lamp oil, twine, flour. That's the list." What I did: I said 'Flour first, before it goes up again.' Then I buy a half-sack of flour and a jar of lamp oil and swing the flour onto my shoulder. Then I said to the fishwife 'Say it louder. Ilse would thank you.' What happened: I was standing -- standing by the market well with the flour on my shoulder and the notice flapping on its nail. The air carried fish, wet stone and bread. How I came into it: irritated, alert, thoughtful.

inferences.text: I concluded that bread is dear because the council's grain stores are short, and nobody at the market can say why they are short. I based that on: the baker says: "Loaf's up a copper again. The council says its stores are short."

turns.content: What I witnessed: I met Oren at the Lantern Inn at noon. The council's men had the long table and were loud with it. Oren sat at his corner table by the stair that goes up to his workshop and waved us over. I heard Oren say: "Mara. Sit, eat. The pie's good today." I heard Oren say, low, sliding a twist of paper across the table: "A new wick. You'll be wanting the green one again, then, once our friends in blue have gone." I heard Oren say: "Trim it low and it won't smoke." I heard Wren say: "We only came in for the pie." What I did: I said 'I'll take the pie. And the wick.' Then I put the twist of paper in my coat pocket without opening it. Then I eat with my back to the council's men and my eyes on Oren. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at Oren's corner table in the Lantern Inn with the pie half eaten and the men's laughter behind me. The air carried mutton, ale and lamp smoke. How I came into it: guarded, hungry, uneasy.

What I witnessed: Two of the council's men at the East Landing steps opened every pot on a tinker's handcart before they let him aboard. A woman with a crate of hens came after him. Wren had gone up to the boathouse to dry the map, so I crossed alone with them. I heard the tinker say: "Every pot. Every pot, like a grown man could fold himself up in a stewpot." I heard the woman say: "My hens have been searched twice this week." What I did: I said 'They're thorough today.' Then I push off and take the Heron across on the slack side of the current. Then I help the woman carry the hen crate up the West Landing steps. Then I said to the tinker 'Mind the bottom step, it's slick with weed.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the West Landing steps with the empty Heron tied to the ring below me. The air carried wet hens and tin. How I came into it: amused, tired, watchful.

What I witnessed: Ilse was on the cold bench before the Drowned Saint's niche, with a candle she had set burning there. The sexton was sweeping the aisle. I heard Ilse say: "Hesk's notice came first, and then the fire came after it. Tell me that's chance, Mara." I heard Ilse say: "I'll stand up in front of the whole council and say it to their faces if I have to." I heard the sexton say: "Keep your voice down in the Saint's house, Ilse." What I did: I said 'I don't think it's chance.' Then I sit down beside her on the bench. Then I said 'Then say it. They ought to hear it from you.' Then I sit with her until the candle is half gone. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the bench by the Drowned Saint's niche with Ilse's shoulder against mine. The air carried candle smoke and cold stone. How I came into it: sad, loyal, angry.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Councillor Hesk: he gains by the mill burning. His eviction notice came first and the fire finished what the notice began. I based that on: Ilse says: "Hesk's notice came first, and then the fire came after it. Tell me that's chance, Mara."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren had made fish soup, and Tobin sat on the low stool away from the window. Oren's new wick lay on the table where I had dropped it out of my pocket, and Tobin turned it over with one finger. I heard Tobin say: "Where's this from?" I heard Tobin say: "How many nights have you crossed for him, with the green one at the bow?" Then Tobin put the wick down and climbed to the loft without finishing his soup. I heard Wren say: "He's been like that since the men came." What I did: I said 'From Oren Dask. A new wick for the green lantern.' Then I said 'Three nights. Why?' Then I watch the loft hatch he went through. Then I said to Wren 'He'll tell it when he's ready to tell it.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with his soup going cold across from me. The air carried fish soup and lamp oil. How I came into it: puzzled, uneasy, patient.

inferences.text: I concluded that Tobin's fear has to do with Oren's crossings, not only with the council's men. He asked how many nights I had crossed with the green lantern and left his supper when I said three. I based that on: Tobin says: "How many nights have you crossed for him, with the green one at the bow?"

turns.content: What I witnessed: The council's men came down to the steps at first light with their packs on and their pikes sloped, the sergeant last, settling his bill at the inn door. Aldous stood at the head of the steps with his tally board. I heard Aldous say: "Seven to cross, with packs. The council pays by chit." I heard the sergeant say to Aldous: "Keep that notice up. We'll be back the day there's word." I heard Wren say: "They're going west, then. Up the toll road." What I did: I said 'Seven, and the packs in the middle of the deck.' Then I set the plank to the steps and count them aboard one by one. Then I take the chits from the sergeant and hand them to Aldous. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the head of the plank with the last of the chits in my hand. The air carried cold and boot grease. How I came into it: relieved, careful, alert.

What I witnessed: The sergeant stood beside me at the stern most of the way across, watching the reeds. I heard the sergeant say: "If a thin man in a blue coat ever asks you for a crossing, ferrywoman, you send word up the hill. He's wanted for more than running. The granary count came up short the week he ran." I heard Wren say: "Is that what the warrant says?" I heard the sergeant say: "The warrant says find him." What I did: I said 'I take whoever pays and asks.' Then I steer us through the midstream pull with the rudder oar and bring us onto the West Landing steps. Then I set the plank and watch them go up the toll road in a file. What happened: I was standing -- standing on the West Landing steps watching seven blue coats get small on the toll road. The air carried wet road and reeds. How I came into it: relieved, uneasy, curious.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: the council believes he had a hand in the grain that went missing from its stores, and that is why ten silver hangs on him. I based that on: the sergeant says: "He's wanted for more than running. The granary count came up short the week he ran."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Coming back east I had a woman with a basket of eggs and two marsh boys with eel traps. The river was up and fast and brown from rain somewhere upriver, carrying branches and broken reed mats. I heard one of the boys say: "Heron's quick this morning!" I heard Wren say: "The river's up a hand since yesterday. I cut a mark on the West Landing post." What I did: I said 'Rain upriver. It'll bring bigger wood down by afternoon.' Then I keep the bow upstream and let the current carry us across on the slant. Then I said 'Hands inside the rail, both of you, or the eels will have you.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern as we came into the East Landing steps, the egg basket held up out of the splash. The air carried river water and eel slime. How I came into it: lighter, watchful, easy.

What I witnessed: With the council's men gone, Aldous stood a jug of cider for the ferry and the dock at the Lantern Inn. Bram sat with his bandaged hands round his cup. The long table where the men had eaten was bare and scrubbed, and Oren's stair door was shut. I heard Aldous say: "The landing's ours again. Drink, Mara, you've earned it with that lot tramping your deck." I heard Bram say: "The left bandage comes off the day after tomorrow." I heard Aldous say: "And then he's back on your pole, if you'll have him." I heard Wren say: "To the end of the searching." What I did: I said 'I'll have him, and gladly.' Then I drink and pass the jug to Wren. Then I said to Bram 'Light work first. Fares and lines.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the bench in the Lantern Inn common room by the hearth, with Aldous across the table from me. The air carried cider and pipe smoke. How I came into it: relieved, warm, cheerful.

What I witnessed: Tobin came down from the loft for the first time in two days and sat on the step inside the water door, where a patch of sun came in off the river. Wren sat on an upturned bucket drawing the slip. I heard Tobin say: "First sun I've had on my face in a week." I heard Wren say: "Hold still. I'm drawing the slip and you're in it." I heard Tobin say: "Then leave me out of it. Draw the boat." What I did: I said 'Five minutes in the sun, then back from the door.' Then I work tar into the seam of the Heron's bow board with my thumb. Then I said 'Sun's free. Take it while it's there.' What happened: I was crouched -- crouched by the slip with the tar pot warming on the step beside me. The air carried tar and sunlit river. How I came into it: content, watchful, gentle.

What I witnessed: A carter's load of split wood crossed west with his horse. The river was higher than in the morning and full of wood; a whole willow went by with its roots in the air. I heard the carter say: "That one would stove a boat in." I heard Wren say: "There's another behind it, low in the water. You can only see it when it rolls." What I did: I said 'I see it.' Then I hold the Heron upstream and let the willow pass ahead of the bow. Then I bring us onto the West Landing steps and set the plank, and the carter leads his horse off. Then I said 'Mind the wood going home. The river's in a temper.' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the West Landing steps with the brown river loud behind me. The air carried wet bark and horse. How I came into it: alert, careful, tired.

What I witnessed: Halfway back from the West Landing, running empty, a waterlogged log rolling just under the surface came down on us and struck the blade of the rudder oar. The oar wrenched sideways and the lashing that holds it to the stern post parted with a crack. Wren caught the loose oar before the river took it. At the boathouse Tobin came down to the slip to help. I heard Wren say: "I've got it -- it's still in the crutch, just." I heard Tobin say: "Tarred line's on the hook. I'll hold it square, you lash." What I did: I said 'Let the oar ride slack. I'll pole us in.' Then I pole the Heron into the boathouse slip without the rudder. Then I cut away the frayed lashing, soak new tarred line in the bucket, and re-lash the rudder oar to the stern post with Tobin holding it square: eight round turns, four frapping turns, the end seized, the way Petra taught me. Then I swing the oar through its arc twice to test it. Then I said 'That'll hold. A log gets one try at my oar, not two.' What happened: I was crouched -- crouched at the Heron's stern with tar on my hands and the new lashing hard under my palm. The air carried tar and river water. How I came into it: shaken, focused, satisfied.

inferences.text: I concluded that the old lashing had chafed thin where it crosses the stern post; a sound lashing would have let the log bend the blade, not part. I based that on: the cut ends of the old lashing are worn flat on one side.

turns.content: What I witnessed: The first crossing west carried a cart of empty barrels going back to the cooper upriver. The river had dropped in the night and run clearer. I heard Wren say: "It's not creaking anymore, the oar." I heard the carter say: "Cold enough for gloves this morning. Winter's coming down the river." What I did: I said 'New line. It'll creak again once it's learned the work.' Then I bring the bow round at midstream and feel the oar answer clean under my arm. Then I said 'Barrels stay chocked till we touch the steps.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the oar under my arm and my breath showing. The air carried cold river and barrel pitch. How I came into it: steady, satisfied, awake.

What I witnessed: I brought Ilse six eggs and a loaf. She was at the sexton's table with paper, ink and a list half written. I heard Ilse say: "The sexton says the sergeant asked him about the fire before they left. Asked him to stop telling people it was set, more like." I heard Ilse say: "I'm writing it all down: the notice, the fire, the men tramping through here. Then I'll stand before the council with it." I heard Ilse say: "You've always been the one who tells me straight, Mara. Read it and tell me if it's straight." What I did: I said 'Write it all. I'll read it when you're done.' Then I put the eggs and the loaf on the table. Then I take her inky hands in mine until they stop shaking. I did not answer the rest. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the sexton's table across from Ilse with her hands in mine and her list between us. The air carried ink, bread and cold ash from her shawl. How I came into it: guilty, loyal, sad.

inferences.text: I concluded that I cannot go on lying to Ilse. I have lied to her twice about Tobin: when she asked after a stranger in a blue coat and I said I hadn't seen anyone about the boathouse, and when I told her he was a cousin from downriver. I based that on: Ilse says: "You've always been the one who tells me straight, Mara."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Bram came to the market with us to carry, though his hands were still in bandages, and at the rope stall he haggled with the rope seller over a coil of tarred line like a man buying a horse. He caught my eye over the coil and grinned. I heard Bram say: "Two coppers less, or she buys at the chandler's upriver." I heard the rope seller say: "Tarred line's dear since the river went quiet at night." I heard Wren say: "We should keep a spare lashing aboard, after yesterday." What I did: I said 'Two coils. One for the locker on the Heron, one for the boathouse.' Then I pay what Bram got him down to. Then I said 'And a ball of marline for seizing.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the rope stall in the Market Square with two coils over my shoulder. The air carried hemp, tar and onions from the next stall. How I came into it: practical, amused, content.

What I witnessed: I met Oren on the West Landing at half past one, waiting at the steps with a handcart under wet sailcloth. He crossed east with us and leaned on the rail beside me at the stern while Wren took his fare. I heard Oren say: "Mara. I hear the sergeant's lot are three villages up the toll road by now." I heard Oren say: "That's a handsome new lashing on your oar." I heard Oren say: "Keep the green one trimmed. When the moon's thin and the river's down, I'll have work for you." I heard Wren say: "Two coppers for the cart, same as anyone." What I did: I said 'If the river's down.' Then I steer us across with the new lashing tight and quiet. Then I said 'Your cart's dripping on my deck.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with Oren's elbow on the rail beside mine and the East Landing coming up. The air carried wet sailcloth and lamp oil. How I came into it: wary, tempted, cool.

What I witnessed: When I came in, Tobin was standing back from the crack of the water door, white in the face. He had watched Oren's handcart come off the Heron at the steps. I heard Tobin say: "The man at your stern. The one who leaned on the rail. That was Oren Dask." I heard Tobin say: "I've seen him before. Not here. At night." Then Tobin climbed the ladder to the loft and pulled the hatch down. I heard Wren say: "Tobin, wait--" What I did: I said 'Where have you seen him?' Then I go to the foot of the ladder. Then I said up the ladder 'Tobin. Where?' Then I stand a long time with my hand on the third rung. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the foot of the loft ladder looking up at the shut hatch. The air carried tar and cold. How I came into it: alarmed, frustrated, worried.

What I witnessed: Tobin did not come down for supper. All evening I heard his boots cross the loft boards, turn, and cross again. I heard Wren say: "He hasn't eaten since noon." I heard Wren say: "Whatever it is, it's about Oren." What I did: I said 'Then it's about me as well. I'm the one who carries Oren's loads.' Then I fill a bowl and set it at the foot of the ladder. Then I said up through the hatch 'There's soup at the foot of the ladder. Come down when you want. I'm not going anywhere.' Then I bank the stove and sit by it. What happened: I was sitting -- sitting by the banked stove listening to the boards creak overhead. The air carried smoke and cooling soup. How I came into it: anxious, sleepless, tender.

What I witnessed: Bram came down to the steps with the left bandage off: new pink skin across his palm, and the old forge scar still white along the side of his left hand. The right was still wrapped. A dairy cart with four churns crossed west. I heard Bram say: "Left one's off. Look -- new skin right up to the old scar." I heard Bram say: "I can pole with the left. Let me take her off the steps." I heard the dairyman say: "Mind my churns, lad." What I did: I said 'One length of the pole, then rest it.' Then I take the rudder oar and let Bram set the pole and push us off. Then I said 'Good. Long push, short recover. Let the pole do the work.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with my hand on the oar, watching Bram's back as he poled. The air carried milk and cold river. How I came into it: pleased, protective, easy.

What I witnessed: I climbed the back stair of the Lantern Inn to Oren's workshop because he had sent word my money was waiting. The long room was warm from the solder pot, and a dozen lanterns with green glass hung along the back wall, more than I had ever seen in one place. I heard Oren say: "Your pay for the last crossing. I'd have brought it down, but the inn was crawling with blue coats." I heard Oren say: "Green glass is the hardest to get right. Too dark and nobody sees it; too light and everybody does." I heard Oren say: "When the moon's thin. Same as before." When I asked about the lanterns, I heard Oren say: "Fishermen. Fools. Poets. Everybody wants a little colour on the water." What I did: I said 'I said if the river's down.' Then I count the coins in my palm and close my fist on them. Then I said 'Who needs a dozen green lanterns, Oren?' Then I look along the row of them on the back wall. What happened: I was standing -- standing in Oren's workshop above the Lantern Inn with the coins in my fist and the green glass behind him. The air carried hot solder and lamp oil. How I came into it: wary, uneasy, curious.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he makes more green lanterns than any honest trade could want, and he does not care that I saw them. I based that on: a dozen green-glassed lanterns along his workshop wall, and Oren says: "Too dark and nobody sees it; too light and everybody does."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Ilse came down to the steps and asked to be taken along the bank to the mouth of the side channel, to see the mill once from the water. Wren came too. From the channel mouth the mill was a black shell, and the wheel stood with half its paddles burned to stubs. I heard Ilse say: "Hold her here. No closer. I only want to see it the way it looked the morning I came to it a bride, from the water." I heard Ilse say: "One night, and thirty years of that wheel are gone." I heard Wren say: "I drew it on the map the way it stood before. I won't draw it any other way." What I did: I said 'I'll hold her here as long as you want.' Then I set the pole into the channel bottom and hold the Heron steady against the current. Then I say nothing and let her look. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the pole braced, the mill's black shell up the channel and Ilse still at the bow. The air carried wet ash and reed. How I came into it: sorrowful, patient, tender.

What I witnessed: A farmer's red cow refused the plank at the West Landing and then refused to leave the Heron at the East Landing. Wren held a turnip under her nose while I leaned on her rump. Oren stood in the Lantern Inn's waterfront door, laughing at us. I heard the farmer say: "She's never liked water. She doesn't like anything." I heard Oren say: "You'll want a lantern on that cow, Mara, or she'll walk off the end of the landing." I heard Wren say: "Two more weeks of chaining and the marsh is done. The council gets its map by the end of the month." What I did: I said 'Lean into her with me, Wren. On three.' Then I set my shoulder to the cow and push until she clatters down the plank onto the landing. Then I said 'End of the month. Then what will you do with yourself?' What happened: I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with cow on my coat and Wren laughing beside me. The air carried cow and wet planks. How I came into it: amused, warm, wistful.

What I witnessed: When I took the green lantern down from its nail, Tobin came down the ladder at the sound and stopped on the bottom rung. I heard Tobin say: "Don't. Don't take that out again." I heard Tobin say: "Not like this. Let me tell it properly. After supper. Both of you." I heard Wren say: "We'll be here." What I did: I said 'I'm only fitting the wick. Nobody is crossing tonight.' Then I set the green lantern on the table, fit Oren's new wick and trim it low, and leave the lantern dark between us. Then I said 'After supper, then. All of it.' What happened: I was sitting -- sitting at the table with the dark green lantern in front of me and the wick trimmed. The air carried lamp oil and onions frying. How I came into it: tense, resolved, wary.

What I witnessed: After supper Tobin sat with his hands flat on the table on either side of the dark green lantern. I heard Tobin say: "Before I ran I stood the night watch on the council's grain stores. Some nights carts came for grain that was never written in the book. The men who loaded them hung green lanterns on the shafts, and the one who paid the watch to look away was Oren Dask." I heard Tobin say: "Those crossings of yours, with the green one at your bow -- that's where the grain goes. Stolen grain, out of the council's own stores, over your ferry in the dark." I heard Tobin say: "I took his coin twice. When the count came up short they needed a man to hang for it, and I ran. That's the part I never told you." I heard Wren say: "The council's own stores. That's why the bread's gone up." What I did: I said 'Every crossing? All three nights I hung that lantern at the bow?' Then I stand up and look down at the lantern. Then I said 'I never asked what I carried for him. I'll have it from Oren himself.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the table with my hand on the green lantern's cold handle. The air carried lamp oil and the stove going out. How I came into it: shocked, angry, ashamed.

inferences.text: I concluded that every load I carried for Oren under the green lantern was grain stolen out of the council's own stores -- the town's winter bread. I based that on: Tobin says: "Those crossings of yours, with the green one at your bow -- that's where the grain goes."

turns.content: What I witnessed: As I went out of the boathouse I heard Wren say: "Mara, it's gone eleven. Wait for morning." Her voice came from the doorway behind me, and I did not look back. The landing was dark and empty under the curfew, and the moored boats knocked together on the slack water. The Lantern Inn still had a light in its taproom. Inside, the innkeeper was stacking stools on the tables and one old carter sat over the last of his ale. I heard the innkeeper say: "If it's the lantern-maker you want, he's up in his workshop. He works late, that one." A line of lamplight showed at the top of the back stair. What I did: I walked straight from the boathouse along the landing to the Lantern Inn, with what Tobin had just told me about the grain going round and round in my head. Then I pushed the inn door open and said 'Is Oren upstairs?' Then I crossed the taproom to the foot of the back stair. What happened: I was standing inside the Lantern Inn at the foot of the back stair with one hand on the rail. The air carried spilled ale, pipe smoke and lamp oil. How I came into it: anger, resolve, dread.

What I witnessed: Oren was at his bench under two hanging lamps, soldering a pane of green glass into a lantern frame. Finished lanterns hung from the beams, green and plain. I heard Oren say: "Mara Vell, at this hour. Has the Heron sprung a plank?" When I told him what I knew, he set the iron down in its stand and wiped his fingers on a rag, slowly, and did not deny any of it. I heard Oren say: "That's a heavy thing to carry up a stair at night. Who handed it to you?" What I did: I climbed the back stair and opened the workshop door without knocking. Then I said 'I know what your green lanterns carry across, Oren. Grain. Out of the council's own stores.' Then I said 'Never mind who. I've crossed in the dark with your green light at my bow, and I want to know what I was showing the way for. That grain is what this town eats in February.' What happened: I was standing just inside the workshop door with his bench between us. The air carried hot solder, lamp oil and new tin. How I came into it: anger, resolve, disgust.

What I witnessed: Oren came round the bench and stood close, still smiling, his voice low and easy. I heard Oren say: "Here's how it is, Mara. You keep poling and keep quiet. The river doesn't care what's in a sack, and neither should you." I heard Oren say: "The council's men are looking hard at boats this month. A ferry pilot who's crossed after curfew with a green lamp at her bow would have a great deal to explain. I'd hate that for you." Then he went back to his bench and picked up the iron again, as if I had already gone. What I did: I said 'Is that a threat?' Then I said 'You'll get nothing more from me tonight.' Then I lifted the latch to go. What happened: I was standing in the workshop doorway with my hand on the latch and the dark stair behind me. The air carried solder smoke. How I came into it: anger, fear, shame.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he was not surprised that I knew, only curious who had told me. He has been expecting someone to find out, and he had his answer ready. I based that on: he set the iron down slowly, asked who had handed it to me, and told me to keep poling and keep quiet without denying a word of it.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren was sitting up by the stove with the lamp turned low and her map rolled on her knees. Tobin was halfway down the loft ladder, gripping the rungs, his face white in the lamplight. I heard Tobin say: "Did you tell him it was me? Mara, did you say my name?" I heard Wren say: "What did he say to you?" What I did: I said 'I didn't say your name. I didn't say anyone's.' Then I said 'He told me to keep poling and keep quiet. And he said the council's men are looking hard at boats, and I'd have a great deal to explain.' Then I barred the boathouse door and sat down on the bench with my boots still on. What happened: I was sitting on the bench by the stove with my back against the wall. The air carried stove smoke and river damp. How I came into it: tired, angry, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: he is more afraid of Oren than of the council's men. He asked whether I had said his name before he asked anything else. I based that on: Tobin coming halfway down the ladder and saying: "Did you tell him it was me? Mara, did you say my name?"

turns.content: What I witnessed: Mist lay so thick on the Aune that I could not see the West Landing until we were halfway over. Bram worked the bow pole with his hands still healing from the mill beam. A carter sat on the tail of his empty cart, bound for the toll road. Wren was aboard with her chain and satchel, dropping a sounding line over the side every twenty strokes and calling out the depths. I heard Bram say: "You look like you never went to bed, Mara." Then Wren came back to the stern beside me. I heard Wren say: "Seven feet here. Will he do anything, do you think?" What I did: I said 'I went late. That's all.' Then I said to Wren, low, 'He'll smile at me today. That's what worries me.' Then I steered us through the mist with the long rudder oar while Bram poled. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in the middle of the river. The air carried mist, cold mud and wet rope. How I came into it: tired, uneasy, watchful.

What I witnessed: At the West Landing the mist was lifting off the reeds. Up the side channel the black shell of the old mill showed against the grey, its wheel stopped and charred. Wren shouldered her chain to go. I heard Wren say: "The eastern reed beds today. Then the reaches along the toll road, and after that it's all ink." Two women with baskets of eggs and a goatherd with six goats were waiting to cross for market. One goat jumped the rail as they loaded, and Bram caught it by the horn and hauled it back aboard. I heard the goatherd say: "Mind his feet, lad, he kicks." What I did: I said to Wren 'Be back at the landing before the bell.' Then I took the fares, counted the goats twice and tied the gate across. What happened: I was standing at the mooring post on the West Landing with the bow rope in my hand. The air carried goat, wet reeds and old smoke from the mill. How I came into it: tired, steady, sad.

What I witnessed: Halfway back across, the goats crowded to the downstream rail and the Heron listed a hand's width. The egg women held their baskets in their laps. I heard one of the egg women say: "Flour's dear this autumn. They say the council granary's running short." I heard Bram say: "Do you want them moved, Mara?" Bram pushed the goats back to the middle with his knees. What I did: I said 'Move them amidships, and keep them there.' Then I leaned on the rudder oar to bring the bow up into the current and held her steady until the list came off. Then I thought of the grain going over under green lanterns, and said nothing to the egg women. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with the East Landing coming up out of the mist. The air carried goat and river water. How I came into it: tired, angry, quiet.

inferences.text: I concluded that the grain going over under Oren's green lanterns is why flour is dear in Saltmere this autumn, and that the whole town is paying for those crossings, my own among them. I based that on: an egg woman on the ferry saying: "Flour's dear this autumn. They say the council granary's running short."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Aldous called me into the dock office as I tied up. A new notice was pinned beside the tide board: a deserter, a thin young man last seen in a torn blue coat, with a reward for word of him. I heard Aldous say: "The council's men brought that round at first light. They're asking after a deserter again, and they want a list from me of every boat that moves after dusk." I heard Aldous say: "You've crossed late a few times this month, Mara. I've not written it down. I'd like not to have to." He did not look up from his tally book while he said it. What I did: I said 'I cross when people need crossing, Aldous. You know that.' Then I read the notice through twice and kept my face still. Then I said 'I'll keep to daylight for now.' What happened: I was standing by the dock office door with my hat in my hands. The air carried ink, tar and the wet wool of my coat. How I came into it: wary, tired, guilty.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Aldous: he knows about my night crossings and has kept them out of his books, and he is warning me that he cannot go on doing it with the council's men asking for lists. I based that on: Aldous saying: "You've crossed late a few times this month, Mara. I've not written it down. I'd like not to have to."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The chapel sexton rode across with a handcart of cabbages for the chapel house, sitting on the cart's shaft. The sun had burned the mist off and the river lay brown and flat. Bram poled at the bow. I heard the sexton say: "Ilse was asking after you this morning, Mara. She sat up half the night again. She can't settle since the mill." I heard Bram say: "My father says she's stopped eating her supper." What I did: I said 'I'll take her something at midday.' Then I said 'Sit still on that shaft or you'll have the cabbages in the river.' Then I steered us across for the East Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with the town side close. The air carried cabbage, river weed and warm planking. How I came into it: tired, worried, fond.

What I witnessed: Ilse was at the table in the chapel house kitchen with her shawl on, though the stove was lit. Her eyes were red at the rims. She took the loaf and the smoked fish from me and set them down without looking at them. I heard Ilse say: "I couldn't sleep again last night. I was at the window gone eleven, and I saw somebody on the landing walking toward the Lantern Inn, fast, the way you walk when you're angry. Was that you, Mara? Where were you last night?" She watched my face while she waited. What I did: I lied to Ilse. I said 'Not me. I was asleep in the boathouse by ten. The Heron wore me out yesterday.' Then I said 'Eat the fish while it's fresh.' Then I sat down across from her and looked at the table instead of at her. It was a plain lie about where I had been the night before, and I told it to her face. What happened: I was sitting at Ilse's table in the chapel house with my hands around a cup I did not drink. The air carried woodsmoke and stale bread. How I came into it: guilt, tenderness, fear.

What I witnessed: We carried a cart of firewood and two drovers over to the West Landing. The wind had got up from the south and put a chop on the water. I heard Bram say: "You've not said a word since the chapel house, Mara. Is Ilse worse?" I heard one of the drovers say: "Hold her steady, pilot, the load's shifting." What I did: I said 'Ilse's tired. So am I.' Then I braced the rudder oar against the chop and called to Bram to lean on the downstream pole. Then I counted it up while I steered. That is three lies I have told Ilse now. The first was when she asked about a stranger in a blue coat and I said I'd seen no one around the boathouse. The second was that Tobin is my cousin from downriver. The third was today, about last night. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with both hands on the rudder oar. The air carried wet bark and spray. How I came into it: guilt, weariness, resolve.

inferences.text: I concluded that lying to Ilse comes easier each time, and that frightens me more than Oren or the council's men do. I based that on: today's lie came out of me without a stumble, and I only felt it an hour later, out on the river with the chop under us.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I met Oren on the West Landing. He came down the toll road behind a carter's mule with a crate on his shoulder and set it on the planks as if nothing had passed between us last night. I heard Oren say: "Afternoon, Mara. One for the town side, and mind the crate. It's all green glass, and it cost me dear." Bram lifted the crate aboard, and Oren thanked him by name and pressed a copper into his hand. Wren came out of the reeds a little after with mud to the knees and her chain over her shoulder, and Oren lifted his hat to her. I heard Wren say: "The eastern reed beds are done, Mara. Only the reaches by the toll road left to chain." What I did: I said to Oren 'The fare's the same as anybody's.' Then I held out my hand for his coin and did not smile. Then I said to Wren 'Get aboard before you sink.' What happened: I was standing at the Heron's gate on the West Landing with Oren's coin shut in my fist. The air carried mule, marsh mud and the cold coming off the water. How I came into it: anger, wariness, contempt.

What I witnessed: Oren sat on his crate amidships with his hat tipped back and talked to Wren the whole way over. I heard Oren say: "A surveyor out in the marsh at dusk wants a lantern that won't blow out. Tin hood, a deep chimney, and a green pane on the side. Green carries in mist, where a plain flame only glares." I heard Wren say: "I'm mostly out of the reeds before dusk." I heard Oren say: "Lovely evening for poling, Mara." Bram looked from him to me and kept his eyes on his pole after that. What I did: I said nothing to Oren the whole crossing. Then I said to Wren, low, while he was turned away, 'Don't buy a lantern from him.' Then I steered wide of the moored barges toward the East Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in the middle of the river with the town side coming close. The air carried tar and the first cold of evening. How I came into it: anger, contempt, unease.

What I witnessed: Rain was drumming on the boathouse roof before light. Tobin came down the loft ladder for bread while the door was still barred, and ate standing by the stove. I heard Tobin say: "I should go, Mara. Up the toll road tonight, before Oren works out who told you. I've brought this on your house." I heard Wren say: "The council's men are on the toll road day and night. You'd not get a mile." Wren was cutting bread at the table with her map weighted flat under the teapot. What I did: I said 'Wren's right. You stay in the loft until I say different.' Then I said 'Oren doesn't know it was you. He knows somebody talked, and that's all he knows.' Then I put the last of the cheese in Tobin's hand. What happened: I was standing by the stove in the boathouse with the kettle starting to sing. The air carried rain, woodsmoke and bread. How I came into it: protective, tired, stubborn.

What I witnessed: Wren had gone out to the pump with the buckets, and Tobin had gone back up to the loft. The green lantern was where I had left it after my last night crossing, its glass dull with old soot. Overhead the loft boards creaked once as Tobin settled. What I did: I picked up the green lantern and turned it over in my hands. Then I carried it out to the slipway and held it over the water, meaning to drop it in the Aune. Then I did not. I brought it back inside, wrapped it in a piece of sacking and put it in the chest under the loft ladder, unlit, with the oil still in it. Then I said aloud to nobody 'Not yet.' What happened: I was kneeling by the chest under the loft ladder with both hands flat on the shut lid. The air carried lamp oil and wet sacking. How I came into it: anger, doubt, shame.

inferences.text: I concluded that dropping the green lantern in the river would tell Oren I had broken with him, while hiding it tells nobody anything, and I am not ready to tell him that yet. I based that on: I stood on the slipway holding it over the water and could not make my hand let go.

turns.content: What I witnessed: The rain came down steady and the river was pocked all over. We carried a farmer and a pig in a slatted crate to the West Landing, and the pig screamed the whole way.
