Bram's oilskin was too short for him and the rain ran off it into his boots. I heard Bram say: "Why'd you not give Oren the time of day yesterday? He gave me a copper extra for lifting that crate." I heard the farmer say: "Pig's never been on water. He'll settle." What I did: I said 'Keep his copper, Bram. But don't carry anything else for him.' Then I said 'Lean on your pole. The current runs stronger in the rain.' Then I kept us straight on the line with the rudder oar. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in the middle of the river with rain running off my hat brim. The air carried rain, pig and wet oilskin. How I came into it: irritable, wet, careful.

What I witnessed: The market was half empty in the rain and the sellers had their awnings down low. Wren was at the stationer's stall buying ink and a pen-knife for her fair copy. Two of the council's men in oiled capes were nailing a fresh notice to the market cross, and one of them stopped me. I heard the council man say: "Ferry pilot, isn't it? We're after a deserter, a thin young man last seen in a blue coat. If he's crossed this river, he's crossed it on your boat." I heard Wren say: "She crosses fifty people a day. She can't know every face." What I did: I said 'I take fares, not names. If I see a blue coat I'll look twice.' Then I bought lamp oil, a coil of tarred line and salt from the stalls. Then I walked Wren out of the square by the chapel lane. What happened: I was standing under the chapel wall at the edge of the market square with the oil jar under my arm. The air carried rain on stone and wet canvas. How I came into it: wary, steady, protective.

What I witnessed: The rain came down harder and Wren pulled me into the Lantern Inn to wait it out. I met Oren at the inn. He was coming down the back stair with a lantern in each hand for a customer, and he stopped at our table as easy as you please. I heard Oren say: "Mara, Wren, in out of the wet. Hot cider's on me." Then he turned to Wren. I heard Oren say: "I've a marsh lantern half made for you. Tin hood, green side-pane. You'll not lose your way in the reeds with it." I heard Wren say: "That's kind, but I'm nearly done with the reeds." He paid for the cider at the bar before I could stop him. What I did: I said 'We'll pay for our own.' Then I put my coins on the table and pushed his cider back across to him. Then I sat with my back to the wall where I could see the stair. What happened: I was sitting at a table in the Lantern Inn's taproom with wet sleeves and the rain loud on the windows. The air carried hot cider, wet wool and pipe smoke. How I came into it: anger, wariness, pride.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: he wants Wren to carry one of his green-paned lanterns into the marsh, so that his light is in her hands as well as mine. I based that on: Oren telling Wren in the inn: "I've a marsh lantern half made for you. Tin hood, green side-pane."

turns.content: What I witnessed: The rain eased to a drizzle after noon. We carried a family with a handcart of firewood and a crate of hens back from the West Landing, and Wren rode with us, taking soundings with her weighted line. Bram poled at the bow. A grain barge lay moored below the dock with its hatches under tarpaulin and nobody aboard. I heard the mother say: "We'd have been over yesterday, but the toll road was stopped. The council's men were turning out every cart." I heard Wren say: "Nine feet off the barge's bow. Deep for this side." What I did: I said 'Keep the hens out of the wet if you can.' Then I looked a long while at the covered barge as we passed it. Since Tobin told me about the grain, I cannot look at a covered hatch without wondering what is under it. Then I set us on a long slant for the East Landing to spare Bram's hands. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river, steering for the town side. The air carried drizzle, hens and wet firewood. How I came into it: thoughtful, wary, tired.

What I witnessed: The rain stopped, and Wren wanted the old names of the channels before she inked them, so I left Bram minding the Heron at the West Landing and walked the reed path with her. She unrolled a corner of the map on a dry tussock. I heard Wren say: "The council's old map calls them all just 'channel'. What do the river people call them?" The reeds were brown and beaten flat by the rain, and a heron got up out of the shallows ahead of us. What I did: I said 'That's the Eel Cut. The bend past it is Widow's Reach, and the narrow one that silts up every spring is Petra's Gut. Petra named it herself, because she ran aground in it every spring for thirty years.' Then I pointed out each one with a reed stem, and Wren wrote the names in pencil along the lines. What happened: I was standing on the reed path in the marsh with my boots sunk to the ankle. The air carried wet reeds, mud and cold water. How I came into it: fond, calm, sad.

What I witnessed: Back at the West Landing the light was going yellow and low. Bram had the Heron swept out and the poles stacked. The curfew bell began from the town side, slow and flat across the water. I heard Bram say: "That's the bell, Mara. Last crossing." I heard Wren say: "Three names I didn't have this morning. The map's nearly whole now." A goatherd came running down the bank with two kids under his arms, shouting for us to wait. What I did: I said 'Get aboard, and quick about it.' Then I held the gate for the goatherd and his kids. Then I put Wren's map case in the dry locker under the stern seat. What happened: I was standing at the Heron's gate on the West Landing with one hand on the rope as the bell finished. The air carried evening cold and goat. How I came into it: tired, content, watchful.

What I witnessed: After supper, with the door barred and the shutters closed, Tobin came down from the loft and sat mending the torn seine by the stove. Wren had her map spread on the table under the lamp, inking in the names I gave her. I heard Tobin say: "He'll want to know who told you. Oren's patient. He'll ask round quiet, and he'll wait." I heard Wren say: "Then nobody tells him anything. That's not hard." Tobin worked the net needle without looking up. What I did: I said 'He can ask all he likes. Nobody comes up that ladder but us.' Then I sat down across from Tobin and took the other end of the seine to hold the mesh taut for him. Then I said 'Mind the knots. They're Petra's.' What happened: I was sitting by the stove in the boathouse with a fold of wet net across my knees. The air carried stove smoke, tar and ink. How I came into it: tired, protective, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: he knows Oren's ways better than he has told us. He talks of Oren's patience and how he asks round quiet, like someone who has watched him work. I based that on: Tobin saying by the stove: "He'll want to know who told you. Oren's patient. He'll ask round quiet, and he'll wait."

turns.content: What I witnessed: A cold clear morning, with geese going south over the river in long lines. The chapel sexton rode the first crossing west with a letter for a farm on the toll road. Bram poled at the bow. I heard the sexton say: "Ilse's going to petition the council against the eviction. She says Councillor Hesk can sign what he likes, the mill was a Harrow mill before he was born." I heard Bram say: "My father says nobody's ever won a petition against Hesk." What I did: I said 'Then Ilse can be the first.' Then I watched the geese go over for a while. Then I steered us in toward the West Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with my breath showing in the cold. The air carried cold river water. How I came into it: hopeful, cold, stubborn.

What I witnessed: Four of the council's men came down the East Landing with staves and went through every boat tied there, the Heron first. They lifted the stern seat, opened the lockers and prodded the bilge with a stave. Aldous stood by with his tally book and said nothing. Bram stood at the bow with his fists closed. Wren came down from the boathouse to watch, with ink still on her fingers. I heard one of the council's men say: "There's a deserter on this river somewhere, and he didn't swim across it." Oren came down from the inn with two new lanterns on a pole and handed them to the men. I heard Oren say: "Your new lanterns, gentlemen, as ordered. Plain glass, just as the council likes." He nodded to me pleasantly. What I did: I said 'Mind how you go in my lockers. Those are my good ropes.' Then I stood on the planks with my arms folded while they searched, and did not once look toward the boathouse. Then I said to Bram 'Stay where you are.' What happened: I was standing on the East Landing beside the Heron's bow post as the council's men climbed out of her. The air carried wet planks and lamp oil. How I came into it: fear, anger, steadiness.

inferences.text: I concluded that Oren sells lanterns to the same council men who watch the river for green lights, and that he likes standing beside them while they search my boat. I based that on: Oren handing two new lanterns to the council's men in the middle of the search, saying: "Plain glass, just as the council likes," and nodding to me.

turns.content: What I witnessed: When the council's men had gone off down the landing, Wren and I climbed the loft ladder. Tobin was crouched behind the net-bales in the dark with his knees drawn up, and he did not move until he heard my voice. I heard Tobin say: "I heard them. Every stave on every plank. Did they come to the door?" I heard Wren say: "They searched the boats and went. They never looked at the house." What I did: I said 'It's us, Tobin. They searched the landing, not the boathouse. They've gone on toward the dock office.' Then I sat down on the loft boards beside the net-bales where he could see me in the light from the gable slit. Then I said 'Stay up here today. No smoke, no noise. I'll bring your dinner up.' What happened: I was sitting on the boards in the boathouse loft beside the net-bales. The air carried dust, old nets and tar. How I came into it: relieved, protective, tired.

What I witnessed: Ilse came down to the landing with her shawl over her head and tried to pay her fare like a stranger, which she has never done. She sat on the bench amidships and looked upriver toward the side channel the whole way across. I heard Ilse say: "I'm going to look at it. Somebody has to, before Hesk's men come and pull the walls down." I heard Ilse say: "The sexton said the fire was set. I knew it before he said it. Hesk wanted the land, and now there's nothing standing in his way." Bram kept his eyes on his pole. What I did: I said 'Put your money away, Ilse. You've never paid me and you're not starting now.' Then I said 'I'll wait at the West Landing as long as you need.' Then I steered for the West Landing and did not hurry. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river, with Ilse's coin still on the bench where I had pushed it back to her. The air carried cold water and woodsmoke from the town. How I came into it: sorrow, anger, tenderness.

What I witnessed: From the West Landing I could see Ilse small and far off up the side channel, standing on the bank by the mill race and looking at the black beams. She did not go in. Bram and I ate bread and cheese on the gate rail while we waited. I heard Bram say: "Should one of us go up after her?" After an hour she came back down the bank with her hem wet from the race and nothing in her hands. I heard Ilse say: "I couldn't go in, Mara. I stood at the door and I couldn't put a foot over it." What I did: I said to Bram 'No. Let her be.' Then I put my coat round Ilse's shoulders and handed her down into the Heron. Then I said 'Sit by me at the stern.' What happened: I was standing at the Heron's gate on the West Landing with Ilse's elbow in my hand. The air carried old wet ash and reeds. How I came into it: sad, patient, worried.

What I witnessed: Ilse sat by me at the stern going back, with my coat round her shoulders. Halfway over she put her hand on my arm. I heard Ilse say: "Thirty-one winters since you pulled me out of the ice, Mara. You'd tell me if something was wrong with you, wouldn't you? You've been somewhere else all week." I heard Bram say: "Barge coming down, Mara." What I did: I said 'I'd tell you what I could, Ilse.' Then I said 'Hold on now. There's a barge.' Then I leaned on the rudder oar and took us across the barge's wake bow-on. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with the barge's wash slapping the side. Ilse had taken her hand back and was looking at the water. The air carried cold spray. How I came into it: guilt, love, unease.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse: she knows I am keeping something from her, and she is waiting for me to bring it to her myself rather than catching me out in it. I based that on: Ilse saying: "You've been somewhere else all week," and then taking her hand back and looking at the water when I answered.

turns.content: What I witnessed: Wren was in the dock office copying the old river chart off Aldous's wall for the depths below the landing. Aldous had a council paper on his desk, a ruled list headed After Dusk, with columns for boat, pilot and passengers. I heard Aldous say: "Councillor Hesk's clerk sent this. Every crossing after the bell, written down and signed for, and handed over at the end of every week." I heard Aldous say: "And the council's ordered a dozen new lanterns for the watch from Oren Dask. Plain glass. Funny thing to buy from him, I'd have said." I heard Wren say: "He's busy, then." What I did: I said 'Write mine down as none, Aldous. I'm keeping to daylight.' Then I signed my name at the top of the empty column. Then I looked at the chart over Wren's shoulder and showed her where it was wrong about the shoal below the chapel. What happened: I was standing at Aldous's desk in the dock office with the pen still in my hand. The air carried ink, tar and a cold stove. How I came into it: wary, tired, determined.

What I witnessed: The last crossing came in with a carter and an empty wagon, and the curfew bell began as we tied up. Lamps were being lit along the landing, and one of the new plain-glass lanterns hung outside the dock office. Wren came down to meet me with the chart she had copied rolled under her arm. I heard Wren say: "Your shoal was right. Aldous's chart is twenty years out of date." Bram coiled the bow line and went off up the landing toward the dock office, holding his hands away from his sides the way he does when they ache. I heard Bram say: "Night, Mara. Night, Wren." What I did: I said 'Night, Bram. Soak those hands.' Then I made the Heron fast fore and aft and chained the pole rack. Then I said to Wren 'Supper. I'm done with people for today.' What happened: I was standing on the East Landing beside the Heron's stern post as the bell stopped. The air carried lamp smoke and cold river water. How I came into it: tired, relieved, quiet.

What I witnessed: With the shutters closed, Wren unrolled the marsh map on the table for Tobin to see. Nearly every channel was on it now, the reed beds hatched in ink and the names I gave her lettered along the water. Tobin held the lamp close and looked at it a long time. I heard Tobin say: "You've drawn the back cuts too. The ones behind the mill channel." I heard Wren say: "I've drawn everything that holds water. That's the job." Tobin put the lamp down and went back to his net without saying any more. What I did: I said 'Those cuts were Petra's eel grounds. Nobody uses them but eels.' Then I looked at the back cuts on the map, and at Tobin's face, and said nothing else. Then I put more wood in the stove. What happened: I was standing by the table in the boathouse with the map lit under the lamp. The air carried ink, stove smoke and fish. How I came into it: uneasy, curious, tired.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin: the back cuts behind the mill channel mean something to him, and I think the green-lantern boats use them. I based that on: Tobin holding the lamp close over Wren's map and saying: "You've drawn the back cuts too. The ones behind the mill channel," and then going quiet.

turns.content: What I witnessed: I met Oren on the East Landing in the grey before the first crossing. He came down with a tin of lamp oil and a coil of new wick in his hand. Bram was untying the bow line and Wren was stowing her chain aboard. I heard Oren say: "You'll be wanting a new wick for the green one, then. The old one smokes, I'd guess, if you've been keeping it in the dark." I heard Oren say: "No charge. A lantern-maker looks after his lanterns." When I did not take them, he set the tin and the wick on the mooring post and walked back up toward the inn. What I did: I said 'Keep your wick, Oren. I've no use for it.' Then I said 'Bram, cast off.' Then I left the tin where it sat on the post. What happened: I was standing at the Heron's gate on the East Landing with the bow line in my hand and Oren's tin still on the post. The air carried cold fog and lamp oil. How I came into it: anger, unease, contempt.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren: the wick was not a gift. It was a reminder that the green lantern is his, that I have used it, and that he can speak of it in front of Bram whenever he likes. I based that on: Oren saying on the landing, with Bram standing by: "You'll be wanting a new wick for the green one, then."

turns.content: What I witnessed: Halfway across, Wren came back to the stern with her collar up against the fog. Bram was at the bow and could not hear us over the water. I heard Wren say: "He said that about the green one in front of Bram on purpose." I heard Wren say: "He's reminding you that you're tied to him. That's all that was." The fog was thinning off the reeds on the west side. What I did: I said 'I know what he's doing. He gave me that lantern, and he wants me never to forget it.' Then I said 'Bram doesn't need to know any of it, so don't tell him.' Then I set the rudder oar over and brought us round the shoal. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with Wren beside me. The air carried fog and wet wool. How I came into it: tense, tired, grateful.

What I witnessed: Wren needed her last bearings from the milestone on the toll road, so I left Bram with the Heron at the West Landing and carried her chain up the road. Carts were coming down toward the ferry with turnips and firewood, and a council man at the toll gate was looking under every tarpaulin. Wren set her compass on the milestone and sighted back across the river on the chapel tower. I heard Wren say: "Chapel tower, eighty-one degrees. Mill chimney, forty. That's the last of the chain-work, Mara. Everything after this is ink." The council man turned to a carter. I heard the council man say: "Lift that sack. And that one. All of them." What I did: I said 'Petra would have liked your map. She hated the council's.' Then I held the chain end on the milestone while Wren wrote. Then I watched the council man lift sacks at the toll gate until Wren was done. What happened: I was standing on the toll road beside the milestone with the chain over my shoulder. The air carried cart dust and wet grass. How I came into it: calm, fond, watchful.

What I witnessed: Back at the West Landing there was a lull, with nobody on the road. Bram sat on the gate rail picking at the new pink skin on his palms. The old forge scar on his left hand showed white beside the new burn marks. I heard Bram say: "The forge one doesn't hurt anymore. This one itches like fury." I heard Bram say: "My uncle upriver used to say a smith's not a smith till he's been burned twice. I'm a ferry hand burned twice." Wren sat on the bank with her notebook, working her sums. What I did: I said 'Stop picking at it, or it'll scar worse than the forge one.' Then I said 'You're a good hand, Bram, burned or not.' Then I gave him the salve tin from the stern locker. What happened: I was sitting on the gate rail of the Heron at the West Landing beside Bram in the thin sun. The air carried warm tar and reeds. How I came into it: fond, easy, tired.

What I witnessed: We carried Wren back, along with a woman going up to the chapel with a basket of apples for the Drowned Saint and a carter with a calf tied in his cart. Bram poled at the bow. The calf bawled until Wren gave it her fingers to suck. I heard the woman say: "They say the deserter's out in the reed marsh, living on eels. My son's seen smoke out there." I heard the carter say: "They say a lot of things. If he's any sense he's halfway to the sea by now." What I did: I said 'There's always smoke in the marsh in autumn. The reed cutters smoke their eels.' Then I took an apple from the woman for her fare when she offered it. Then I kept us on the line for the East Landing. What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river, eating the apple. The air carried apples, calf and river water. How I came into it: easy, wary, amused.

What I witnessed: I went up to the chapel of the Drowned Saint between crossings to light a candle for Petra, as I do at the turn of every season. Ilse was at the side table under the window with the sexton, a sheet of paper in front of her and a pen in her hand. I heard Ilse say: "It's my petition to the council against Hesk's notice. The sexton says forty names might make them read it. I have eleven." I heard Ilse say: "Will you put yours to it, Mara? You don't have to stand before the council. Just your name." What I did: I said 'Give me the pen.' Then I signed my name under the eleven, in the big letters Petra taught me. Then I lit the candle for Petra at the Saint's feet and stood a while. Then I said 'I'll ask my passengers. You'll have your forty.' What happened: I was standing before the Drowned Saint in the chapel with the candle burning and Ilse behind me. The air carried candle wax, cold stone and damp. How I came into it: loyal, quiet, hopeful.

inferences.text: I concluded that Ilse is putting all her grief into the petition, because it is the one thing left that she can do with her own hands. I based that on: Ilse at the chapel table with her pen, saying: "It's my petition to the council against Hesk's notice. The sexton says forty names might make them read it. I have eleven."

turns.content: What I witnessed: On the afternoon crossings I asked every passenger whether they would put their name to Ilse's petition at the chapel, and Wren rode with us writing down the ones who said yes. A drover said he would, and two women from the West Landing said they would go up on market day. I heard the drover say: "Hesk's notice on a widow's mill, after a fire like that? I'll sign it twice." I heard Bram say: "My father can't sign, being dockmaster. But he says he'll not stop anyone who does." I heard Wren say: "That's seven promised today." What I did: I said 'Seven, and Ilse's eleven, and mine. That's nineteen.' Then I chalked the count on the stern board. Then I said to Bram 'Tell your father I understand.' What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with chalk on my fingers. The air carried a cold wind off the marsh. How I came into it: hopeful, busy, tired.

What I witnessed: Supper was eel stew and the last of the bread. Tobin came down and ate with us at the table, and Wren had the map pinned flat on the wall where the stove would dry the ink. I heard Tobin say: "I'd sign Ilse's petition, if they'd take the name of a man the council wants." I heard Wren say: "Don't joke about that, Tobin." I heard Tobin say: "I'm not joking. I'm saying I would if I could." He wiped his bowl with his bread and carried the bowls to the bucket to wash. What I did: I said 'Your name stays off every paper in Saltmere, Tobin. That's how you stay safe.' Then I said 'You can wash the pot as well, since you're up.' Then I sat back and looked at Wren's map on the wall with the reed beds inked in. What happened: I was sitting at the boathouse table with my boots off and my feet to the stove. The air carried eel stew, ink and woodsmoke. How I came into it: warm, worried, tired.

What I witnessed: Tobin had gone up to the loft, and I could hear him turning over on the boards above us. Wren sat by the stove with her knees drawn up, cleaning her pens. I heard Wren say: "How did you meet Oren, Mara? Tell it from the start." What I did: I said 'There's not much to it. It was at the East Landing, at dusk. My lamp fell and smashed on the planks. A man stepped out of the crowd holding up a lantern with green glass in it, and the first thing he ever said to me was "You'll be wanting the green one, then." Then he told me his name, Oren Dask. I had heard the name once before, from Aldous at the dock office, when he was telling me about the curfew.' Then I said 'I took his lantern. I should have let my lamp lie broken and walked home in the dark.' Then I put another log in the stove. What happened: I was sitting by the stove in the boathouse with the stove door open. The air carried woodsmoke and pen ink. How I came into it: rueful, tired, quiet.

inferences.text: I concluded that Oren had me picked out that first evening, and was standing ready with the green lantern before my lamp ever hit the planks. I based that on: remembering, as I told it to Wren, how quickly he stepped out of the crowd holding it up, and that his very first words to me were already about the green one.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Wren was at the table under the window with a blank marsh sheet pinned flat at each corner and the ink pot open. I heard Wren say: "Two sheets left. The channels behind the toll road, and the eel weirs below the willows. Then it's only lettering." I saw Tobin come halfway down the loft ladder and stop where the window light does not reach. I heard Tobin say: "Carts on the landing road already. I counted four from the gable slit."
What I did: I said 'Then stay on the ladder till they're past. Porridge first, maps after.' Then I rake out the stove, set the pot on and stir in the last of the oats. Then I said 'Wren, the weirs flood at the top of the tide. Measure them before ten or you'll be wading.' Then I carry a bowl to the foot of the ladder so Tobin does not have to cross the window.
What happened: I was standing at the stove with the spoon in my hand and the oats thickening. The air carried oat steam and wet mist coming under the door.
How I came into it: tired, watchful, steady.

What I witnessed: Bram was waiting on the East Landing with his pole over his shoulder; the new skin on his palms from the night of the fire had nearly closed. Two carters drove a cart of turnips up the ramp, and a woman with a basket of hens came after it. Wren sat on the rail with the surveyor's chain coiled and the satchel between both boots. I heard Bram say: "The council's men were in the dock office at first light. Da says they asked after a man in a blue coat again." I heard Wren say: "Again? That's three times this week."
What I did: I said 'They can ask the river. Bow pole, Bram, and keep the turnips off my feet.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and bring the Heron's head round into the current. Then I count the fares into the tin: two carters, one cart, one woman, six hens. Then I said 'Wren rides free. The council's paying for that map, not me.'
What happened: I was standing at the stern with both hands on the rudder oar and the East Landing falling behind us. The air carried mist off the water and wet turnip.
How I came into it: wary, dry, alert.

What I witnessed: The carters led the turnip cart off the ramp and up the toll road. Wren stepped ashore, shouldered the chain and set off along the reed path toward the channels behind the toll road. Past the reeds I could see the mill's black chimney on its side channel and the wheel standing still. A goatherd was waiting at the head of the ramp with eleven goats on a rope line. I heard the goatherd say: "Eleven head to the East Landing. What's your price for goats that won't stand still?" I heard Bram say: "Same as for goats that will."
What I did: I said 'A copper a head, and you hold the billy yourself.' Then I watch Wren until the reeds close over the satchel. Then I said 'Bram, rope off the downstream rail. Goats run to the low side when the deck tilts.' Then I take the goatherd's coppers and drop them in the tin.
What happened: I was standing at the head of the West Landing ramp with the fare tin under my arm. The air carried the sour smell of old char from across the reeds.
How I came into it: steady, wry, tired.

What I witnessed: Halfway across, the billy goat put its forefeet up on the rudder platform and Bram hauled it down by the horns. At the East Landing I saw Aldous at the top of the ramp in his dock coat with the tally board under his arm. I heard Aldous say: "Mara. Oren Dask left word for you last night. He wants you at the Lantern Inn tomorrow, after the noon crossing." I saw Aldous set his mouth tight on the name. I heard Aldous say: "He didn't say what for. He never does. And the council's men have put a reward on that deserter. It's nailed up in the market." I saw Bram look at his father and then at me.
What I did: I said 'Tell him I heard. Nothing more than that.' Then I hold the ramp chain while the goats go off in a heap. Then I chalk the crossing on Aldous's tally board with the chalk on its string.
What happened: I was standing at the foot of the East Landing ramp with the chalk still in my fingers. The air carried goat and wet planking.
How I came into it: wary, irritated, tired.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Aldous Toller: he does not like carrying Oren's word and wanted me to see that he does not. I based that on: Aldous passing on Oren Dask's message with his mouth set tight, adding that Oren never says what for, and Bram looking from his father to me.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: A new notice was nailed to the post by the market well with the council's seal in red wax at the foot. It read: "Tobin Reyes, deserter, about twenty-eight years, thin, last seen in a blue coat. Ten silver for word of him at the council house." I heard a fishwife at the next stall say: "Ten silver. My man would sell his own brother for four." I heard the bread seller say: "They say Councillor Hesk wants the widow's mill land cleared before winter. Poor Ilse Harrow, and her mill not cold yet."
What I did: I said 'Two loaves, the dark ones.' Then I pay the bread seller and put the loaves in my sack. Then I buy a flask of lamp oil and a hank of tarred twine at the chandler's stall. Then I read the notice once more and walk away from it at the same pace as before.
What happened: I was walking out of the Market Square toward the waterfront with the sack over my shoulder. The air carried fish brine and warm bread.
How I came into it: cold, careful, angry.

inferences.text: I concluded that the reward puts a price on Tobin that any passenger who ever glanced up at my loft could try to collect. I based that on: the notice by the market well offering ten silver for word of Tobin Reyes, deserter, last seen in a blue coat.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Wren came in at dusk with marsh mud to the knees and laid the toll-road sheet on the table with every channel inked. I heard Wren say: "The toll-road sheet's done. One left, the weirs." I saw Tobin on the bottom rung of the loft ladder with a net across his knees, mending a tear.
What I did: I said 'There's a notice by the market well with your name on it, Tobin, and your coat. Ten silver. The coat stays in the loft.' Then I set the loaves and the oil on the shelf. Then I said 'And Oren wants me at the Lantern Inn tomorrow after the noon crossing. He sent word through Aldous.' Then I cut the bread and give Tobin the heel.
What happened: I heard Tobin say: "Ten silver, is it? I'm worth more than I thought." I heard Wren say: "What does Oren want with you?" I said nothing to that. I was sitting at the table across from Wren with the bread knife in my hand. The air carried lamp oil and river damp.
How I came into it: tired, protective, uneasy.

What I witnessed: A squall came down the Aune at first light and rain drove flat across the deck. Wren had come over for the weirs and turned back at the sight of the marsh in the rain, and crouched by the rail with the map case buttoned inside an oilskin. The chapel sexton came aboard at the West Landing with four bundles of cut reed for the chapel roof and sat on them under a sack. I saw Bram bailing at the bow with the wooden scoop. I heard the sexton say: "The saint sends rain on the just and the unjust alike, Mara, but mostly on ferries." I heard Bram say: "Water's over the boards at the bow. I'm bailing as fast as it comes."
What I did: I said 'Keep bailing, we're nearly over.' Then I put my weight on the rudder oar and hold the Heron square to the gusts. Then I said 'Sexton, your reeds are getting wetter on the way home than they were in the marsh.' Then I tie off at the East Landing and help him lift the bundles onto his handcart.
What happened: I was standing on the East Landing in the rain, soaked through, with reed chaff stuck to my sleeves. The air carried cold rain and wet reed.
How I came into it: wet, dogged, amused.

What I witnessed: I met Oren at the Lantern Inn, at the corner table of the taproom under the hanging lanterns, with a box of new glass chimneys at his elbow. I heard Oren say: "Mara. Sit. You look like the river's been at you." I heard Oren say: "Tonight. The timber staithe at ten, forty sacks. You'll want the green one lit and hung at the bow by ten." I heard Oren say: "You remember what I told you in the workshop. Keep poling, keep quiet, and everybody stays dry. How's that loft of yours, by the way? Dry, I hope. Damp gets into everything."
What I did: I said 'I'll stand.' Then I stand at the end of his table with my hands in my coat pockets. Then I said 'Forty sacks is a heavy load for one pole.' Then I said 'My loft is my business.' Then I turn toward the taproom door without touching the cup he pushed at me.
What happened: I was standing in the taproom of the Lantern Inn between his table and the door, the cup untouched behind me. The air carried pipe smoke and hot lamp oil.
How I came into it: angry, cornered, cold.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he knows who sleeps in my loft, and he asked after it so that I would know he knows. I based that on: Oren saying 'How's that loft of yours, by the way? Dry, I hope. Damp gets into everything,' straight after telling me to keep poling and keep quiet.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: The curfew bell had rung hours since and the waterfront was dark. Wren stood between me and the door with arms folded. I heard Wren say: "You told me yourself he walked out of a crowd holding a green lantern the evening you met him. He's been holding it out to you ever since." I heard Wren say: "Let me come. Two poles are quicker than one." I saw Tobin at the foot of the ladder with his collar turned up. I heard Tobin say: "The sacks will carry the stores' stamp. Don't let his carters see you read it."
What I did: I said 'No. You stay here with Tobin and bar the door behind me.' Then I take the green lantern down from its nail and check the oil and the wick without lighting it. Then I said 'I'll carry his sacks. And I'll count them, and I'll look at what's on them.' Then I pull on my oilskin and put a stub of chalk in the pocket.
What happened: I was standing at the boathouse door with the green lantern unlit in my hand. The air carried cold damp and the river smell at night.
How I came into it: grim, determined, afraid.

What I witnessed: At the timber staithe below the East Landing three carters with shuttered lamps loaded forty sacks onto the Heron's deck in four rows, the grain heavy and dry in the hessian. I heard a carter say: "Forty. Count them if you like, ferrywoman." No other light showed anywhere on the river.
What I did: I said 'I will.' Then I walk the rows and count the sacks with my hand on each one: forty. Then I light the green lantern Oren gave me and hang it at the bow. Then I push off from the staithe after the curfew and pole out into the dark with the green lantern at the bow and nothing else lit on the water.
What happened: Out in the current a green light opened once on the West Landing and shut again, and I steered for it. I was standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my arm, the green lantern swinging at the bow and the sacks dark between us. The air carried cold river damp and the dry smell of grain.
How I came into it: grim, tense, alert.

What I witnessed: I met Oren on the West Landing in the dark. He was standing at the head of the ramp with a shuttered lantern, green glass showing at the crack, and two carts waited behind him on the toll road. The carters swung the sacks off the deck, and in the lantern light I saw the council's stamp on every one, the town tower in black on the hessian. I heard a carter say: "Easier when the old mill took them. Now it's all the way up the toll road raw." I heard Oren say: "Hold your tongue and lift." I heard Oren say: "Good light, Mara. I saw your green from the reeds before I heard your pole. Clear glass shows a face; green shows a friend." I saw him hold out a purse.
What I did: I said 'Keep it.' Then I count the sacks off the deck as they go: forty. Then I said 'You'll have my crossing. You won't have my hand on your coin.' Then I take the green lantern down from the bow and put it out.
What happened: I was standing on the West Landing beside the Heron's ramp with the cold lantern in my hand while the carts went up the toll road. The air carried horse sweat and grain dust.
How I came into it: angry, steady, sick.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the old mill: it ground the stolen council grain before the fire, so the stamp was gone before the flour went up the toll road. I based that on: a carter on the West Landing saying it was easier when the old mill took them, and the council's stamp on all forty sacks.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Wren unbarred the boathouse door at my knock and held the lamp up to my face. I heard Wren say: "You're back. Was it forty?" From the dark of the loft I heard Tobin say: "Was the stamp on them?"
What I did: I said 'Forty. The town tower on every sack.' Then I take the lamp from Wren and climb the loft ladder with it. Then I said 'A carter on the West Landing said it was easier when the old mill took them. Ilse's mill, Tobin.' Then I hang the cold green lantern on the loft nail behind the bales.
What happened: By the lamp I saw Tobin sitting behind the net-bales with his knees drawn up, awake. I heard Tobin say: "Then you've carried the council's grain across the council's river, and before the fire your friend ground it for them." Wren stood at the foot of the ladder. I heard Wren say: "Ilse can't have known." I was sitting on the top rung of the loft ladder with the lamp beside me. The air carried tar and dust off the net-bales.
How I came into it: exhausted, sick, resolved.

What I witnessed: Wren had the weirs sheet pinned out but was watching me instead of inking. I heard Wren say: "You didn't sleep." I saw Tobin at the foot of the ladder with his bowl in both hands. I heard Tobin say: "Millers write everything down. Sacks in, flour out, who paid, what night. The widow will have written down more than she knew."
What I did: I said 'Ilse would never have ground stolen grain if she'd known. She'd have taken it for an order like any other.' Then I pour the tea and drink mine standing. Then I said 'If she wrote it down, the book may have burned with the mill. I'll ask her today.' Then I lace my boots and take my coat from the peg.
What happened: I was standing at the door with my coat half on and the tea still hot in me. The air carried tea steam and the mist off the Aune.
How I came into it: tired, resolved, worried.

What I witnessed: A tinker drove his cart onto the deck at the East Landing with every pot on it ringing, and Wren climbed on after with the chain. I heard Bram say: "You look like you poled all night, Mara." I heard the tinker say: "Mend a kettle for my fare, ferrywoman? Your stern lamp's dented." I heard Wren say: "The weirs today. I'll be back for the noon boat if the water lets me."
What I did: I said 'Coin, not kettles.' Then I said 'I slept badly, Bram. Bow pole.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and take us across on the slack of the tide. Then I hand Wren the end of the chain over the rail at the West Landing.
What happened: I was standing at the stern of the Heron at the West Landing with the tinker's pots still ringing up the toll road. The air carried hot tin and river weed.
How I came into it: tired, short, watchful.

What I witnessed: Two of the council's men in grey coats were waiting at the top of the East Landing ramp, one with a halberd, stopping every passenger coming off. I heard the man with the halberd say: "Ferrywoman. A man named Tobin Reyes, a deserter, thin, in a blue coat. Has he crossed on your boat?" I saw Aldous watching from the dock office door with his pipe unlit, and across the waterfront I saw Oren standing in the Lantern Inn's doorway with his arms folded, watching too. I saw Bram stop coiling the stern rope.
What I did: I said 'I carry whoever pays the fare. I don't keep a book of coats.' Then I go on handing the passengers' bundles up the ramp. Then I said 'If your deserter wants to cross, he can pay a copper like anybody.' Then I nod at Bram to finish the rope.
What happened: I was standing on the East Landing ramp with a passenger's bundle in my arms and the halberd a pace from my shoulder. The air carried pipe smoke and the cold off the water.
How I came into it: guarded, steady, cold.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the council's men: they ask at the ferry now because someone has told them the deserter never left Saltmere. I based that on: the man with the halberd naming Tobin Reyes at the East Landing and asking whether he has crossed on my boat, with Oren watching it from the inn door.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Ilse was at the chapel house table hemming a sheet, with the eviction notice pinned to the wall above the bread crock. I heard Ilse say: "You don't come up here at this hour unless something's wrong."
What I did: I said 'I need to ask you about the mill. Did it grind council grain this summer? Night orders? Did you write them down?' Then I sit down across from her and take one end of the sheet so she can hem the other. Then I said 'If there's a book, tell me where it is and I'll fetch it for you. Tomorrow, first thing, with a bar.'
What happened: I heard Ilse say: "Night orders, yes. Every sack went in the ledger. Sacks in, flour out, who paid, which night." I heard Ilse say: "It's under the hearthstone in the tin box, wrapped in oilcloth. If the fire didn't get under the stone, it's there still. I can't go into that shell, Mara. I can't." I was sitting at Ilse's table holding the end of her sheet. The air carried soap and old smoke caught in her shawl.
How I came into it: careful, tender, determined.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: she has known since the fire that the ledger might still be under the stone, and has left it there because going into the shell is worse to her than losing it. I based that on: Ilse telling me exactly where the tin box is and saying she can't go into that shell.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Oren came down the East Landing ramp for the noon crossing with a crate of lantern glass under one arm and paid his copper like anybody. Halfway across he came and stood beside me at the stern and watched the water. I heard Oren say: "Good glass is all in the cooling, Mara. Cool it too fast and it cracks the first cold night." I heard Oren say: "You were up late. So was I. The river's very quiet after the bell." I saw Bram at the bow pole, not looking round.
What I did: I said 'Stand forward of the oar. You're in my way.' Then I bring the Heron's head up into the current so his crate slides against his shins. Then I said 'Your glass is your business. The river's mine.' Then I drop his copper in the tin without looking at it.
What happened: I was standing at the stern with both hands on the rudder oar and Oren a pace forward of me, the West Landing coming up. The air carried river weed and the smoke of his pipe.
How I came into it: hostile, controlled, wary.

What I witnessed: I found Wren knee-deep at the eel weirs with the chain pegged across the channel and the field book propped on a stake. I heard Wren say: "I missed the noon boat. The weirs are bigger than they look from the bank." I heard Wren say: "What do the marsh folk call this channel? It isn't on any chart. And the one that bends back on itself by the willows?"
What I did: I said 'Petra called this one the Long Elbow, and that one the Drowned Lane. Nobody else calls them anything.' Then I wade in and hold the far end of the chain while Wren reads the measure. Then I said 'Tomorrow I'm going into the mill for Ilse's ledger. Come with me and hold the lamp.'
What happened: I heard Wren say: "I'll hold the lamp." I was standing on the bank of the Long Elbow with marsh water running out of my boots. The air carried reed rot and the cold coming in from the west.
How I came into it: easier, fond, resolved.

What I witnessed: Tobin was on the bottom rung of the loft ladder splicing a new eye into the stern rope. I heard Wren say: "I'll bring the field lamp. It throws further than yours." I heard Tobin say: "Go early, before the council's men are on the toll road. And if the book's there, don't open it on the West Landing."
What I did: I said 'First light, then. Bram can hold the Heron at the West Landing while we go up the side channel.' Then I lay the iron pry bar, a coil of line and a square of oilcloth by the door. Then I eat my supper standing. Then I said 'Tobin, if anyone knocks while I'm gone, you're not here.'
What happened: I was standing by the door with my bowl, the pry bar at my feet. The air carried tar from the splice and boiled potato.
How I came into it: restless, determined, uneasy.

What I witnessed: Wren was already dressed, the field lamp trimmed and the satchel over one shoulder. Overhead I heard Tobin turn over in the loft and the boards creak under him. I heard Wren say: "The tide's on the turn. If we go now we'll be up the side channel before the mist lifts."
What I did: I said 'Bring the lamp. I'll bring the bar.' Then I shoulder the pry bar and the coil of line and push the oilcloth inside my coat. Then I pull the boathouse door to behind us and wedge it. Then I walk with Wren along the waterfront to the East Landing.
What happened: I was standing at the top of the East Landing ramp with the pry bar on my shoulder, looking for Bram in the mist. The air carried mist and the first smoke from the inn's chimneys.
How I came into it: tense, purposeful, cold.

What I witnessed: Bram took us over on the bow pole with no other fares, the mist flat on the water. At the West Landing I saw the side-channel path running up through the reeds toward the mill's black chimney. I heard Bram say: "How long do I hold her?" I heard Wren say: "An hour, if the stone comes up easy."
What I did: I said 'Hold her an hour. If the council's men come down the toll road, take her back across and come for us after.' Then I step off onto the West Landing with the pry bar. Then I start up the side-channel path with Wren behind me carrying the lamp.
What happened: I was at the foot of the side-channel path on the West Landing with the reeds over my head on both sides. The air carried wet char from somewhere ahead.
How I came into it: tense, quiet, resolved.

What I witnessed: From the sill of the old mill's burned shell I saw the roof gone and the main beam down across the grinding floor, black, with wet ash drifted against the walls. Through the gap where the wall had been I saw the wheel standing still in the side channel, its paddles charred to stumps. The hearthstone at the kitchen end was cracked across but still in its bed. I heard Wren say: "Mind the beam. Left of it there's still a floor."
What I did: I said 'Hold the lamp low, on the stone.' Then I go into the burned shell over the sill and step left of the beam to the hearth. Then I work the pry bar into the crack at the hearthstone's edge, lever it up and slide it aside. Then I lift the tin box out of the hollow under it, wrapped in oilcloth and dry, and take out Ilse's ledger with its pages whole. Then I wrap the ledger in my own oilcloth and button it inside my coat.
What happened: I was standing in the mill's burned doorway with Ilse's ledger inside my coat, looking back at the fallen beam. I remembered Ilse and me as girls, sitting at the edge of the race with our feet over the water. The air carried wet ash and cold char.
How I came into it: grieved, careful, resolved.

inferences.text: I concluded that whoever set the mill fire wanted the mill gone, and either did not know the ledger lay under the hearthstone or could not find it. I based that on: the ledger dry and whole in its tin under the stone while the rest of the mill burned, and the sexton saying at the landing at dawn after the fire that it was set.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Bram had the Heron waiting at the West Landing with the ramp down and no fares aboard. Halfway across I looked back and saw the mill's black chimney standing small over the reeds on its side channel. I heard Bram say: "You found it, then. You've a face like you found it." I heard Wren say: "Not a page burned. The stone kept it."
What I did: I said 'Pole, Bram. East Landing, and then I'm going up to the chapel house.' Then I keep one hand flat on the ledger inside my coat and the other on the rudder oar. Then I said 'Not a word of this on the dock, Bram. Not to anyone.'
What happened: I heard Bram say: "Not a word." I was standing at the stern of the Heron in mid-river with my coat buttoned over the ledger. The air carried the mist burning off and the char smell still in my sleeves.
How I came into it: relieved, wary, purposeful.

What I witnessed: Ilse unwrapped the oilcloth on her table and sat down hard when she saw the ledger whole. She turned the pages back to the summer. I saw the night orders in her own hand: "Night order, council stamp, thirty sacks ground, carted west, paid in coin," then the same again, and again, all through the summer and into this autumn, the last one four nights before the fire. I heard Ilse say: "The carters said it was the council's own grain for the council's own bread, ground at night because the stores wanted it quiet. I wrote it down like any other order." I heard Wren say: "That's more than six hundred sacks."
What I did: I said 'The ledger shows the grain, Ilse. Every sack of it, in your hand, with the night it came.' Then I run my finger down the night orders and count the nights twice. Then I said 'Keep this book where nobody can get at it. Not on that shelf, and not under your bed.'
What happened: I was standing at Ilse's shoulder with my finger on the last night order. The air carried damp paper and old smoke.
How I came into it: grim, certain, protective.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: the night orders in Ilse's ledger are his green-lantern grain, ground at her mill so the council's stamp was gone before the flour went up the toll road. I based that on: the ledger's night orders of council-stamped sacks paid in coin, and the carter on the West Landing saying it was easier when the old mill took them.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: The sexton unlocked the iron-bound chest in the vestry, and Ilse laid the ledger in it wrapped in my oilcloth. Under the painted saint with the river at her knees, Ilse stood with her hand flat on the lid. I heard Ilse say: "I'll put it before the council with a petition. Councillor Hesk's notice, the night orders, and the fire that was set. All of it, in writing." I heard Wren say: "I'll write it fair for you. My hand's clean, and I know how the council likes its papers laid out." I heard the sexton say: "The key stays on my belt, and my belt stays on me."
What I did: I said 'Good. Let Wren write it.' Then I watch the sexton turn the key and try the lid. Then I said 'Ilse, don't speak of the ledger in the market. Not to anyone.' Then I put my hand over hers on the chest lid.
What happened: I was standing in the vestry beside Ilse with my hand on hers. The air carried candle wax and cold stone.
How I came into it: solemn, protective, hopeful.

inferences.text: I concluded that Ilse means to fight the eviction in the open now, and that her petition will make her as much of a target as the ledger was. I based that on: Ilse saying she will put the ledger before the council with a petition naming Councillor Hesk's notice, the night orders and the fire that was set.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Tobin was waiting at the foot of the ladder when Wren and I came in. I heard Tobin say: "Well?" I heard Wren say: "More than six hundred sacks, every night written down in her own hand." I heard Tobin say: "Then it's in writing. Men have been ruined by less writing than that."
What I did: I said 'It's locked in the vestry chest, and the sexton has the key on his belt.' Then I sit on the bench and pull my boots off. Then I said 'Ilse thanked me three times. She doesn't know I've carried his sacks under the green lantern.' Then I think of the lies I have told Ilse this autumn, and I say nothing more.
What happened: I was sitting on the bench with one boot in my hand, not looking at Tobin. The air carried tar and cold supper.
How I came into it: weary, ashamed, steady.

What I witnessed: Fog sat on the Aune so thick that the East Landing was only the clank of its chain. A carter led a lame grey mare down the West Landing ramp onto the deck, the mare blowing at the water. Wren stood at the mare's other side with a hand on her neck. I heard the carter say: "She threw a shoe on the toll road. The smith's on your side." I heard Bram say: "She's shaking, Mara. I'll hold her head." I heard Wren say: "Talk to her, Bram. Horses like a voice."
What I did: I said 'Talk, then, both of you. I'll steer.' Then I ring the bow bell three times before we push off. Then I steer by the clank of the East Landing chain and the chapel bell behind it.
What happened: I was standing at the stern steering into the fog, the mare's breath steaming at the rail. The air carried wet horse and cold river.
How I came into it: calm, careful, alert.

What I witnessed: Aldous was at his desk in the dock office with the tally book open and the stove ticking. Ilse's chest and three sacks of her things saved from the mill were still stacked under the window, where they have stood since the fire. I heard Aldous say: "The widow wants her things up the hill, then? She's staying at the chapel house for good?" I heard Aldous say: "The council's men were in again yesterday. They've raised the reward on that deserter to fifteen silver." I saw Wren look at me and then at the floor.
What I did: I said 'For good. She won't go back across, and she's right not to.' Then I clear the coil of rope off the top of the chest. Then I said 'Fifteen silver. They must want him badly.' Then I lift one end of Ilse's chest to try the weight while Wren takes the other.
What happened: I was standing in the dock office with one end of Ilse's chest off the floor. The air carried stove heat and ink.
How I came into it: brisk, wary, purposeful.

What I witnessed: Bram met us at the dock office door and took the other end of Ilse's chest from Wren, and Wren took up two of the sacks. Ilse had the chapel house door propped open at the top of the chapel lane. I heard Ilse say: "Under the window, Bram. That's where it'll stay." I heard Ilse say: "The sexton says this house is mine for as long as I want it, and I want it. I'm not going back across, Mara. There's nothing over there now but a chimney." I saw her hang the old mill key on a nail by the door.
What I did: I carry my end of the chest up the chapel lane and set it down under the window. Then I carry the last sack in and set her pots out on the shelf beside the bread crock. Then I said 'Then it's home.' Then I said 'You'll want a better lock on that door. I'll bring one.'
What happened: I was standing in Ilse's kitchen in the chapel house with her pots on the shelf and her chest under the window. The air carried whitewash and soap.
How I came into it: warm, sad, steady.

What I witnessed: The market was half empty in the wind, the awnings cracking. A boy in an inn apron ran up to me at the chandler's stall. I heard the boy say: "The lantern-maker says will you come up to the workshop when you've a moment, missus. He says it's about your lamp." I heard the chandler say: "They're saying the miller's widow means to put a petition to the council. Against Councillor Hesk's notice, if you can believe it."
What I did: I said 'A lock and hasp, the heavy one, and the screws for it.' Then I pay the chandler for the lock and a tin of tallow. Then I said 'Tell the lantern-maker I heard.' Then I look across at the upper windows of the Lantern Inn, where the workshop lamps are burning in daylight.
What happened: I was standing at the chandler's stall with the lock in my hand, looking toward the Lantern Inn. The air carried wind-blown straw and tallow.
How I came into it: wary, irritated, alert.

What I witnessed: Oren's workshop above the inn was hot from the little glass furnace, and lanterns hung from every beam, clear and amber and green. I saw Oren set a purse on the bench between us. I heard Oren say: "Your crossing money. You left it on the West Landing." I heard Oren say: "I'd have said you'd be wanting the green one again before long, the way the nights are drawing in." I heard Oren say: "I hear the widow's taken the chapel house and is writing to the council. Did she save anything from the fire? Papers? Millers do love their papers."
What I did: I said 'I said keep it, and I meant it.' Then I push the purse back across the bench with one finger. Then I said 'What Ilse saved is Ilse's business. Leave her be.' Then I turn to the workshop stairs without waiting for an answer.
What happened: I was standing at the top of the workshop stairs with my hand on the rail and the heat of the furnace on my back. The air carried hot glass, solder and lamp black.
How I came into it: angry, wary, cold.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he has heard there might be a book, and he is fishing to learn whether the fire missed it. I based that on: Oren asking whether the widow saved anything from the fire, papers, and saying millers do love their papers, the same morning she took the chapel house for good.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: Two crates of hens and a woman with a barrow of cabbages came aboard at the East Landing. Bram poled at the bow with rag wound round his palms against the wet. I heard the woman with the cabbages say: "Mind the hens. They bite." I heard Bram say: "You've said four words since noon, Mara. Is it Da? Is it me?"
What I did: I said 'It isn't you, Bram. It isn't your father either.' Then I steer us wide of the snag off the timber staithe. Then I said 'Don't take any errand from the lantern-maker, whatever he pays. Give me your word on it.'
What happened: I heard Bram say: "You have it." I was standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my arm, watching the West Landing come up. The air carried cabbage and wet feathers.
How I came into it: preoccupied, protective, tired.

What I witnessed: Wren had the weirs sheet pinned out under the lamp with the channels inked and the names lettered in. I heard Wren say: "Petra's names are on it now. The Long Elbow, the Drowned Lane. They'll be on the council's copy for good." I saw Tobin sitting on the floor with his back against the ladder.
What I did: I said 'Oren asked me today whether Ilse saved any papers from the fire. Millers love their papers, he said.' Then I sit down by the map and look at Petra's names in Wren's lettering. Then I said 'And Aldous says the reward's fifteen silver now. I'll put the new lock on Ilse's door in the morning.'
What happened: I heard Tobin say: "He knows there's a book, or he guesses it. Either way he'll want it." I heard Wren say: "It's in the chapel vestry. He'd have to rob the Drowned Saint." I was sitting at the table beside the map with the lamp between us. The air carried ink and the cold coming under the door.
How I came into it: uneasy, fond, watchful.

What I witnessed: Wren was still asleep in the spare room with the door shut. Tobin was sitting by the cold stove with his blue coat folded on his knees. I heard Tobin say: "Fifteen silver now. Someone on this river will think of me every time they're short." I heard Tobin say: "When the reward's forgotten I'll go downriver. I won't stay and bring the council's men to your door."
What I did: I said 'Not yet. Nobody goes downriver while the council's men are watching the barges.' Then I kneel and light the stove and set the kettle on. Then I said 'You'll go when I say the river's clear, and I'll take you myself. Put that coat back in the loft.'
What happened: I was kneeling at the stove with the kettle just set on and Tobin's shadow on the wall behind me. The air carried cold ash and kindling smoke.
How I came into it: protective, tired, stubborn.

inferences.text: I concluded that the raised reward has set Tobin thinking of leaving alone, and that he would go some night without telling me if I did not forbid it. I based that on: Tobin saying he will go downriver when the reward is forgotten and will not bring the council's men to my door, with his blue coat folded on his knees.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: The first crossing carried a cart of split oak and two drovers west, and Wren rode along with the sighting staff to take one last bearing from the West Landing mooring post. On the West Landing I saw two of the council's men at the head of the toll road, stopping the carts and lifting the sacking to look under it. I heard Bram say: "They're searching the carts now, not just the boats." I heard Wren say: "One bearing from the mooring post and the map's closed."
What I did: I said 'Let them search. Firewood's firewood.' Then I bring the Heron alongside the West Landing and drop the ramp. Then I steady Wren's sighting staff against the mooring post while Wren takes the bearing.
What happened: I was standing on the West Landing beside the mooring post, watching the council's men lift the sacking on the first cart. The air carried split oak and river mist.
How I came into it: watchful, calm, wary.

What I witnessed: Wren sat at Ilse's table writing the petition fair, with the ledger open beside the page, and the sexton waited by the door to carry the book back to the vestry. I heard Ilse say: "Write that the eviction notice for the mill was signed by Councillor Hesk, and that the mill burned after it." I heard Ilse say: "And write out the night orders, every one, with the nights." I heard Wren say: "Six pages of night orders. They'll have to read every one." I heard Ilse say: "You'll come to the council house when they hear it, Mara?"
What I did: I said 'Write it plain, Wren. Councillors don't read past the first page unless they're made to.' Then I fix the new lock and hasp on Ilse's door, three screws to each plate. Then I hand Ilse both keys. Then I said 'One for you and one for the sexton. I've the river to keep, Ilse. I'll wait for the word.'
What happened: I was standing at Ilse's door with the turnscrew in my hand, trying the new lock. The air carried ink and whitewash.
How I came into it: hopeful, protective, uneasy.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the eviction notice: it and the fire came too close together to be strangers, and Ilse's petition now says so in writing under Councillor Hesk's own name. I based that on: Ilse having Wren write that the notice was signed by Councillor Hesk and that the mill burned after it.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: In the Lantern Inn I met Oren at the bar of the taproom, talking with two carters over cider. He lifted his cup to me. I heard Oren say: "The ferrywoman. The widow's petition is all over town, Mara. Brave woman. Brave women need good friends." I heard Oren say: "Tell her from me: a lantern's no use if you hang it where the wind can get at it."
What I did: I said 'Two mutton pies, wrapped.' Then I pay the pot-boy and wait at the end of the bar with my back to the wall. Then I said 'Ilse has all the friends she needs.' Then I take the pies and go to the door without looking at him again.
What happened: I was standing in the inn doorway with the hot pies in a cloth and the waterfront wind in my face. The air carried mutton fat and cider.
How I came into it: cold, angry, guarded.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he meant the lantern talk as a threat to Ilse, and he wanted me to carry it to her for him. I based that on: Oren saying brave women need good friends, and telling me to tell her a lantern's no use if you hang it where the wind can get at it.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: The afternoon crossing carried a carter with a load of cabbages and a girl driving three geese. Bram ate the last of his pie at the bow between pole strokes. From mid-river I saw the mill's black chimney standing over the reeds on the west bank. I heard Bram say: "The wheel's still there. You could build a mill round a wheel." I heard the girl with the geese say: "My gran says the widow's mill made the best flour on the river."
What I did: I said 'The wheel's charred to the axle, Bram. Nobody's building anything round it.' Then I steer us across the run of the current. Then I take the girl's copper and drop it in the tin.
What happened: I was standing at the stern, watching the mill's chimney from the river until the reeds hid it. The air carried goose and the cold of the afternoon wind.
How I came into it: sad, quiet, steady.

What I witnessed: Aldous came out of the dock office at dusk and rang the curfew bell on its post, twelve strokes. Wren came down the landing road with the map case under one arm. I heard Aldous say: "Last boat in, Mara? Then tie her up. The council's men are walking the waterfront tonight with lamps." I heard Aldous say: "There's a new notice on my door. Anyone carrying after the bell loses their boat to the council." I heard Wren say: "Then nobody's carrying after the bell."
What I did: I said 'She's in.' Then I make the Heron fast to the rings at the East Landing with a double hitch at bow and stern. Then I read the new notice on the dock office door twice. Then I said 'Come on, Wren. Supper.'
What happened: I was standing on the East Landing at the dock office door with the notice in front of me and the last stroke of the bell going away over the water. The air carried lamp smoke and cold.
How I came into it: wary, tired, grim.

inferences.text: I concluded that the curfew now puts the Heron herself at stake: one more crossing under the green lantern and the council could take Petra's ferry from me. I based that on: Aldous saying anyone carrying after the bell loses their boat to the council, and the new notice nailed on the dock office door.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: After supper Wren laid all the marsh sheets edge to edge across the boathouse floor, the whole marsh from the toll road to the river. I heard Wren say: "That's the last channel inked. All that's left is the title and the council's seal." Tobin came down the ladder and knelt at the edge of the map. I heard Tobin say: "So that's where I've been hiding. It's smaller than it feels." I heard Wren say: "Everything is, on paper."
What I did: I said 'It's good work, Wren. Petra would have liked it.' Then I kneel and put my finger on the boathouse, a small square at the river's edge. Then I said 'Roll it up before somebody kicks the lamp over. The council's men are on the waterfront tonight.'
What happened: I was kneeling on the boathouse floor at the edge of the marsh map with Wren and Tobin across from me. The air carried ink, tar and the river's cold.
How I came into it: tender, tired, uneasy.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren at the table under the lamp, inking the reed marsh onto the big sheet, with the toll road bend still in pencil. I heard Wren say: "Two more days. Then the bend is the only blank left on it." I heard the loft boards creak overhead, the slow steps Tobin Reyes takes when he cannot sleep.
What I did: I said 'Two more days, then. Do not ink the river where it was in the spring.' Then I take Ilse's ledger out of its hiding place and fold back the oilcloth far enough to see the cover and the grain pages, dry and whole. Then I wrap it again and put it back where it was. Then I take the lantern out to the slip, check the Heron's bow and stern lines, come back in and bar the door.
What happened: I was standing -- standing with my back against the barred door and the lantern in my hand. The air carried lamp oil, wet rope and the river at night.
How I came into it: protectiveness, tense, drained.

inferences.text: I concluded that the ledger is safer in the boathouse than anywhere in town until Ilse's petition is heard; nobody looks for a miller's book in a ferry pilot's house. I based that on: You fold back the oilcloth and see the ledger dry, its grain pages whole, where you left it.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Bram Toller come down the East Landing at a run with his coat half on and take the bow pole without being told. I saw a carter lead an empty cart and a grey horse aboard, and a goatherd lift his three goats over the side one by one. I heard the carter say: "Mind the horse. He don't like the water slapping." I heard Bram Toller say: "Mist's lying thick on the far side, Mara."
What I did: I said 'Then we go slow. Wren, stand at his head and talk to him.' Then I chock the cart wheels, cast off the stern line and lean on the rudder oar to bring the Heron's nose into the current. Then I call the strokes for Bram as we go out into the mist.
What happened: I saw Wren stand at the horse's head with one hand on its neck, talking nonsense to it until it stopped stamping. I was standing -- standing at the stern with both hands on the rudder oar and the East Landing gone grey behind us. The air carried cold mist, horse and goat.
How I came into it: calm, absorbed, contentment.

What I witnessed: I saw the carter take the grey horse and his cart up the West Landing toward the farms, and two market women come down the bank with apple baskets and a crock of eggs between them. I saw Wren set her compass on the landing post and sight across the side channel at the black chimney of the old mill, then write the bearing in her book. I heard Wren say: "Burned or not, that chimney is still the best mark on this side." I heard Bram Toller say: "Father says the council sits tomorrow. Half the marsh wants to be in town for it."
What I did: I said 'Write it down and do not stand looking at it.' Then I take the women's fares and lift the egg crock aboard with both hands. Then I said 'Tomorrow, Bram. You are sure.'
What happened: I heard Bram Toller say: "Noon bell tomorrow. It's the widow's petition they're hearing, and a lot of others besides." I was standing -- standing on the West Landing planks with the bow line in my hand and the mill chimney black across the channel. The air carried wet reeds and woodsmoke from the cottages.
How I came into it: guarded, sadness, calm.

What I witnessed: I saw Oren Dask come down the West Landing bank alone with a crate on his shoulder, straw sticking out between its slats and his boots wet to the ankle from the marsh path. I heard Oren Dask say: "You'll be wanting the fare first, then. Here -- and one more for the crate. It's glass." I heard the crate clink when Bram Toller took it from him. I heard Oren Dask say: "The miller's widow has her petition in, I'm told. Tomorrow, is it? You'll be up at the hall holding her hand."
What I did: I said 'I pole a ferry. Sit on your crate if you want it whole.' Then I put his two coins in my pocket without looking at them. Then I push off from the West Landing and keep my eyes on the East Landing and not on him the whole way over.
What happened: I met Oren on the West Landing this morning and carried him and his crate across. I saw him shoulder the crate at the East Landing and walk up toward the Lantern Inn without looking back. I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my hand, watching him go. The air carried straw, river mist and the marsh mud on his boots.
How I came into it: guarded, suspicion, tense.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he was out in the reed marsh in the night, after the curfew, on some business that needed glass carried back to town. I based that on: Oren Dask comes down the West Landing bank on the first morning crossing with marsh mud to the ankle and a crate of glass on his shoulder.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Tobin Reyes come down the loft ladder when I barred the street door, and sit on the bottom rung with a bowl of the soup. I heard Wren say: "That crate of Oren's rang like a chapel bell every time the boat rocked." I heard Tobin Reyes say: "If he's carrying glass over to the marsh and back again, it isn't to sell to reed-cutters." I saw Wren look at me and say nothing more.
What I did: I said 'Eat your soup. What Oren carries is between him and the council now.' Then I cut the bread three ways and give Tobin the heel because he likes it. Then I take the bow net down from its peg and start on the tear near the float line while my soup cools.
What happened: I was sitting -- sitting on the upturned bucket with the net across my knees and the netting needle going. The air carried barley soup, tarred twine and the stove.
How I came into it: connected, calm, guarded.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse Harrow at the chapel house table with her petition copied out fair and a cup of cold tea beside it. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "They sit tomorrow at the noon bell. Councillor Hesk at the head of the table, and his name still on the notice." I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Bring the ledger in the morning, Mara. I want it in my own hands when I stand up in front of them." I saw her press her thumb hard against the table edge, the way she did when we were girls and she would not cry.
What I did: I said 'I will bring it before the first crossing. It is dry, and it is where I put it.' Then I sit down across from her and read the petition through once, slowly. Then I said 'It is plain and it is true. Say it the way you wrote it and do not let them hurry you.'
What happened: I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Plain and true. Petra used to say that about a good crossing." I was sitting -- sitting at the chapel house table with Ilse across from me and the petition between us. The air carried candle wax, cold tea and damp stone.
How I came into it: protectiveness, tenderness, tense.

What I witnessed: I heard the rudder oar's pin knock in its socket at the end of every sweep, a dry click it has not made before. I saw Bram Toller look back from the bow. I heard Bram Toller say: "That's the pin talking. It's been at it since this morning." I saw Wren lay her hand flat on the oar beside mine to feel it. I heard Wren say: "There's play in it. A finger's width, maybe more."
What I did: I said 'It is worn thin where it bears. It will hold today if nobody leans on it like a fool. Tomorrow the old one comes out and a new one goes in.' Then I take the Heron over the rest of the way with short, easy sweeps, the firewood cart rocking in the waist. Then I look down at the pin head and see the bright ring of wear around it.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with one hand on the rudder oar and the other over the pin head, the East Landing coming up. The air carried split oak from the firewood cart and the first cold of the evening.
How I came into it: serious, absorbed, calm.

What I witnessed: I heard the chapel bell ring the curfew while I was making the Heron fast. In the dock office I saw Aldous Toller take an iron pin from the drawer of the store cabinet and weigh it in his palm. I heard Aldous Toller say: "Last one that size in the store. Fit it before you take her out again." I heard Aldous Toller say: "And you'll have company at the landing tomorrow night. Grain barge called the Moth, down from upriver, tying up below the crane till first light." I saw Bram Toller hang his coat on the peg behind his father's chair.
What I did: I said 'Put it on my slate, Aldous. I will fit it in the morning before the first crossing.' Then I take the pin and close my fist on it, cold and heavy, and put it in my coat pocket. Then I said 'Below the crane is where the goats come off. Tell the bargemen to keep their lines out of the way.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing by the dock office stove with the new pin heavy in my pocket and Wren at my shoulder. The air carried coal smoke and wet wool.
How I came into it: calm, resolve, connected.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse Harrow open the chapel house door before I could knock, already in her dark good dress with her hair pinned tight. I saw her take the oilcloth bundle from me, fold the cloth back and lay both hands flat on the ledger's cover. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "You'll not come up to the hall with me. No. I know. You never have, for any of it."
What I did: I said 'I do not go to council business, Ilse. I will be at the landing when you come down.' Then I fold the oilcloth back over the corner of the ledger so the damp cannot get at it. Then I hold her by both shoulders for a moment and let her go.
What happened: I heard Ilse Harrow say: "The landing, then. Wait for me there." I saw her shut the door, and her lamp move away inside. I was standing -- standing on the chapel house step in the dark before dawn with my hands empty. The air carried a hard cold and tallow from the chapel.
How I came into it: protectiveness, tense, hopeful.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin Reyes come down the loft ladder once the slip doors were shut, and take the weight of the rudder oar on his shoulder without a word. I saw Wren hold the lamp close over the crutch at the Heron's stern. I heard Tobin Reyes say: "Old pin's worn to a waist. Another week and it would have sheared in the middle of the river."
What I did: I said 'Hold it level. When I say, lift a hair.' Then I set the drift against the old pin of the rudder oar and knock it out with the mallet, three blows, and catch it in my palm. Then I scrape the socket clean, grease the new iron pin from the dock store with tallow and drive it home through the crutch and the rudder oar. Then I peg it and swing the rudder oar hard over each way, twice. Then I said 'There. That is the last thing she needed before the winter.'
What happened: I saw the rudder oar swing clean on its new pin with no click and no play. I heard Wren say: "That's the rudder oar mended, then." I was standing -- standing on the slip at the Heron's stern with the old pin in my pocket. The air carried tallow, lamp smoke and the river through the cracks of the slip doors.
How I came into it: absorbed, satisfaction, connected.
