What I witnessed: I saw a goatherd drive six goats aboard at the East Landing with a hazel switch, and Bram Toller stand in the gap at the side to keep them in. I heard Bram Toller say: "Pin's quiet. You've done it already?" I saw the East Landing busier than a market day, people walking up toward the market square and the hall in their good coats. I heard Wren say: "Half the marsh is in town for the sitting."
What I did: I said 'Before you were out of bed, Bram.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and feel it swing without a click. Then I catch myself watching the hall roof over the market square while we cross, and make myself look at the water.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the goats bleating against my knees and the West Landing coming up. The air carried goat, cold water and the town's chimneys.
How I came into it: tense, anticipation, guarded.

What I witnessed: I saw the Lantern Inn half empty at the noon bell, most of the town gone up to the hall. I saw Oren Dask at the table nearest the fire with a pack at his feet, roped and buckled, and his good boots on. I heard Oren Dask say: "You'll be wanting a fresh wick for the green one, then. First thing I thought when you came in." I saw him lay two wicks on the table, coiled in paper. I heard Oren Dask say: "Is she up there with them now? With her book?"
What I did: I said 'Ask her yourself when she comes out.' Then I leave the wicks lying where he put them while I pay for two hot pies for Wren and me. Then I pick the wicks up after all and put them in my coat, because a wick is a wick. Then I said 'Going somewhere, Oren.'
What happened: I heard Oren Dask say: "Nowhere you'd need a ferry for." I met Oren at the Lantern Inn at noon and came away with two wicks and no answer. I was standing -- standing in the inn doorway with the pies wrapped in a cloth and Wren beside me. The air carried pie crust, ale and the fire.
How I came into it: suspicion, guarded, tense.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Oren Dask: he is packed to leave Saltmere and is only waiting to hear what the council makes of Ilse's ledger. I based that on: Oren Dask sits by the fire with a roped pack at his feet and his good boots on, and says: "Is she up there with them now? With her book?".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw a reed-cutter bring a cart stacked with thatching bundles aboard at the West Landing, the load higher than the horse's ears. I heard Bram Toller say: "A man off the hall steps says they're still reading. Doors shut since the noon bell." I heard Wren say: "Tomorrow I'll go out to the toll road bend and finish it. It's the last blank on the map. One day's chaining and it's done."
What I did: I said 'Then go over on the first crossing and come back on the last. The light goes early now.' Then I said 'Bram, lean on the far side of that load.' Then I bring the Heron across with the reed cart rocking and the wind pushing at the bundles like a sail.
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the stern with the wind on my right cheek and the East Landing ahead. The air carried cut reed and river wind.
How I came into it: absorbed, anticipation, tense.

What I witnessed: I saw Ilse Harrow come down the East Landing from the market square with her hands empty and her shawl crossed over her chest. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "They kept the ledger. They read it, every page, and they kept it." I heard Ilse Harrow say: "Hesk sat at the head of the table and wrote and never once looked up. They've sent men to count the grain in the council's own stores. The answer on the mill comes when the count is done, and not before." I saw Bram Toller stop coiling the stern line to listen.
What I did: I said 'Then they believed it enough to count.' Then I step off the Heron onto the planks and take her cold hands in mine. Then I said 'Come and sit by the stove in the boathouse for an hour.'
What happened: I heard Ilse Harrow say: "No. I want the chapel quiet and my own bed. But I'll take your arm as far as the steps." I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with Ilse holding my arm while the light went yellow over the water. The air carried woodsmoke from the town and the river going cold.
How I came into it: relief, hopeful, protectiveness.

inferences.text: I concluded that the council believed the ledger enough to count its own stores, which it would not trouble to do on a widow's word alone. I based that on: Ilse Harrow says: "They've sent men to count the grain in the council's own stores.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw a grain barge come down on the current with her brown sail furled and MOTH painted on her stern boards, and two bargemen pole her in below the crane. I saw Aldous Toller come out of the dock office with his slate to take their names and their lading. I heard Aldous Toller say: "Grain and hides for the downriver towns. Off at first light, they say." I heard the chapel bell ring the curfew.
What I did: I said 'Your lines are over the goat ramp. Shift them aft three yards or I will move them for you in the morning.' Then I tie the Heron off at her own rings for the night and ship the poles. Then I said 'Bram, go home to your supper. Wren, take the lantern.'
What happened: I saw the bargemen shift their lines aft without arguing. I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with the Moth's high side dark below the crane and the curfew bell still humming. The air carried damp grain, tar and the cold coming down off the hills.
How I came into it: drained, calm, guarded.

What I witnessed: I saw the Moth's bargemen take in their lines below the crane at dawn, and Oren Dask come down the East Landing at a fast walk with the roped pack on his back and no crate. I saw him step from the planks aboard the grain barge called the Moth and go aft to the stern without once looking at the dock office. I saw the Moth swing out into the current heading downriver, and Oren Dask lift a hand to me from the stern. I heard Oren Dask say: "Keep the green one, Mara. It's yours now."
What I did: I keep both hands on the pole and do not lift one back. Then I watch the Moth go down past the chapel steps and round the bend until her stern is gone. Then I said 'Wren. Get aboard. We have a crossing to make.'
What happened: The last I saw of Oren Dask was his raised hand over the Moth's stern at dawn, going downriver. I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with the pole in both hands and the bend empty. The air carried river mist and the smoke of the first chimneys.
How I came into it: guarded, resentment, relief.

inferences.text: I concluded that Oren Dask is running ahead of the council's count and does not mean to come back up the river. I based that on: Oren Dask boards the Moth at dawn with his pack and no crate, lifts a hand from the stern and says: "Keep the green one, Mara. It's yours now.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Wren step off onto the West Landing with the surveyor's chain over her shoulder, the map board under her arm and her satchel full. I heard Wren say: "The bend, the ditch and the culvert, and I'm done. I'll be on your last crossing." I saw Bram Toller hand her bread and cheese tied up in a cloth.
What I did: I said 'The last crossing goes at the bell, and the bell goes early now. Be on this landing before it rings, or you sleep in a reed stack.' Then I watch her go up the bank toward the toll road with the chain clinking. Then I take a carter and his load of cabbages aboard for the East Landing.
What happened: I was standing -- standing on the West Landing planks with the bow line in my hand and Wren getting small along the toll road. The air carried wet reeds, cabbages and the first sun on the marsh.
How I came into it: protectiveness, calm, anticipation.

What I witnessed: I saw a carter's wife lead a red cow aboard at the East Landing on a halter, taking her over to the bull at the marsh farms, and Bram Toller stand at the cow's head with his hand on her neck. I heard the carter's wife say: "She's never been on the water. She'll stand if you talk to her." I heard Bram Toller say: "Easy, girl. It's only the river." I heard Bram Toller say: "Father says the council's men are at the grain stores with their tallies already."
What I did: I said 'Keep talking to her, Bram. Do not stop until her feet are on grass.' Then I take the Heron out slow and flat, with no hard sweep of the rudder oar to set the cow dancing.
What happened: I saw the cow stand like a post with her ears turning to Bram's voice. I was standing -- standing at the stern halfway across, with the West Landing coming up. The air carried cow, river and thin cold sunshine.
How I came into it: calm, absorbed, amusement.

What I witnessed: I saw the West Landing empty in the last light except for a goatherd bringing his goats down to drink. I heard the goatherd say: "Your surveyor? Out at the bend of the toll road at mid-afternoon, with her chain across the ditch. Long way out." I heard the chapel bell begin the curfew from across the river. I heard Bram Toller say: "That's the bell, Mara. We have to go."
What I did: I said 'One more minute.' Then I stand up on the bow and look up the toll road until the light is gone off it. Then I said 'All right. Push off.' Then I take the Heron back across without her and make her fast at the East Landing on the last stroke of the bell.
What happened: I was standing -- standing on the East Landing with the stern line made fast and my eyes on the far bank. No lamp showed anywhere on the West Landing. The air carried river mud, cold and frost coming.
How I came into it: dread, tense, protectiveness.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Wren: she lost the light at the toll road bend finishing the map and is walking back along the ditch in the dark, slow with the chain, rather than lying hurt. I based that on: The goatherd says: "Out at the bend of the toll road at mid-afternoon, with her chain across the ditch. Long way out.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw the carters in off the toll road at the long table in the Lantern Inn with their boots steaming by the fire. I heard a carter say: "Saw a lass with a chain at the bend of the toll road at sundown, setting stakes by a lamp. She waved us on." I heard the innkeeper say: "Oren Dask's rooms are bare. Paid to the end of the month, took his glass and his tools and went down on the Moth at first light. Not a word to me why." I saw the stair up to the workshop dark, and no light under its door.
What I did: I said 'Did the lass still have her lamp lit when you passed.' Then I put a coin on the table for the carter's ale.
What happened: I heard the carter say: "Lit, aye. Swinging it about like a churchwarden." I let my breath go, and asked nothing about Oren. I was standing -- standing by the long table in the Lantern Inn with the cold door at my back and the fire in front. The air carried wet boots, ale and woodsmoke.
How I came into it: relief, tense, resolve.

What I witnessed: I saw Tobin Reyes come down the loft ladder when he heard me take the green lantern off its hook. I heard Tobin Reyes say: "You're going over. After the bell." I heard Tobin Reyes say: "I'll keep the stove up and the slip door on the latch."
What I did: I said 'Wren is on the far side with no light, and I am not leaving her in the reeds all night with frost coming.' Then I fit one of the fresh wicks in the green lantern and light it. Then I hang the lit green lantern at the bow, pole the Heron out of the slip and cross the river after curfew with the green light going ahead of me on the water. Then I bring her in at the West Landing, where Wren is sitting on the bottom step with the chain in her lap and her own lamp burned out. Then I said 'Get in. Do not say anything clever.'
What happened: I heard Wren say: "The bend's done. All of it. I'm sorry, Mara." Out on the river I saw no green light anywhere on the reed marsh or the West Landing, and nobody hailed us from either landing. I was standing -- standing at the stern on the way back, with the green lantern lit at the bow and Wren huddled on the thwart. The air carried lamp oil, cold and the black river.
How I came into it: resolve, tense, protectiveness.

inferences.text: I suspected this about the green lantern: it means nothing on the river any more; nobody answered it from the reed marsh and nobody hailed it from either landing. I based that on: You cross after curfew with the green lantern lit at the bow and see no green light anywhere on the reed marsh or the West Landing, and nobody hails you.

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw white frost on the East Landing planks and on the Heron's rails and thwarts, the first frost of the year, and the mooring lines gone stiff and grey with it. I saw Bram Toller come down the landing blowing on his hands. I heard Bram Toller say: "First frost. Father says it's come early by a week." I heard Wren say: "I'd like it noted that I was out in it last night." His nose was stuffed and red.
What I did: I said 'It is noted. Scrape the thwarts before anyone sits on them.' Then I knock the frost off the bow line against the bollard and work it soft in my hands. Then I break the thin skin of ice in the bailing bucket and tip it over the side.
What happened: I was standing -- standing on the frosted planks with the bow line in my hands and my breath smoking. The air carried frost, woodsmoke and mist lifting off the river.
How I came into it: contentment, calm, connected.

What I witnessed: I saw a shepherd bring nineteen ewes aboard at the West Landing, the frost on their backs turning to steam as the sun came over the town roofs. I heard the shepherd say: "Down to the town fold before the hard weather. They'll stand if the dog lies down." I saw the dog lie down in the bow. I heard Wren say: "Nineteen. I counted twice, because the first time it came to eighteen and a half."
What I did: I said 'The half is the black-faced one standing on the others.' Then I lean on the rudder oar and feel it swing clean and stiff on its new pin in the cold. Then I take us over slow, the ewes packed shoulder to shoulder and breathing steam.
What happened: I saw Bram Toller laugh so hard he had to hold the bow pole with both hands. I was standing -- standing at the stern with the rudder oar under my hands and the sheep's breath rising round me. The air carried wet wool, melting frost and sheep.
How I came into it: amusement, calm, absorbed.

What I witnessed: I saw two of the council's men going stall to stall in the market square with a paper in their hands. I heard one of the council's men say: "A deserter. Thin, about so high, a torn blue coat when he was last seen. There's silver at the hall for anyone who's seen a stranger like that." I saw the fish seller shake her head. I saw Wren lean close to me. I heard Wren say: "Keep walking, Mara."
What I did: I said 'Two pounds of the salt cod. The dry end, not the wet.' Then I pay the fish seller and take the cod in its paper, and buy lamp oil and a pair of grey wool socks for Wren at the next stall. Then I walk past the council's men at an ordinary pace with the basket on my arm, and do not look at their paper.
What happened: I was walking -- walking out of the market square toward the landing with Wren beside me and the basket on my arm. The air carried salt fish, cold and the smoke of the chestnut brazier.
How I came into it: guarded, threatened, tense.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Tobin Reyes: the council's men have his looks from someone who saw him in the autumn, and silver at the hall will loosen a tongue before the winter is out. I based that on: One of the council's men says: "A deserter. Thin, about so high, a torn blue coat when he was last seen. There's silver at the hall.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw Ilse Harrow at the chapel house window with her mending in her lap and the needle not moving. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "No answer yet. They're still counting. The sexton says the stores are short by whole cartloads." I heard Ilse Harrow say: "And they say Oren Dask's gone downriver on the Moth. Has he sent any word back, Mara? To anyone?"
What I did: I said 'No word from him. The innkeeper says he paid to the end of the month and took his glass and his tools.' Then I sit down on the bench under the window beside her. Then I said 'You put the ledger in their hands. Whatever they answer, that part is done, and it was right.'
What happened: I heard Ilse Harrow say: "You kept it dry for me. Thank you, Mara." I could not answer that. I have told Ilse three lies this autumn -- that I had seen no one round the boathouse, that Tobin was my cousin from downriver, and where I was one night -- and she thanked me for keeping her ledger safe. I was sitting -- sitting on the bench beside Ilse with my hands between my knees. The air carried cold chapel stone and her mending wool.
How I came into it: guilt, tenderness, sadness.

inferences.text: I suspected this about Ilse Harrow: she expects the council to refuse her and is bracing for it, though all she says is that they are still counting. I based that on: Ilse Harrow sits at the window with her mending in her lap and the needle not moving, and says: "No answer yet. They're still counting.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw a cooper roll four empty barrels aboard at the East Landing and lash them himself, going over to the marsh farms for the apple pressing. I saw Bram Toller take the bow pole with his left hand, the old forge scar on it shiny with the cold. I heard Bram Toller say: "River's dropped a hand this week. You can see the old piles by the chapel steps." I heard Wren say: "Then I'll put a note on the map. Water level as of the first frost."
What I did: I said 'Put the spring level on it too, or the next surveyor will drown somebody.' Then I steer wide of the chapel piles with the rudder oar and take the Heron across on the slack water under the far bank.
What happened: I saw the barrels knock hollow against each other in the waist of the boat. I was standing -- standing at the stern with the West Landing coming up. The air carried cold sun, river weed and oak staves.
How I came into it: calm, absorbed, connected.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren set her compass on the West Landing post and take a last sight on the chapel tower across the river, then one on the black chimney of the old mill across the side channel. I heard Wren say: "That closes it. Every line on the map meets now." I saw her write the two numbers in her book and rule a line under them.
What I did: I said 'Then close the book and get aboard. The bell goes within the hour, and I am not crossing for you twice in two nights.' Then I hold the Heron against the landing with the pole while she climbs down with the board. Then I look once across the channel at the mill chimney, and then at the water.
What happened: I saw Bram Toller grin at Wren and say nothing. I was standing -- standing in the Heron's stern at the West Landing with the pole set against the bottom and the chimney black against the low sun. The air carried cold reeds and the last of the sun.
How I came into it: satisfaction, sadness, calm.

What I witnessed: I heard the chapel bell ring the curfew as I made the Heron fast. In the dock office I saw Aldous Toller at his slate with the council's tally sheets pinned up beside it. I heard Aldous Toller say: "They're still counting at the stores. Two days now. The hall won't answer the widow till the last sack is tallied, and Hesk won't hurry it." I saw Bram Toller warming his hands at the stove beside his father.
What I did: I said 'She has waited this long. She can wait a day more, and so can I.' Then I write the day's fares on my slate under his: the sheep, the cooper's barrels, nine crossings. Then I said 'Goodnight, Aldous. Goodnight, Bram.'
What happened: I was standing -- standing at the dock office door with Wren beside me and the dark come down on the landing behind us. The air carried coal smoke and frost coming again.
How I came into it: drained, hopeful, calm.

What I witnessed: I saw Wren at the table inking the last line of the marsh map, the toll road bend, with Tobin Reyes holding the lamp close for her. I saw the green lantern on its hook by the door, cold and unlit. I heard Wren say: "Do you think Oren will send word? To anyone?" I heard Tobin Reyes say: "Men like Oren don't write letters."
What I did: I said 'No word from Oren, and there will not be. I have not seen Oren since the Moth took him round the bend yesterday at first light, and I do not expect to see him again.' Then I take the green lantern down, wipe the soot off its glass with my sleeve and hang it back on its hook without lighting it. Then I lean over Wren's shoulder to look at the finished map.
What happened: I saw Wren lift her pen and blow on the ink. I was standing -- standing behind Wren's chair with one hand on its back and the whole marsh under the lamp. The air carried ink, lamp oil and the stove.
How I came into it: sadness, contentment, guarded.

inferences.text: I concluded that no word will come from Oren Dask, and that he meant it that way when he lifted his hand from the Moth's stern. I based that on: Wren says: "Do you think Oren will send word? To anyone?" Tobin Reyes says: "Men like Oren don't write letters.".

turns.content:
What I witnessed: I saw frost again on the slip and on the boathouse window, thicker than yesterday. I saw Tobin Reyes come down the loft ladder in his stocking feet and take the two poles from the rack without being asked. I heard Tobin Reyes say: "I'll carry them as far as the slip door and no further. Morning, Wren." I saw Wren roll the finished map, tie it with tape and lay it on the high shelf above the stove.
What I did: I said 'Morning, Tobin. Stay inside the doors today. The men from the council are still asking at the market.' Then I take the poles from him at the slip door. Then I push the slip door open on the frost and the white mist over the river, and look back once at the two of them by the stove before I go out to the first crossing.
What happened: Tobin is still with us. I was standing -- standing in the slip doorway with the poles on my shoulder and Tobin Reyes and Wren behind me in the warm. The air carried frost, woodsmoke and the river.
How I came into it: protectiveness, contentment, hopeful.

past.content: The oldest thing I remember is the reed marsh on the West Landing, across the Aune from Saltmere. Da cut reeds and Mam wove them into mats, and our house stood on stilts where the reeds gave way to open water. I was not allowed past the end of the duckboards. I used to sit there with my feet over the edge and watch Petra's ferry, the Heron, cross to the town and back.

The winter I was seven the river froze along the edge of the reed marsh. A girl whose family had come to the marsh that autumn went out on the ice to free a duck frozen in by its feet, and the ice broke under her. I lay flat, pushed a reed pole out to her and pulled until she was up on the thick ice. The girl was Ilse Harrow. Mam sat us both by the stove in one blanket. That is how Ilse and I met.

After the ice Ilse and I were never apart. We set eel traps in the side channels, cut ourselves a reed boat and poled it badly through the marsh until we learned better. When we got lost in the tall reeds we listened for the wheel of the old mill and followed the sound back to the landing. Mam said she could find either of us by looking for the other.

When I was ten I started hanging about the West Landing to watch old Petra work the Heron. She let me coil her mooring lines and paid me in apples. Her voice carried clean across the river and her arms were as thick as the pole. I told Ilse that one day I would have a ferry of my own, and Ilse said she would ride free.

Petra taught me to pole the summer I was eleven. Plant the pole by the bow, lean your weight into it, walk it back along the deck, and pull it free before the river keeps it. The river kept it before the morning was out and I had to swim after it. Petra did not laugh. She said everyone pays the river something once, and better a pole than a person.

Petra made me learn to read the river before she let me near the rudder oar. A smooth slick on the water means a snag underneath. Brown water standing up in ridges is running over a bar. After rain upstream the current sets hard toward the West Landing, so you aim high to land square. She said the Aune tells you everything twice, once on top and once under your feet.

I steered the Heron alone for the first time when I was fifteen. Petra's back was bad that morning, so she sat on a bollard at the East Landing and watched. I took a carter, his cart and two goats over to the West Landing and back again. My hands shook on the rudder oar the whole way, but I landed square both times. Petra only nodded. That was worth more to me than praise.

The flood year I was seventeen. It rained for most of a month and the Aune came up over both landings. The reed marsh went under and our stilt house went with it. Petra and I ran the Heron for three days, carrying marsh folk and their goats up to the chapel of the Drowned Saint on the high ground. Afterwards Mam and Da went west along the toll road to Da's brother's farm. I stayed with the river, and Petra gave me her back room.

The thickest fog I ever crossed in was the autumn I was nineteen. From the stern I could not see the bow. Petra had me take the Heron over by sound alone: the chapel bell behind us on the East Landing, the weir on the mill channel ahead, and the water talking against the hull. We came in a pole's length from the landing. I have trusted my ears on the river ever since.

Ilse married the miller from the old mill the summer we were twenty-one. They were wed in the chapel of the Drowned Saint, and afterwards the whole wedding party crossed back to the West Landing on the Heron with ribbons tied to the rails. Petra took the pole that day so I could stand at the bow beside Ilse. She laughed the whole way over. I had never seen her so happy.

At twenty-two I bought the old boathouse on the East Landing with six years of saved fares. The roof leaked and the slip was half silted, but it was mine and nobody else's. I spent that autumn mending the roof and digging out the slip. It has a berth for the Heron, a net loft reached by a ladder, and a small spare room I have hardly used. I have lived there ever since.

Aldous Toller was made dockmaster the year I turned twenty-six. He had been the tally clerk in the dock office as long as I could remember. Straight away he started writing every crossing in a book, fares and freight both. Petra grumbled that the river had done without a book for a hundred years. I found I did not mind him. He is fair, and his sums are right.

The year I was twenty-eight a carter's horse took fright at a pike jumping and went over the side of the Heron in midstream, cart and all. Petra cut the traces and I went in after the horse's head. Between us we swam it to the West Landing. The cart drifted onto the bar and we got it back the next day. The carter never crossed with us again and told everyone it was our fault.

By the time I was thirty Petra's knees would not take the pole any more. She sat on a stool on the landing and called corrections at me across the water while I did the work. Passengers took her for the pilot and me for the hand, and I let them. She still read the river better from the bank than anyone did on it.

Ilse's husband drowned the spring I was thirty-two. The river was high and he went down to clear weed from the mill wheel and slipped. The mill race took him under the wheel before anyone could reach him. I helped bring him up out of the reeds below the mill. We buried him from the chapel of the Drowned Saint. Ilse did not cry at the grave. She cried that night in the mill kitchen with her head on my shoulder.

After he died Ilse kept the old mill going alone. She learned the stones and the sluice by getting them wrong until she got them right, and the carters came back to her one by one. Every week I brought her loads across on the Heron, and on slow evenings I poled over to sit on the mill step with her and say nothing much. It was the best part of most weeks.

The winter I was thirty-four the Aune froze from bank to bank, which Petra said it had not done in forty years. We hauled the Heron up the slip and people walked across on the ice. I hated every day of it. I kept going down to the landing to look for open water, the way Petra taught me, and I thought about the winter I pulled Ilse out.

Two autumns ago Petra's chest went bad. She coughed through the nights, and by the turn of the year she could not get as far as the landing. I did the crossings alone and sat with her in the evenings and told her what the river had done that day, the bars, the snags, who had crossed. She corrected me even then. She said she would see the spring.

Petra died two winters ago, with ice along the edges of the river. She did not see the spring. She left me the Heron. She had told Aldous Toller so in front of witnesses, and he wrote my name into the dock book under hers and said nothing else, which was kind of him. We buried her from the chapel of the Drowned Saint. The next morning I took the Heron across, because she would have.

The spring after Petra died I painted the Heron's name on her bow myself. Petra had done it every spring for forty years in the same white paint with the same chipped brush. I used her brush. Ilse rowed over from the mill to watch and told me the letters were crooked. They were. I left them.
